discriminating_test: Compare the per-transit G residuals of nearby stars of similar magnitude at the same transits (especially 539.38, 507.23, 864.52), and check those transits' scan angles; alternatively, see whether DR4's denser epoch photometry shows a coherent 0.6% depression over days 507-864 rather than scattered single-transit lows.

evidence.feature: Within-pair inconsistency: 539.38 fov1 0.974 vs 539.45 fov2 1.002 (3.5 sigma apart); 507.23 vs 507.40 differ by 1.7%
Visits at 681 and 702 inside the dip window are at or above the median (1.005, 1.002)
sigma_visit 0.00153 vs G robust_sigma 0.008 and median_flux_err 0.0061: noise model underestimated, depth_g_err too small
Low single transits also occur outside the window (t=0 at 0.982, 321.71, 357.44, 490.40), so the window is not special
BP and RP scatter (9%, 7%) far exceeds their errors; simultaneous BP 1.51 / RP 1.37 spike at 119.93 with normal G suggests a neighbour in the BP/RP window at some scan angles
RP depth -0.067+-0.030 and BP -0.023+-0.051: no usable colour, ratio undefined
G scatter modestly above errors, abbe 0.65; K-dwarf colour (bp_rp 1.38, G-Ks 2.2) with no IR excess
NEOWISE W1/W2 changes consistent with zero within large errors; ztf_after changes of -0.9% (g) and -0.2% (r), below ZTF noise
ruwe 1.03, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, BP/RP excess 1.25 within expectation at this colour and magnitude

explanation: Most likely a noise detection. The 0.6% 'episode' on this faint (G=17.9) K-type star rests on a few low single transits (539.38 at 0.974, 507.23, 864.52) whose partner transit 106.5 min later is normal, which a year-long dimming of the star cannot do. Visits 681 and 702 inside the window sit above the median. sigma_visit (0.0015) is far below the real scatter between visits (robust sigma 0.008 against errors of 0.006, pair differences of 1.5-2.8%), so the formal 7.5-sigma depth is overstated. BP and RP are too noisy to give a colour. ZTF and NEOWISE cannot reach 0.6%. Low-level spot modulation of the star is the main astrophysical alternative.

discriminating_test: Run a box-least-squares search on archival high-cadence photometry (ZTF/ATLAS/Catalina or TESS FFI) for recurring ~20% eclipses with periods under ~1 day. Also check the Gaia transit-level flags and scan angles of the two dimmed epochs, and whether nearby stars dropped on the same transits.

evidence.feature: Episode deficit comes entirely from two single-transit drops of about 18-20% (G 0.818, 0.800); the other visits in the window are near 1.00
Both drops appear at the same moment in G, BP (0.775, 0.799) and RP (0.753, 0.781) with similar depths (grey)
Drops occur in different fields of view (fov 1 and fov 2)
Normal fov-2 transit 4.2 h before the dimmed transit at t=763.7; dimming lasts well under a few hours
BP-RP = -0.2, parallax_snr -0.2 at G=18.3, high galactic latitude: distant hot subdwarf/BHB-like star, not a nearby white dwarf
No WISE/2MASS counterpart; a G=18.3 quasar would be bright in W1, and quasars are rarely this blue
Otherwise quiet light curve (robust sigma 0.014 vs err 0.009), so no large-amplitude pulsation or flicker
Only two outlier transits, 182.5 d (half a year) apart, with 22.9 d 'repeat' period just an 8-cycle alias; the partner transit at t=946 is missing
ruwe 0.96, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, BP/RP excess 1.1: no sign of a resolved neighbour

explanation: The 354-d, 2.9% 'episode' is not a real slow fade. Two single transits, t=763.74 (fov 1) and t=946.22 (fov 2), each about 20% low, produce the whole deficit. The other ten visits in the window average about 1.00. Both drops show in G, BP and RP at once and are close to grey, which rules out a one-band cosmic ray. The source is very blue (BP-RP -0.2), has no measurable parallax at G=18.3 and no WISE detection. That fits a distant hot subdwarf or other hot halo star. A short-period eclipsing binary (sdB+dM-like) caught in eclipse in 2 of 41 brief transits is the most likely cause. A transit-level Gaia artefact (window or attitude flux loss) is the main alternative.

discriminating_test: Run a periodogram on each ZTF season (or a TESS sector): a stable ~1.2-1.3 d period whose amplitude grows as the seasonal median fades confirms a spot cycle; a constant rotational amplitude under the fade would instead point to an occulting dust structure.

evidence.feature: Gaia t=252-254 dense sampling: smooth ~4% peak-to-peak modulation, maxima about 1.25 d apart, fov1/fov2 on one curve
Short-term variation larger in the faint state (t=691: 0.974 to 0.892 in 0.4 d; ZTF bins at 1290-1470 have minima 3-8% below median vs 1-3% when bright)
ZTF g and r show a quasi-cyclic multi-year rise and fall (~7-10%) that continues the Gaia fade; W1 tracks it at ~1-2%
NEOWISE W1 change -0.0135+/-0.007 matches star_temperature (-0.017) better than dust_in_front (-0.0045); grey (-0.064) and hot shells excluded
Ks-W3 about 0, W1-W2 = 0: photosphere only, no inner-disk excess
BP/RP depth ratio 1.68+/-0.31 (z_grey 2.2): chromatic, consistent with cooler spots or dust
ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, BP/RP excess factor normal for its colour, ruwe 1.33 below 1.4
Fade of 6% at G=14.9 is far larger than any residual Gaia calibration drift, and ZTF confirms it independently

explanation: A young, rapidly rotating spotted K/M star (M_G about 7 at BP-RP 1.94, above the main sequence) with a multi-year activity cycle. The dense Gaia run at t=252-254 shows a smooth ~4% modulation with period about 1.25 d, and in the faint state the fast changes are larger (8% within 0.4 d at t=691), so the amplitude grows as the mean fades, which is what more spot coverage does. ZTF shows the same quasi-cycle: faint at 1300-1500, bright at 2050-2700, faint again at 3150-3500, recovering by 4000, with larger scatter when faint. The BP/RP ratio of 1.68 and the NEOWISE W1 dimming (-1.4%, close to the star-temperature prediction) fit cooling. There is no IR excess.

discriminating_test: Run a box-least-squares period search on the 705 ZTF r epochs together with the Gaia dip times. A strict period of a few days that folds all the ~0.6-flux r points and the Gaia dips into one flat-bottomed eclipse window, ideally with a secondary eclipse, would confirm a detached eclipsing binary. If no such period exists, dipper/debris/artefact explanations become more likely.

evidence.feature: ZTF i, r and g at t~2950.9-2951.0 progressively deeper (0.85, 0.63, 0.55) within ~2 h; similar g-partial/r-deep pairs at 2218.9, 2627.8, 3640.0, 3663.99
Faintest ZTF r epochs cluster at a common floor of 0.56-0.66 flux; Gaia G deepest 0.586
Gaia dips are single transits with adjacent transit 106-254 min away normal, occurring in both fov 1 and fov 2; partial ingress points at 506.30 and 606.01 right after normal transits
G, BP and RP all drop at the same transit (e.g. t=35.62: 0.59, 0.43, 0.55)
Visit-mean abbe 1.11, slope_z 0.83: no smooth fade; the 338-d 'episode' is an averaging artefact of single-transit dips
|b| 0-5 deg, G=18.7, bp_rp_excess 1.39, noisy BP: crowded field could mis-assign or truncate transits
Dip duty cycle ~4% in ZTF r with hour-scale events, no long-duration fades

explanation: The detected 338-day 'episode' is not a slow fade. It is visit means pulled down by single-transit drops (t=395, 506, 606, 733; also 35.6) in which G, BP and RP all dim together, in both fields of view, with a normal transit 106-254 min before or after. So each event lasts a few hours and has sharp edges. ZTF shows the same thing on its own: about 14 single-epoch r points that bottom out near flux 0.56-0.66, and sequences within one night that deepen across bands, e.g. t~2950.9 with i 0.85, then r 0.63, then g 0.55 within about 2 hours. Similar g-ingress-then-deep-r pairs appear at 2627.8, 3640.0 and 3663.99. Short, recurring, flat-floored ~40% eclipses point to a detached eclipsing binary with a period of a few days, possibly blended in this crowded plane field.

discriminating_test: Take an identification spectrum, or check archival LAMOST/SDSS/DESI spectra, for Balmer and He emission lines on a white-dwarf continuum. Finding them would confirm a cataclysmic variable and an outburst decline as the cause.

evidence.feature: brightening to ~1.7x in G, BP and RP at t=121-137, then a monotonic decline to the pre-outburst level of ~0.95
M_G ~11.8 and BP-RP 0.28 (white-dwarf region), parallax SNR 22, ruwe 0.94
G-W1 ~2.3, W1-W2 ~0.1: excess consistent with a cool donor star
10-16% G changes within 12 h at t=27, seen in both fields of view, errors ~1%
dip depth 0.136 is the inside mean against an outside median inflated by outburst visits; early and late levels agree
ipd_frac_multi_peak 0 and normal BP/RP excess factor 1.12
BP/RP depth ratio and NEOWISE changes have large errors and do not discriminate

explanation: M_G ~11.8 with BP-RP 0.28 puts this on or near the white-dwarf sequence. G-W1 ~2.3 is a strong infrared excess that fits a late-M or brown-dwarf companion (W1-W2 ~0.1), and G changes by 10-16% within hours. Taken together, this looks like an accreting white dwarf (a cataclysmic variable). Gaia caught a brightening to 1.7x in G, BP and RP at t=121-137, and the flux then relaxed through 1.15 (t=305) and ~1.0 back to ~0.95, about where it started (t=0-27). The detected 'drop' is that return to quiescence after an outburst or high state. It is measured against a median pushed up by the bright visits, so nothing is actually blocking the star. ZTF shows ongoing flickering and a slow fade.

discriminating_test: Run a period search on the ZTF g/r light curve (or the Gaia epoch photometry) and fold it. A strict period with a repeating ~35% flat-bottomed primary and ~7% secondary would confirm a detached eclipsing binary. Dips that do not recur would point back to a dipper.

evidence.feature: Deep dips are isolated single transits that recover to 1.0 within hours, with partial depths at the fov pair (ingress and egress)
Four independent minima all at 0.64-0.67 (consistent, possibly flat-bottomed depth)
Dips present simultaneously in G, BP and RP and in both fov 1 and fov 2
Per-dip BP/RP depth ratio about 1.0-1.5, nearly grey, slightly blue-deep, as for a hotter star being eclipsed
Light curve otherwise flat, no brightening above 1.03, recurring shallow ~7% dips
ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, ruwe 0.98, normal BP/RP excess 1.19
Low galactic latitude, no WISE match, so no infrared constraint on a disk
Slow-change 'episode' built from visit means that mix in-eclipse and out-of-eclipse epochs

explanation: The 283-day 'episode' comes from averaging visits. The flux is really flat near 1.0 (maximum 1.03, no brightenings), interrupted by short, deep single-transit dips. Four epochs (t=226.19, 357.52, 504.59, 508.77) sit at a consistent 0.64-0.67, which suggests a flat-bottomed primary eclipse about 35% deep. The 106.5-min fov partners catch ingress or egress (0.88, 0.925), and the flux is back to 1.0 within 4-6 h, so each eclipse lasts a few hours. About 10% of epochs are in eclipse, which fits a period of order days. G, BP and RP dim together at the same epochs and in both fields of view, nearly grey with BP slightly deeper. Several ~7% dips (around 0.93) look like a secondary eclipse. Together this is a detached eclipsing binary (EA).

discriminating_test: Get an optical spectrum (SDSS/DESI/LAMOST archive, or a cross-match to Milliquas / Gaia DR3 QSO candidates) and check for broad emission lines at a cosmological redshift.

evidence.feature: W1-W2 = 1.1 mag, W2-W3 = 3.6 mag (AGN wedge colours)
G - W1 ~ 2.9 with BP-RP 0.695: large mid-IR excess for an F/G-coloured source
parallax_snr 0.5, ruwe 1.02, |b| 20-25 deg: consistent with zero parallax, not a nearby disk star
ZTF g and r vary aperiodically by ~30-40% over ~2700 d, larger amplitude in g than r (bluer when brighter)
Abbe 0.175 and a rise-then-fade in Gaia G: smooth red-noise variability, no strict recurrence
W1 rises ~500-700 d after the Gaia optical high, and W1 brightens while G fades in the Gaia window
Large outliers in single BP/RP epochs (e.g. RP 4.35 at t=180) with no G counterpart
G change consistent between fov 1 and fov 2 transits

explanation: Most likely a quasar/AGN, with the Gaia fade being ordinary stochastic AGN variability. W1-W2 = 1.1 and W2-W3 = 3.6 are classic AGN mid-IR colours. G-W1 ~ 2.9 is far too red in the IR for a star with BP-RP 0.7. Parallax SNR 0.5 fits zero parallax. The variability is aperiodic red noise: low Abbe ratio, a rise then a fade in Gaia, and ZTF swinging between about 0.82 and 1.2 over years with no recurrence. It is bluer when brighter (ZTF g change 0.198 vs r 0.147), as AGN are. W1 rises roughly 500-700 d after the optical peak, as expected from dust-torus reverberation. BP/RP are too noisy at G=18.6 to constrain colour.

discriminating_test: Check the Gaia epoch photometry of nearby stars with similar G and BP-RP on the same early transits (t=0-54) for the same few-percent, BP-heavy excess. Alternatively, compare the absolute (not median-normalised) ZTF/PS1 magnitudes with the Gaia pre- and post-change levels to find which level is the star's true baseline.

evidence.feature: Only the first 5 epochs (t=0-54, start of mission) are high; the rest are flat, so the 'dip' is an early excess decaying over ~150 d
Excess is larger in BP (~11%) than RP (~5%), as early contamination or calibration residuals would be; ratio 1.65+/-0.65
fov 1 and fov 2 agree at t=0 and t=54; ruwe 0.98, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, normal BP/RP excess
Smooth monotonic decay (abbe 0.13), like the tail of a brightening (e.g. microlensing u~2-3)
Ratio 1.65 matches dust (z_dust -0.07) but is only 1 sigma from grey
No IR excess (Ks-W1, W1-W2 photospheric), and the star is quiet in ZTF 2018-2025
W1 is ~8-10% brighter in the faint phase, against grey/dust/temperature predictions of <=0; real significance is ~2-3 sigma
M_G ~5-6 at 1.9 kpc with moderate extinction: a G/K dwarf, not a giant or B star

explanation: The 'drop' is really a raised level in only the first five Gaia epochs (t=0-54, early in the mission). It sits about 6% high in both fields of view and is larger in BP, then decays smoothly to baseline by t~170 and stays flat to t=923. My leading reading is a residual from early-mission calibration (chromatic contamination), with a decaying brightening a close second: a microlensing tail or a change in stellar activity. A slow dust ingress is also possible. The BP/RP ratio of 1.65+/-0.65 cannot tell grey, dust and cooling apart. There is no IR excess. W1 is apparently brighter during the faint phase, but less significantly than the quoted error suggests; only ~550 K re-emission would fit it. ZTF is normalised per field, so it cannot show whether the level later recovered. My confidence is low.

discriminating_test: Cross-match against Milliquas or the Gaia DR3 QSO candidate table, or get an archival SDSS/DESI/LAMOST spectrum: broad emission lines at a nonzero redshift would confirm an AGN.

evidence.feature: W1-W2 = 1.0 mag and W2-W3 = 3.0 mag (AGN/QSO WISE colour locus)
G - W1 about 4.8 for bp_rp 0.755: mid-IR far too bright for a stellar photosphere
parallax_snr -1.6 at G 18.8 and |b| 40-45 deg: no detectable parallax, consistent with a very distant or extragalactic source
whole G light curve varies smoothly by about +/-20% (abbe 0.22); the detected fade is one trough among several
BP depth 0.27 vs RP depth -0.02: chromatic, larger variation in the blue (bluer when brighter)
NEOWISE W1/W2 change about -2% to -4%, far below the grey prediction of -17%
ruwe 1.01 and ipd_frac_multi_peak 0: point-like, no resolved neighbour
both fields of view track each other in G at the paired epochs

explanation: Most likely a quasar/AGN, and the 'fade' is one low point of its stochastic variability. The source has no measurable parallax (SNR -1.6), lies at |b| 40-45 deg, and at G=18.8 has W1=14.0, so G-W1 is about 4.8, far above a bp_rp=0.755 photosphere. Its WISE colours W1-W2=1.0 and W2-W3=3.0 sit squarely in the AGN locus. The G light curve wanders smoothly between 1.28 and 0.84 over the whole span (abbe 0.22, robust sigma 17%), which looks like red-noise AGN variability, not one discrete event. BP varies more than RP, the usual bluer-when-brighter behaviour, not grey blocking. W1/W2 show no matching drop during the fade, so it is not grey occultation, and the WISE flux is dominated by hot dust that varies on its own timescale.

discriminating_test: Check Gaia epoch photometry, per-CCD G fluxes and scan angles of nearby stars of similar magnitude crossed in the same transits at t = 550.8, 679.3 and 702.6 d. A shared deficit, or a scan-angle or window-edge dependence, would make it instrumental; a deficit confined to this star would favour spots or occultation.

evidence.feature: Only one G epoch below 3 sigma (702.58 d, 0.983); the RP flux at that transit is 1.006 +/- 0.010
Both FOV1 and FOV2 transits are low at 550.8 d and 702.5 d, and the 679 d visit is low too
Outside visits are stable to about 0.16%, near the noise level, over 900 days
MG about 7.5 with bp_rp 1.73: a main-sequence K dwarf, not an evolved star
Ks-W1 = 0.1, W1-W2 about -0.2, W3/W4 only upper limits: no warm dust
A 152-day episode covering three consecutive visits, with normal visits before and after
ruwe 0.98, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, normal BP/RP excess factor
Colour ratio -0.28 +/- 1.7 and no NEOWISE visits inside the dip

explanation: A shallow (0.6-1.7%) dimming across three consecutive Gaia visits on a quiet, photospheric K dwarf (MG about 7.5, no IR excess). Both fields of view are low at 550 d and 702 d, so a field-of-view offset is unlikely. But most of the significance comes from one G transit (702.58 d, -1.7%) whose RP at the same time is normal, and BP/RP are too noisy to pin the colour (ratio -0.28 +/- 1.7). The most likely single cause is spot evolution on a roughly 21 d rotator dimming the star for one season. Transit-level Gaia artefacts (window-edge flux loss, scan-angle contamination, leftover calibration error) are about as likely taken together. A 150-day episode does not look like an eclipse; a disk occultation is still possible.

discriminating_test: Run a box least-squares period search on the ZTF g+r epochs (more than 1800 points). A strict period of order 0.5-2 d that phases every ~0.5-depth dip into a primary (and possibly secondary) eclipse window, with Gaia's dips falling on the same ephemeris, would confirm an eclipsing binary; no coherent period would reopen the alternatives.

evidence.feature: Dips appear in one transit and vanish in the next, 106.5 min apart, in both fov 1 and fov 2 (e.g. 790.65 fov1 1.00 vs 790.72 fov2 0.54; 857.14 fov1 0.55 vs 857.21 fov2 1.01)
Deep dips are matched in G, BP and RP and roughly grey (0.54/0.58/0.54; 0.55/0.59/0.53)
ZTF g and r (about 2 arcsec PSF) show many independent dips down to a repeatable floor of about 0.46-0.50 over 7 years
Consecutive ZTF exposures minutes apart stay at about 0.5 (1352.077-1352.093, 2306.235-2306.240, 2999.768-2999.777), so eclipses have flat or broad bottoms lasting tens of minutes
Out-of-dip light curve is flat: G robust sigma 0.027, no epochs above 3 sigma, no brightenings
ZTF median level after 2020 is unchanged (g -0.7%, r +0.9%), so there is no secular fade
Depth up to about 50% rules out a planet; ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, normal BP/RP excess and ruwe 0.98 point to a single unresolved stellar source
Negative parallax and G=18.3 at |b| 15-20 deg suggest a distant star; no luminosity or energy-budget constraint is possible

explanation: This looks like a detached Algol-type eclipsing binary, and the 'fade' is an artefact of sampling. The star is flat (G max 1.045, nothing above 3 sigma) apart from short, deep dips that switch on and off between transits 106.5 min apart, in both fields of view. The deepest dips are grey: at t=790.72, G 0.54, BP 0.58, RP 0.54. ZTF sees the same kind of dip all through 2018-2025, with a floor near 0.46-0.50 that is held for 10-25 min, plus shallower ingress/egress points; about 9% of ZTF r epochs are low. A floor near 50% fits a central eclipse of two similar stars. The 193-day 'fade' is just a cluster of eclipse hits late in Gaia's sampling. ZTF shows no lasting level change after 2020.

discriminating_test: Check one TESS sector (or the ZTF light curve) for strictly periodic eclipses: an Algol should show primary eclipses ~60% deep, deeper in blue, and ~10% secondaries, deeper in red, at a fixed period of days. No recurrence would revive the occultation and instrumental options.

evidence.feature: Flux changes by 18% within 106.5 min (t=357.87 to 357.95) and by 14% between FOVs at t=544.7; normal at t=169.7 and 383.4
Deep dips deeper in BP than RP (ratio 1.16+-0.10, z_dust=-5.63): consistent with a hot star eclipsed by a cooler one
Shallow dip at t=970.7-970.8 is deeper in RP (~12%) than BP (~6%): secondary eclipse of the cooler star
Dips seen consistently in G, BP and RP and in both fields of view; G=9.4, ipd_frac_multi_peak=0, normal BP/RP excess
W1-W4 flat at ~7.9 mag, photospheric; no warm-dust excess
M_G ~1.5 at BP-RP 0.68 (about 2 mag above the main sequence) and ~4% out-of-eclipse scatter: evolved and/or binary light with ellipsoidal or reflection modulation, typical of Algols
W2 visits low at t=378.9 (0.85+-0.10) and t=1458.8 (0.73+-0.06): eclipse-affected NEOWISE visits seen at other times

explanation: Most likely an Algol-type eclipsing binary that Gaia sampled sparsely. The 163-day 'episode' is really two separate deep visits (t=220.9 and 357.9) with no epochs between them. The flux changes fast: 0.578 to 0.397 within 106 min at t=357.9, and a 14% drop between the two fields of view at t=544.7. That is eclipse ingress, not a slow fade. The deep dips are deeper in BP than RP (ratio 1.16, far from dust at z_dust=-5.6), as expected when a hot star is eclipsed by a cooler companion. At t=970.7-970.8 the shallow dip is deeper in RP than BP, as a secondary eclipse should be. The star sits about 2 mag above the main sequence and shows few-per-cent out-of-eclipse modulation. Its infrared is photospheric.

discriminating_test: A multi-year light curve calibrated across fields (ZTF g/r or ASAS-SN g, 2018 on) would show whether the fade turns around like a cycle (activity or long-period variability) or keeps going. Its colour would also help: reddening at the interstellar-dust slope points to an occulter. A low-resolution spectrum for spectral type and Ca II/H-alpha activity would be the next check.

evidence.feature: Smooth monotonic fade, Abbe 0.248, slope_z -7.1, seen in G, BP and RP independently
Depth order BP 2.7% > G 1.9% > RP 1.1% (ratio 2.49+-0.76, z_grey 1.95)
Ratio consistent with cooling/spots (~1.5) at 1.3 sigma as well as dust (1.7) at 1.0 sigma
No FoV offset in same-day pairs; shared calibration drift already removed
phot_bp_rp_excess_factor 1.32 matches expectation for BP-RP 1.86 (C* ~0); ipd_frac_multi_peak 0; ruwe 1.28
No IR excess indicated: W1-W2 = -0.2, W3/W4 only upper limits
No NEOWISE visits; ZTF normalised per field so long-term trend untestable
Galactic plane, 870 pc, reddened colours; luminosity class ambiguous (A/F dwarf or subgiant)

explanation: The star fades smoothly by about 2% over 965 d (slope_z -7, Abbe 0.25). The fade shows in G, BP and RP separately, with no offset between fields of view. The colour pattern is BP 2.7% > G 1.9% > RP 1.1%, which is what a cooler star or dust in front would give. A blend would deepen both BP and RP relative to G, and grey blocking is disfavoured at about 2 sigma. The packet cannot tell temperature change from dust: the ratio of 2.5±0.8 fits both, and NEOWISE has no visits. The star is reddened (A_V of roughly 2-4) and sits at 870 pc in the plane. It could be an A/F dwarf or a subgiant. The most likely cause is long-term stellar variability (a spot or activity cycle, or slow irregular variability). A slow dust occultation is next.

discriminating_test: Compare absolute magnitudes in g, r and W1, not the median-normalised ones: Pan-STARRS/SDSS from before 2014 against calibrated ZTF and Gaia DR4 epochs from after 2017. This shows whether the grey ~4.5% deficit persisted (long occultation), recovered, or appears in Gaia only (artefact or injection).

evidence.feature: Smooth monotonic fade (abbe 0.05, slope_z -8.4), seen alike in both FoV 1 and FoV 2 and in G, BP and RP
BP/RP depth ratio 1.19+-0.31 (z_grey 0.6, z_dust -1.65)
NEOWISE W1 change in the window against later visits is +0.008+-0.022, against -0.043 predicted for grey dimming
W1 (1.106, 1.041, 1.073) and W2 (about 1.08-1.11) visits before t=330 are brighter than all later visits, as if the IR stepped down with the optical
Sharp 3% drop over about 88 d into a flat plateau; short-term scatter only about 0.3-0.5% (sigma_visit 0.0044; ZTF scatter at the error level)
ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, RUWE 0.98, normal BP/RP excess, high galactic latitude
Parallax SNR 16 at 1.2 kpc; about 700 pc from the plane; photospheric W1-W2 colour
Lasts more than 474 d with a flat bottom on a K dwarf; t ~ 2R/v rules out a stellar companion as the occulter

explanation: This is a quiet K dwarf (M_G about 6.1, RUWE 0.98, no IR excess). Over about 400 d it fades smoothly by 4.5%, with a sharp 3% drop between t=392 and 480, then holds flat for 500 d. Both fields of view and BP, G and RP agree, which rules out most Gaia artefacts. The colour is about grey (BP/RP ratio 1.19+-0.31). Against the later NEOWISE baseline, W1 shows no dip, which favours a temperature change. But W1 and W2 are brighter by about 5% before the fade, which fits a grey step that never recovered. My leading explanation is a long, flat-bottomed occultation by a large-grain disk. Spot or activity change is less likely: it needs a 4.5% dimming with almost no rotational modulation and a fast, step-like drop. I keep real weight on an injected or otherwise unexplained grey step.

discriminating_test: Plot the Gaia G epoch fluxes against scan angle and check Gaia DR3 for a resolved neighbour within ~2 arcsec: if the fainter G visits after t~390 cluster at scan angles that put the companion outside the G window, the drop is a blend effect.

evidence.feature: ipd_frac_multi_peak 72, phot_bp_rp_excess_factor 2.03, ruwe 4.45
G-only outliers near 1.47-1.49 at t~251-252 (both FoVs) and 789, 0.65 at 97.1, with BP/RP near 1 at the same epochs
Dip depth in G only ~1 sigma; BP and RP depths consistent with zero
NEOWISE W1/W2 changes consistent with zero; no infrared excess (W1-W2 ~0.1, W3/W4 upper limits)

explanation: The 'drop' is a ~1.3% G offset after t~390 d, significant at only ~1 sigma (depth_g -0.0133 +/- 0.0135, slope_z -0.97), with RP flat and BP noisy. The source is clearly blended: ipd_frac_multi_peak 72, BP/RP excess 2.03, ruwe 4.45, and G alone jumps to ~1.48 at several epochs (both fields of view at t~252, again at 789) and falls to 0.65 once, while BP/RP stay near 1. That is a close neighbour moving in and out of the narrow G window with scan angle. A small shift in which scan angles get sampled easily makes a ~1% G-only level change. NEOWISE and ZTF show no matching change. The ZTF single-epoch drops look like deblending outliers. Low-level M-dwarf spot activity is a minor alternative.

discriminating_test: Take the ZTF g/r (or ASAS-SN) light curve from 2018 on and run a periodogram. Semi-regular periods of tens of days, with g amplitude greater than r amplitude, would confirm giant pulsation; a stable rotation period would point to spots. A low-resolution spectrum (e.g. LAMOST) giving the luminosity class would separate an AGB/M giant from an active K giant.

No NEOWISE visits and no ZTF/TESS epochs, so the explanation cannot be tested in other bands or other years

explanation: The 'steady trend' is not monotonic. G falls from 1.06 to about 0.96 by day 780, recovers to about 1.00 by days 876-916, drops to 0.927 at day 955, then rises to 1.03 within 7 days. Same-day pairs agree to about 0.5%, but the visit-to-visit scatter is 2.2%, so this is the star's own red-noise variability on timescales of days to years, and the fitted trend is an alias of it. The source is red (BP-RP 2.19), distant (parallax SNR 3.5), at low Galactic latitude, and has W1-W2 = -0.3. That points to a cool giant with no warm-disk excess. The dimming is reddened (BP/RP ratio 1.9 +/- 0.7), which fits a temperature change. Best guess: semi-regular or irregular giant variability, or spot activity on a giant.

discriminating_test: Periodogram of the full ZTF plus ASAS-SN light curve to confirm a ~100 d primary and ~500 d secondary period, plus a Gaia XP or LAMOST spectrum to confirm an M- or C-type AGB giant (TiO or C2 bands).

Long secondary periods are sometimes attributed to a dusty companion cloud occulting the giant

explanation: A luminous, very red (BP-RP 4.0, G-Ks 5.4) dusty giant at 2.9 kpc (W3/W4 excess from mass loss) showing semi-regular variability: ~100 d pulsations of roughly 0.5 mag in ZTF g on top of slow low states lasting 100-200 d. Low states fall near t~200, 630, 1650, 2160, 3240 and 3690, and highs near 484, 997, ~3000 and 3544. That fits a long secondary period of about 500 d, so the detected 579-682 episode is one LSP minimum. BP dims more than RP (ratio 1.48), as expected when a cool star varies in temperature. The two fields of view agree, G, BP and RP move together, and ZTF independently shows the same behaviour, so an artefact is unlikely. The fades are too shallow for R CrB.

discriminating_test: Pull the per-transit scan angles and the Gaia epoch photometry of nearby stars of similar magnitude for the 753-814 d transits. If neighbours dim together or the dip tracks scan angle, it is instrumental; if not, search ZTF 2018+ and any TESS sectors for a recurrence of a similar slow, grey episode.

evidence.feature: Dimming coherent across visit groups at 753, 798 and 814 d, deepening to ~2.7% then back to normal by 863 d
Dip present in both fov 1 and fov 2 transits within the same groups
At 798 and 814 d, BP and RP dim by about the same amount as G (roughly grey; ratio 0.27 +/- 0.9, z_grey -0.8, z_dust -1.6)
Duration >= 61 d (up to ~140 d) needs a transverse speed of ~0.3 km/s for a compact body crossing a ~1 Rsun star
phot_bp_rp_excess_factor 1.21, about what this colour predicts; ruwe 1.06; ipd_frac_multi_peak 1
Ks-W1 = 0, W1-W2 ~ -0.1: no near/mid-IR excess
Star otherwise quiet (sigma_visit 0.0024, no other comparable dips)
At 753 d G is down 1% while BP and RP in the same transit are up ~1% (about 3 sigma inconsistent in combination)
Isolated BP 1.71 / RP 2.15 spike at 108.98 d with no G: something entered the BP/RP windows once
Weak s_rep at 484 d (possible earlier event near 321 d rests on one noisy point)

explanation: Most likely a slow, shallow, roughly grey occultation of a quiet, reddened F-type dwarf by extended dust (a circumstellar or circumsecondary disk, or a debris cloud). The dip deepens across three visit groups (about 1% at t=753, 1.4% at 798, 2.7% at 814) and is gone by 863. It shows in both fields of view and in G, BP and RP alike, which argues against single-epoch defects and FoV offsets. The clean excess factor, ruwe 1.06 and low ipd_frac_multi_peak argue against a blend. Crossing a 1-1.5 Rsun star in at least 61 d takes about 0.3 km/s, far too slow for a compact eclipser. No IR excess, so not a YSO disk. The colour ratio is poorly constrained.

discriminating_test: Run forced photometry on unWISE time-resolved W1/W2 coadds, which go deeper than NEOWISE single exposures. This checks whether the 2015 IR step is real and centred on the star, not a blended neighbour or a faint-source detection bias. Also compare the absolute calibrated optical level after 2017 (e.g. Pan-STARRS or ZTF zero-pointed photometry) with the pre-step Gaia level, to test whether the dimming persists along with the IR excess.

NEOWISE W1 (0.74 to 1.0) and W2 (0.63 to ~1.05) step up between t=321 and t=494, at the same time as the G drop and persisting for ~9 yr; sizes close to the 1000 K shell predictions (+0.38, +0.82)

ruwe 1.02, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, normal BP/RP excess factor
Abs G ~6.8, bp_rp 1.51, |b| 50-55 deg at 1.5 kpc: an old quiet K dwarf far from star-forming regions

explanation: Gaia G drops about 4% in a step near t~350 d, then fades slowly to the end of the Gaia data (smooth, abbe 0.09, no field-of-view offset). BP fades more than RP, but the errors are too large to say much. NEOWISE W1 and W2 both jump up by about 35% and 65% between t=321 and t=494 and stay high until t~3600. That matches the pipeline's prediction for a 1000 K dust shell absorbing the G deficit (W1 +0.38, W2 +0.82). The neowise_change test misses this because most of its 'outside' visits come after the step. Leading picture: new warm dust, for example collisional debris, around a quiet K dwarf with photospheric 2010 colours. Alternatives: an activity cycle or a Gaia drift, with an unrelated NEOWISE step at faint W1/W2.

discriminating_test: Measure the star's rotation period and activity, for example a ZTF/TESS periodogram or a Ca II H&K or RVS activity index. Also check whether Gaia neighbours of similar G and colour on the same scans show the same residual slope. An active star with Prot of days to weeks favours an activity-cycle fade; a quiet star whose neighbours share the slope points to calibration.

evidence.feature: Only a 0.67% fade over 923 d, slope_z 4.09 from 18 visits; trend driven partly by a high first epoch (1.006) and one low epoch (0.991 at t=733)
ZTF g fades after 2020 (change -0.55%, slope -0.27%/yr, same as the Gaia G slope) while ZTF r is nearly flat (-0.09%, -0.06%/yr)
ZTF g season medians wander by 2-4% (e.g. fade over t~2900-3080, smaller in r), suggesting low-level intrinsic blue variability
Ks-W1 = 0.1, W1-W2 = -0.1, W3/W4 only upper limits: no warm dust
ruwe 1.03, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, bp_rp_excess 1.25 only mildly elevated

explanation: The detected 'dip' is a tiny linear fade: about 0.5-0.7% in G over 923 d (slope_z 4.1 from only 18 visits, Abbe 0.51). The star looks like a reddened solar-type dwarf (G=15.7 at 990 pc, bp_rp 1.33, low |b|). It shows no IR excess, ruwe is 1.03 and there are no multi-peak flags. BP and RP are too noisy to give the colour. The most likely cause is slow intrinsic change of an active star, such as a spot or facula activity cycle. ZTF g keeps fading after 2020 (-0.55%, -0.27%/yr) and wanders by a few per cent from season to season, while r stays nearly flat. That fits activity that is stronger in the blue and does not fit a grey occulter. A Gaia calibration residual at the mmag level, or noise in an extreme-tail search, is a close second.

discriminating_test: Query Gaia for neighbours within ~4 arcsec and plot per-transit G flux against scan angle; a neighbour at the scan angles of the bright and faint transits confirms the blend. ZTF PSF photometry at ~2 arcsec would also show whether the star itself varies.

explanation: A faint (G=18.6) source in the Galactic plane with a very high BP/RP excess factor (2.66) and 8% multi-peak transits, so neighbours very likely contaminate the windows. The G light curve holds single-transit jumps to +78%, +70% and +50%, and paired FoV transits 106.5 min apart differ by 10-40% (1.27 vs 1.70, 1.16 vs 0.96, 0.99 vs 0.88). No star does that; a neighbour entering the window at some scan angles does. The 'drop' is a 4.8% (2.7 sigma) deficit made of two low single transits (0.875 at fov2, 0.880 at the last epoch) against an early baseline inflated by those bright epochs. Abbe 0.91 and slope_z -1.7 mean noise, the BP/RP depths are unconstrained, and the 24.2 d repeat from 14 visits is not credible.

If the comparison stars dim too, or the low points sit at a particular scan angle or window edge, it is instrumental. Fold the dense ZTF r data near 40 d to test for spot modulation.

Weighting the nine epochs by their quoted errors gives a deficit of only about 0.38% +/- 0.16%, roughly 2.4 sigma. Two single-transit low points (394.24 fov2, which has no BP/RP, and 405.67 fov1) carry much of it. Within visits the flux swings by up to 2.8% in hours, which a smooth 48-day dimming would not do. The pipeline's sigma_visit (0.05%) is far below the real per-visit noise (~0.2-0.3%), which inflated s_fade and s_rep. Earlier visits scatter by about +/-0.6% too (32.9 d is as low as the dip). The colours are uninformative, there is no IR excess and ZTF shows no change. A mildly spotted K star is the main astrophysical alternative.

discriminating_test: Take an optical spectrum (or check archival SDSS/LAMOST/DESI spectroscopy and quasar catalogues) for broad emission lines and a redshift; confirming a quasar settles the class.

evidence.feature: W1-W2 = 1.0 mag, W2-W3 = 3.7 mag, W3/W4 hugely in excess of a G=19.6 photosphere
parallax_snr -1.3 at G=19.6, distance poorly constrained
bp_rp 0.82, too blue for a typical reddened YSO but typical of quasars

explanation: Most likely a quasar/AGN with ordinary stochastic optical variability. WISE colours W1-W2 = 1.0 and W2-W3 = 3.7 fall in the AGN region, and the mid-IR is far too bright for a G = 19.6 photosphere. Parallax is not significant (snr -1.3), ruwe is 1.1 and bp_rp = 0.82 fits a quasar. The 'fade' is one segment of smooth red-noise variability across the whole light curve: low at t=0 (~0.83), up to ~1.10 at t~430, then down to 0.80 at t=1023 (abbe 0.30). ZTF shows the same wandering, with brightenings and fadings of tens of per cent over months. BP fading more than RP fits a source that is bluer when brighter. The 79 d 'repeat' is probably spurious, given only 23 visits of red noise.

discriminating_test: Fit per-field ZTF g, r and i slopes over 2018-2025, and compare with Pan-STARRS 2010-2014 epochs, to pin down how the fade depends on wavelength and when it began. Spots or dust predict g/r of about 1.4 and a grey occulter predicts about 1. A Ca II H&K spectrum would then test the activity-cycle explanation.

evidence.feature: Gaia G linear decline -0.88%/yr, slope_z -8.1, abbe 0.19, both FoVs agree, shared drift removed
Independent ZTF g and r continue fading ~1.2%/yr within fields 2018-2025
ZTF g change -3.0% vs r -4.0% (ratio ~0.8), grey not dust- or spot-like

M_G ~5-6 at 1600 pc, a dwarf, not an evolved giant

explanation: A real, slow, near-grey fade of about 1%/yr lasting at least a decade. Gaia G declines smoothly (slope_z -8.1, abbe 0.19, drift-corrected, seen in both fields of view). ZTF g and r keep fading within their own fields from 2018 to 2025 (about 6-8%), with g/r near 0.8-1, where dust or spots would predict about 1.4. NEOWISE W1 hints at a similar ~10% drop. The star looks like a quiet reddened G/K dwarf (sigma_visit 0.4%) with no sign of a blend (ruwe 0.98, multi_peak 0, normal BP/RP excess). An activity cycle is the commonest natural cause of trends like this, but it predicts bluer, smaller changes and more rotational scatter. A slow disk ingress is possible. No listed cause fits well.

discriminating_test: Run a BLS/phase-dispersion period search over ~0.2-5 d on the combined dense ZTF r and Gaia G epochs (or check a ZTF periodic-variable catalogue): one strict period phasing all deep dips into primary and secondary eclipses would confirm the eclipsing binary.

evidence.feature: Repeated single-transit G dips of 13-29%, gone by the paired FoV transit 1.8-4.2 h later
Non-dip G visits inside 224-652 d average ~1.00; the 3.7% episode comes from averaging in eclipse points
ZTF r/g/i independently show frequent dips to 0.62-0.74 at ~5% of epochs; ZTF r 1484.87 drops to 0.705 within 12 min after a normal dense run
Dips appear in both fov 1 and fov 2 and simultaneously in BP and RP
Depth ~30-40% on a K/M dwarf requires a stellar-size occulter

explanation: Most likely a detached eclipsing binary with a period of a few hours to ~2 days. Out of eclipse the star is flat. The 428 d '3.7% episode' is not a real slow fade: the visits inside it that are not dips sit at ~1.00, so the episode is made of single-transit dips (0.71-0.87 at t=224, 430, 493, 646, 652; others at 54 and 110). Each dip is gone by the paired transit 1.8-4.2 h later. Dips are seen in both fields of view and in BP and RP at the same epochs. Independent ZTF r/g/i data show ~5% of epochs dipping to 0.62-0.74, with a sharp ingress after a dense normal run. The ~30% depth is too deep for a planet. No IR excess.

discriminating_test: Run a period search on archival ZTF or TESS photometry of the star. Eclipses a few hours long and about 30% deep that recur at a fixed period of a few days would confirm a detached eclipsing binary. If the ZTF data are flat and dense, a Gaia transit-level artefact becomes the leading explanation.

evidence.feature: Four short dips of 22-31% in G, each one transit long, with normal flux a few hours before or after
Dip at t=485 fades from 0.69 (FoV1) to 0.94 (FoV2) to 1.00 within 6 h, an egress seen in independent transits
G, BP and RP dim together by similar amounts in each dip (nearly grey)
The 53.6 d repeat and the 53 d episode are just the gap between two separate short dips, made by visit averaging
All four deepest epochs are FoV1, three of them unpaired FoV1 transits
No near- or mid-IR excess (Ks 15.1, W1 15.4, W3/W4 upper limits)
ruwe 1.05, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, BP/RP excess only mildly high at |b| 5-10 deg

explanation: The 53-d 'episode' comes from averaging visits. Underneath are four separate single-transit dips of 22-31% (t=485, 646, 699, 862). Each dip has normal transits 4-6 h on either side. All three bands dim together and about equally (per-epoch BP/RP depth ratio ~0.7-1.3, about 1 on average), which fits stellar eclipses. At t=485 the dip is 31% in FoV1 and only 6% in FoV2 106.5 min later, a gradual egress seen in two independent transits. That argues against a one-transit artefact. Eclipses lasting a few hours that catch ~8% of epochs suggest a detached binary with a period of days. There is no IR excess (Ks-W1 is about 0), so a dipper is unlikely. ruwe 1.05 and ipd 0 argue against a blend.

discriminating_test: Check Gaia epoch photometry of nearby stars of similar magnitude and colour for the same step between 238 and 318 d, and check later ZTF/ASAS-SN or Gaia DR4 photometry for continued chromatic dimming or an egress.

evidence.feature: Gradual ~80 d fade followed by continued slow decline, both FoVs equal
BP/RP depth ratio 3.42 +/- 0.80 (z_grey 3.0, z_dust 2.15); G depth consistent with BP/RP weighting
Ratio well above ~1.2-1.5 expected for spots or cooling on an F/G star
No IR excess (Ks, W1, W2 photospheric; W3/W4 upper limits); NEOWISE excludes 1000 K shell
NEOWISE W2 change +8 +/- 5%, matching the 300 K shell prediction of +6% (weak)
Single long drop with no egress across the 993 d span; step-like event could be a star-specific calibration discontinuity
ruwe 1.0, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, modest BP/RP excess factor; BP-only scatter dips at 772-786 and 934 d not seen in G
Inferred M_G ~3.5-4.5: a dwarf, not an evolved or Be star

explanation: G sits flat near 1.025 for 240 d, fades over roughly 80 d (238 -> 298 -> 318 d), then keeps sinking slowly to about 0.996 through the end of the data, with no egress seen. Both fields of view agree, so this is not an FoV offset, and the gradual ingress argues against a sharp calibration step. The fade is strongly chromatic: BP 4.7%, RP 1.4%, and G 2.75%, which matches a BP/RP-weighted mean. That rules out grey occultation at 3 sigma and points to small-grain dust, steeper than interstellar dust, or less likely spots or cooling, which give a ratio near 1.5. The star looks like a reddened F/G dwarf with no IR excess. NEOWISE rules out a 1000 K shell. My leading explanation is ingress into a long dust occultation by a disk or cloud. A star-specific calibration or processing step remains possible.

discriminating_test: Get independent archival optical photometry from 2010 to 2026 (Pan-STARRS, ATLAS, ASAS-SN, current CCD photometry). A real grey ramp should continue, reaching about 0.5 of the 2016 flux by 2026, or show where it starts and whether it curves. If the fade is missing from raw independent data, it is an artefact or injection.

evidence.feature: BP/RP depth ratio 0.971+-0.090 (z_grey -0.3, z_dust -8.1)
W1 and W2 fade at the same fractional rate as G (G 1.123 to 1.0 and W1 1.117 to 1.0 between t=0 and t=913); grey out to 4.6 micron, so not small-grain dust in front and not cooling
Strictly linear decline in flux over 10 years with no deceleration (WISE slope ~-1.4e-4/d before and after Gaia), abbe 0.021
Same trend in both fields of view and in G, BP, RP and WISE; calibration drift removed; ruwe 0.95, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0
Linear fade at constant colour: an opaque edge would need ~0.003 km/s to cover half the star in a decade, so only a gradual grey optical-depth gradient works
Ks-W1 = 0.0 and G-Ks ~1.7 in 1999-2010 catalogue photometry look like a normal photosphere: the fade did not extend back linearly, so it began after ~2010
No IR excess (W1-W2 ~ -0.1, W3/W4 upper limits); dwarf luminosity

explanation: A quiet F/G dwarf (M_G~4, no IR excess) fades almost perfectly linearly in flux at ~4.6%/yr: G, BP and RP drop alike (BP/RP depth ratio 0.97+-0.09, dust excluded at 8 sigma, cooling excluded), and NEOWISE W1 and W2 drop at the same fractional rate over 10 years (~1.16 to 0.66), with no curvature and abbe 0.02. Agreement between two independent instruments and both Gaia fields of view rules out most artefacts. Small-grain dust and temperature change are excluded; an opaque edge cannot cross the star that slowly. The only natural option is a smooth optical-depth gradient of very large grains, as in a circumsecondary disk. That is contrived, so 'no listed explanation fits' (or an injected ramp) is somewhat more likely.

discriminating_test: Run a period search on the Gaia dip epochs together with ZTF or a TESS sector. Recurring eclipses at a fixed period of about 2.07 d or 4.15 d, with stable primary and secondary depths, would confirm the eclipsing binary.

evidence.feature: Dips appear simultaneously in G, BP and RP (separate windows) with matching depths, e.g. 0.729/0.715/0.739 at t=433.29 and 0.774/0.769/0.783 at t=593.99
BP/RP depth ratio 0.98 +/- 0.43, grey
Dips occur in both fov 1 and fov 2 at different scan epochs
Dips last < ~0.25 d (normal transits 0.07-0.18 d either side) and recur in ~10% of epochs over 900 d
Visit-averaged deficit of 2.78% over 12 visits matches the sum of the individual eclipse epochs; out-of-dip flux flat
Maximum depth 27% on an F-type star (bp_rp 0.77, M_G ~3)
ruwe 0.97, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, BP/RP excess 1.2 normal
Ks, W1, W2 equal; no clear infrared excess; NEOWISE W1 change consistent with grey
Dip depths vary from 4% to 27%, irregular at first sight

explanation: The 469-day 'episode' is not a slow fade: out-of-dip G stays at about 1.000. The 2.8% visit-mean deficit comes entirely from single-transit dips (4-27%) at 433.2/433.3, 591.9, 594.0 and 678.9, with more at 49.0, 370.4 and 902.5. Each dip shows in G, BP and RP at nearly the same depth (grey), in both fields of view, and lasts under about 0.25 d, with normal transits 0.07-0.18 d on either side. Roughly 10% of epochs are in a dip, and two dips 2.07 d apart have normal coverage between them. This fits a detached eclipsing binary with a period of a few days around an F-type star (M_G about 3), sampled sparsely. Depths are too large for a planet. The star is quiet otherwise.

discriminating_test: Check the scan angles and Gaia DR3 neighbours within about 4 arcsec for the two dipped transits against the normal ones. A neighbour aligned with the scan direction only at t=402 and t=568 would make this a blend or mismatch. Both dips are 8-14 sigma in G and about 3 sigma each in RP at the same transits, in different fields of view

Colour not dust-like (BP is not dimmed more than RP)
Faint source (G=18.7) at |b| 5-10 deg, a moderately crowded field; BP/RP excess factor 1.19 is normal, ruwe 1.09 and ipd_frac_multi_peak 0 show no resolved neighbour

explanation: The 196-day 'episode' is a gap in the sampling. It really consists of two isolated single Gaia transits (t=402, fov2, G -8%; t=568, fov1, G -14%), with the transits at 375 and 598 normal. The other 15 epochs are quiet at about 1%. RP dims about 12% at both transits, so it is a whole-transit effect, not a defect confined to one CCD. Two short dips out of 17 sparse epochs fit a detached eclipsing binary with a duty cycle of about 10%. ZTF r is too noisy (7%) to confirm, though it has a few clusters of low points. The main tension is that BP does not dim (-6 +/- 4%, z_grey -4). That points towards a faint-source instrumental cause instead, such as a mismatched or blended transit of a bluer, fainter neighbour, or heavy-tailed BP errors at G=18.7.

discriminating_test: Check the ZTF r/i PSF light curve of the source for a matching multi-year fade (and for red-giant variability), and test whether the Gaia G residuals correlate with scan angle or with neighbours within ~3 arcsec. A real fade in ZTF i would favour a pulsating giant; a flat ZTF light curve plus a scan-angle correlation would confirm a crowding artefact.

The 'dip' is an ~8% G fade over 965 d (slope_z -4.2), mostly driven by bright early epochs (t=0, t=192). For a star this red, most of the G flux falls in the RP passband, so a real change on the star (pulsation, dust, cooling) should show in RP. RP is flat instead (-0.007±0.016, about 3.5 sigma from G). G also scatters 2-3.5% between paired transits 106 min apart, well beyond its formal errors, and the excess factor is raised: signs of crowding or calibration noise. My leading cause is instrumental (crowding or calibration of an extreme colour), followed by low-amplitude red-giant variability.

discriminating_test: Check ZTF g/r photometry (or the recurrence test) for a strict period that puts the dips at t=34.17, 575.5 and 876.79 into one or two eclipse phase windows of fixed depth.

BP depth ratio uninformative (ratio_err 2.41); no NEOWISE or ZTF epochs inside the dip

explanation: A very red (BP-RP 5.84, G-Ks 7.5), distant source in the Galactic plane with W3/W4 excess: most likely a dust-enshrouded, reddened AGB/semi-regular giant. The whole G and RP light curve varies smoothly (abbe 0.40) by about 0.4 mag: minimum near day 219, maximum near day 593, minimum near day 781, with a quasi-period of about 550 d (rep_period 547 d). The detected 'dip' at days 770-872 is simply the deepest minimum of this cycle. It is not an isolated event, since the star also rises well above the median. FOV1 and FOV2 agree at every paired epoch, and G and RP track each other. BP is too noisy to constrain colour.

discriminating_test: Run a period search on archival ZTF or Catalina photometry of the source. A strict ephemeris in which ~45-50% deep, ~1 d long eclipses recur at fixed depth would confirm the eclipsing binary. Dips that recur at no period would shift weight to debris transits or unexplained.

evidence.feature: Flat out-of-dip level (most visits 0.96-1.05) with isolated deep dips to 0.53; n_above_3sigma = 0
Dips present in BP and RP at depths similar to G (e.g. t=592: G 0.533, BP 0.505, RP 0.544; t=41: 0.553/0.558/0.570)
Flux changes of 6-7% between the paired FoV transits 106.5 min apart during dips, in both directions (ingress/egress-like)
Normal visits at t=475, 513 and 570 inside the 384-592 'episode'; deep dips also at t=0 and 41 outside it
ruwe 1.02, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, high galactic latitude
G-W1 about 0.7 (photospheric), W1-W2 upper limit not AGN-like, bp_rp_excess 1.13 point-like
Repeat search period 42.8 d with s_rep 10.5; dips at 41 and 384 are about 8 x 42.8 d apart (likely an alias of a shorter orbital period)
High galactic latitude, null parallax, no IR excess

explanation: Algol-type (detached or semi-detached) eclipsing binary. The light curve sits flat near 1.0 and has isolated deep dips (0.53-0.72 at t=0, 41, 384 and 592, plus shallower ones at 530 and 763-795). The 209 d 'episode' is a pipeline grouping of separate eclipses, since visits at 475, 513 and 570 inside it are normal. Each dip shows in G, BP and RP at roughly equal depth (grey) and in both fields of view, and its flux changes by 6-7% within 106 min. That fits eclipse ingress or egress on a timescale of about a day, and it rules out cosmic rays, window-edge losses and slow dust. No epoch is bright, which excludes RR Lyrae. The IR colour (G-W1 about 0.7) and the point-like source rule out an AGN. Given the high latitude and null parallax, it is probably a distant halo A/F binary.

discriminating_test: Pull this source's OGLE-IV or VVV light curve (crowded-field ground photometry spanning the Gaia years): ongoing semi-regular or long-period variability of a few per cent there would confirm red-giant variability. If that photometry shows the star flat, the Gaia trend comes from blending or calibration.

evidence.feature: Very red colour (BP-RP 2.83, G-Ks 4.8), negative parallax, low galactic latitude: distant reddened giant
G trend is noisy rather than smooth (abbe 0.59) with intra-visit scatter of 3-4% against ~0.7% errors
BP and RP vary by factors of up to 3 between transits with no link to G (e.g. t=767.97: G 0.96, BP 3.25, RP 1.43)
phot_bp_rp_excess_factor 1.68, ipd_frac_multi_peak 4, ruwe 1.32 in a Galactic-plane field
Colour depths unconstrained (BP 0.36+-0.35, RP -0.06+-0.10); no WISE or NEOWISE data
Early epochs bright (1.09-1.12) then a slow decline, toward the bulge: could be a microlensing tail, but the shape is not clean
Only 18 visits and no recurrence or single-event structure; the decline is gradual, not an eclipse

explanation: A faint (G=17.9), very red (BP-RP 2.83, G-Ks 4.8), negative-parallax source at |b|<5 deg is most likely a distant, reddened red giant in a crowded field. The detected 'dip' is a modest G trend (-2.9%/yr, slope_z -4.4, abbe 0.59, 18 visits) over 967 d, with ~3-4% scatter within visits, well above the errors. That fits the low-amplitude semi-regular or long-secondary-period variability typical of such giants. BP and RP scatter wildly (BP 0.3-3.2) and do not track G. Together with the high BP/RP excess (1.68), ipd_frac_multi_peak and ruwe 1.32, this points to neighbours contaminating the windows, which could also bias G. The colour depths say nothing about the cause.

discriminating_test: Pull independent optical photometry from Gaia's window (ATLAS or Pan-STARRS 2015-2017). Also compare reprocessed Gaia DR4 epoch G with synthetic G from the epoch BP/RP. If the 10% fade is absent from both, it is a G-only processing artefact or a non-physical signal. If it is present, the BP/RP photometry is the faulty part.

evidence.feature: G depth 0.099+/-0.0013 while BP depth -0.0009+/-0.0059 and RP depth -0.003+/-0.004; BP+RP span the G passband
Achromatic or chromatic change of the star would appear in BP/RP at >15 sigma; it does not
Step identical in fov 1 and fov 2 and across many scan-law groups before and after
ruwe 0.974, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, bp_rp_excess 1.22 normal for bp_rp 1.04
Smooth sigmoid-like decline then 30-epoch plateau (abbe 0.036), not single-epoch
NEOWISE W1 change -0.007+/-0.012 vs grey prediction -0.099
Single high W1 visit at t=1 (1.059+/-0.011) coinciding with G bright phase, unmatched by BP/RP
Long permanent 10% fade over hundreds of days is not periodic spot or pulsation behaviour, and BP/RP show no variability

explanation: The only change is in G: a smooth ~10% decline between days ~150 and ~375, then a flat plateau to day 923, the same in both fields of view. BP and RP together cover the whole G passband, and both stay flat to <1% (depths -0.1+/-0.6% and -0.3+/-0.4%). So no change in the starlight can produce the G drop: not an occulter, dust, a temperature change or intrinsic variability. NEOWISE W1 also fails the grey prediction. The source looks clean (ruwe 0.97, no multi-peak, normal BP/RP excess), so a blend is unlikely. What remains is either a G-only processing or calibration fault, with no known Gaia mechanism at G=15.5 for an isolated star, or a signal that no listed process makes. I split the weight between these.

discriminating_test: Compare this star's per-transit G residuals with those of stars of similar magnitude and colour crossed on the same Gaia scans and CCD rows, and plot them against scan angle and AC position. Alternatively, check whether recalibrated Gaia DR4 epoch photometry reproduces the G-only fade: if it vanishes or is shared, it is instrumental; if BP/RP then show it, the star really changed.

evidence.feature: Achromatic or reddening occultation would dim RP by ~0.9% (or ~0.7% if the star cools); RP flat
Late low level present in both fov 1 and fov 2 (853, 876, 948 pairs)
Dense transit clusters offset as groups (t~105-112 at ~1.008, t~398-409 at ~1.004, t~948-953 at ~0.991), i.e. level tied to particular scan sequences
phot_bp_rp_excess_factor 1.21 is normal for BP-RP 0.95; ipd_frac_multi_peak 0; ruwe 1.05
No IR excess (Ks-W1 0.1, W1-W2 0.0, W3/W4 upper limits); NEOWISE change uninformative (W1 +0.0075+/-0.018)
ZTF after 2020 vs 2018-19: r -0.08%, g -0.34%, i -0.24%, no continuation of a -0.6%/yr fade
Slow non-monotonic ~0.5% G wander over hundreds of days (abbe 0.21) in an old subgiant could be an activity cycle
Repeated deep (~16%) single-night ZTF r-only outliers near 2388, 2607, 2975, 3343 spaced ~368 d are seasonal ZTF artefacts, unrelated to the Gaia fade

explanation: The 0.9% G fade belongs to a slow, uneven G-only trend (-0.6%/yr). Over the same dates RP changes by -0.24+/-0.29% and BP by -0.05+/-0.68%. G flux is essentially BP plus RP, so any real dimming or cooling of this G-type subgiant (M_G ~3.6, BP-RP 0.95, high latitude) would dim RP by ~0.7-0.9%, which is ruled out at 3-4 sigma. Both fields of view share the low level. The normal BP/RP excess, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0 and ruwe 1.05 point to an isolated source. There is no IR excess, and ZTF r shows no further fade after 2020. Most likely this is a residual in the G calibration or processing for this source's transits. A weak activity cycle stays possible.

discriminating_test: Get a long ASAS-SN/ATLAS light curve over 2014-2024 and check the 2019 ZTF deep-dip science images and flags. A recurring cycle of a few per cent with no simultaneous dips confirms a spot cycle and artefacts. Real, grey, simultaneous deep dips would move weight to disk or debris occultation.

evidence.feature: G scatter 4x errors and 2.5% rise in G and RP over ~2 days at t 775-779
Smooth fade (abbe 0.29, slope_z -4.3) followed by ZTF brightening of +2.7 to +3.7% after 2020: fade and recovery over years
Dwarf luminosity (parallax SNR 32, M_Ks ~4.2), so not an evolved pulsator
No IR excess: Ks-W1 0.2, W1-W2 0.0, no inner warm dust
NEOWISE W1 slope -0.0173±0.0041/yr matches grey (-0.0108), not a temperature change (-0.0028)
Deep (0.50-0.77) ZTF points in r and g on four nights in 2019, paired exposures agreeing; none in 2018 or 2022-24
BP/RP scatter (0.037/0.022) well above errors and above G scatter; low-latitude field
Colour ratio BP/RP 0.89±0.70: uninformative
Only 17 visits with fast intrinsic variability; the trend can be inflated by rotation-phase sampling

explanation: A K7-M0 dwarf (M_Ks about 4.2 at 520 pc, IR photospheric, W1-W2 = 0) whose G light curve varies far more than its errors (robust sigma 0.012 against 0.003) and rises 2.5% in about 2 days at t~776-779, which looks like a spotted active star. The 2.6% fade over the Gaia span is smooth (abbe 0.29), within errors in BP/RP, and ZTF shows the star still faint in 2018-19 and about 3% brighter from 2022 on: a fade and recovery over years, the kind of change an activity/spot cycle makes. Tensions: W1 fades about as much as G (-1.7±0.4%/yr), more than a cooling star predicts (-0.3%), and deep (23-50%) one-night ZTF dips cluster in 2019. They point to grey blocking or artefacts, so some weight goes to occultation and systematics.

discriminating_test: Run a periodogram on the dense ZTF r season (t about 1737-1810, about 350 epochs) or on a TESS full-frame light curve, looking for a spot-rotation period of 5-25 d whose amplitude changes; a single spectrum showing Ca II H&K or H-alpha emission would confirm an active star.

evidence.feature: Flux returns to 1.000 at t=574 and 617 inside the episode; changes of 1-1.7% within 10-26 days
Variability outside the episode too (pre-dip level about 1.008, rising to 1.014 at t=928); robust_sigma 0.0098 against errors of 0.0016; abbe 0.31
ZTF g and r season medians vary 1-2% with g amplitude larger than r; ZTF robust sigma above its errors
Late part of the episode (t=674-759): BP down about 2.5%, G about 1.7%, RP about 1.2%, so redder when fainter
Dip seen in both fields of view with no offset between them
Many consecutive dip visits at similar depth over 380 d, which no eclipse duty cycle allows
Ks-W1 = 0.1, W1-W2 = 0, only upper limits in W3 and W4; NEOWISE change consistent with zero and the 1000 K shell excluded; 390 pc from the plane
ruwe 0.97, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, normal BP/RP excess factor
Fitted G depth (0.0127) larger than both BP (0.008) and RP (0.0072), about 2 sigma against RP

explanation: This looks like a low phase in the ongoing low-amplitude variability of a G-type dwarf (M_G about 4.2 after modest extinction), most likely from evolving spots or magnetic activity. The 1.3% 'episode' is not one coherent dip. The flux returns to 1.000 at t=574 and 617, drops by 1% within 10 days, and recovers by 1.7% within 26 days. Outside the episode the G flux also wanders: about 1.008 early, 1.000 at t=300 to 850, then 1.014 at t=928. ZTF g and r show the same 1-2% changes from season to season, with a larger amplitude in g. In the late part of the episode the dip is deeper in BP than in RP. There is no IR excess, the astrometry is clean, and NEOWISE shows no change.

discriminating_test: Run a periodogram on the dense ZTF r and g seasons (e.g. t~1460-1600 and 1800-1900), or on TESS: a stable 3-7 d period whose amplitude and mean level change together would confirm spots. A single low-resolution spectrum would also do it, by showing a late-type photosphere with chromospheric emission rather than a Be star.

evidence.feature: Smooth 17% G fade (abbe 0.121, slope_z -8.95) seen in both fov 1 and 2 and in BP and RP
BP/RP depth ratio 1.39+-0.35, close to the ~1.4 expected for a cooling star
NEOWISE W1 change -0.039+-0.040, matching the star-temperature prediction -0.030; dust shell at 1000 K predicts +0.76
Intra-day G/RP rise of ~4% over 0.75 d at t=0-0.75; ZTF g and r swing by 10-15% on 2-6 d timescales near t=1462-1487 (errors 1.5-3%)
Repeated year-long ZTF lows of 5-8% (t~1911-1965, 2440-2660, 3180-3420) with recoveries in between, not at a fixed period or depth
No IR excess: Ks-W1 0.1, W1-W2 -0.1, W3/W4 upper limits only
BP depth >= RP depth; a dissipating Be disk would dim the red more, and there is no IR excess from a disk
ruwe 1.02, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, normal BP/RP excess factor 1.29; the BP/RP outliers at t=216 and 326 are isolated, single-band and not part of the fade
G=17.2 at ~3 kpc gives M_G ~1.5-4.5 after plausible extinction, a dwarf, subgiant or late-B/A star, not a luminous red giant

explanation: Most likely a magnetically active, spotted dwarf or subgiant (RS CVn/BY Dra-like or young) whose spot coverage changed over years. The Gaia fade is smooth (abbe 0.12), about 17% from t~300 to 1021, and appears in both fields of view and in BP and RP, so it is not instrumental. The BP/RP depth ratio of 1.39+-0.35 matches a cooling photosphere, and the W1 change of -0.04+-0.04 matches the temperature prediction (-0.03). On top of this there are fast changes: +4% within 0.75 d at t=0, and +-7% swings every few days in ZTF g and r near t~1462-1473, as rotational modulation would produce. ZTF then shows repeated year-long lows of 5-8%, which looks like an activity cycle, not eclipses or a single occultation. The lack of an IR excess argues against disk dust.

discriminating_test: Run a BLS/period search on the full ZTF r and g light curves, using the high-cadence nights. Check that one strict period phases all the faint ZTF epochs and the Gaia dips at t=357.12, 411.59, 532.04 and 627.70 into a flat-bottomed primary eclipse (and possibly a shallower secondary), while the in-episode Gaia visits that stayed at normal flux fall outside eclipse.

evidence.feature: Gaia dips are isolated single visits with normal visits interleaved inside the 'episode'; changes of 0.62->0.91 and 0.80->0.635 within 106.5 min
Consistent dip floor near 0.60 in Gaia G/BP/RP and ZTF g, r, i across ~7 years
ztf_r high-cadence run at t~1576.47-1576.52: ~30 points flat at 0.58-0.63 (flat-bottomed eclipse)
Dips seen in both fields of view and all three Gaia bands, roughly grey (ratio 1.51 +/- 0.83)
Dips recur throughout ZTF 2018-2024 (faintest epochs spread over t=1376-4036), with no change after 2020
Quiet out of dip (G robust sigma 0.008, close to errors); no brightenings
ruwe 0.92, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, ZTF PSF photometry shows the full 40% depth
ztf_r bin at t~2127 with 135 epochs and median 0.82, min 0.67: a shallower or partial eclipse, possibly the secondary
Galactic latitude 0-5 deg, G=17.9: a crowded field, so an unresolved eclipsing neighbour is possible
NEOWISE W1/W2 show no change and no mid-IR brightening

explanation: A short-period detached eclipsing binary. The 271-d 'episode' is not a sustained fade: it is four isolated Gaia visits (357, 411, 532, 627) dropping to about 0.62, with normal visits in between. Flux changes by up to 30% within the 106.5-min field-of-view pair, which reads as eclipse ingress and egress. The dips are near-grey and appear in G, BP and RP and in both fields of view. ZTF g, r and i show the same flat floor at about 0.60 throughout 2018-2024, including about 30 high-cadence r points sitting flat for more than 1.2 h. Out of eclipse the star is quiet, the dip duty cycle is about 6-12% and the long-term level does not change. Together these point to total or annular eclipses lasting a few hours, recurring on a period of about a day or a few days.

discriminating_test: Check Gaia epoch G photometry of nearby stars of similar magnitude and colour for the same ~0.9% deficit between days 88 and 330 (residual calibration), and get a TESS/ZTF rotation period and flare rate to confirm an active spotted dwarf.

evidence.feature: Depth 0.0092 in G at only ~5 sigma; BP/RP depth errors 0.044/0.016 leave colour untestable
Outside-window visits at days 844 and 880 (0.982) are deeper than any in-window visit; scatter late in the series reaches ~1-2%
Abbe 0.872, slope_z -0.28, s_fade only 4.15 after many trial windows; flagged by a weak 36.7 d repeat
In-window lows in both FOV 1 and FOV 2 (e.g. 87.88 fov2, 183.30 fov2, 329.45 fov1)
ruwe 1.01, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, BP/RP excess 1.34 normal for bp_rp 2.17
Ks-W1-W2 flat (14.5/14.4/14.4), photospheric; W3 13.1 likely low-SNR; no W4 detection
ZTF g has 17 >3-sigma bright outliers and none faint (flares, or Eddington bias near the limit); Gaia day 777 is +2.4% in both FOVs
242 d duration at 0.9% depth with no recurrence; would need an implausibly large, slow occulter for an eclipse
NEOWISE W1 change 0.0017 +/- 0.052, one visit in window: uninformative

explanation: A weak (0.9 +/- 0.18%) G-only depression over 7 visits (days 88-329) of a faint (G=17.9), likely reddened late-K/early-M dwarf (M_G ~8.7 before extinction, Ks-W2 photospheric). BP/RP and NEOWISE errors are 2-50x the depth, so colour cannot be tested. Both fields of view take part. Visits outside the window show similar or deeper lows (days 844 and 880 at -1.8%, 709-733 low), Abbe 0.87 is close to noise, and the search was triggered by a 36.7 d 'repeat', so this is most likely the star's own low-level variability (spot evolution on an active dwarf; ZTF g has bright outliers that could be flares, and day 777 is bright) or a residual faint-red-star calibration or false-alarm run. No eclipse geometry fits 242 d at 0.9%.

discriminating_test: Measure the star's activity level: a rotation period in the ZTF r light curve plus a chromospheric index (Ca II H&K or H-alpha spectrum, or a GALEX NUV excess). An active, fast-rotating K dwarf makes an activity cycle the default. A quiet, slow rotator shifts weight to residual Gaia calibration drift, which a comparison with same-magnitude neighbours' DR4 epoch trends would then test.

evidence.feature: Smooth monotonic trend, 1.7% over 2.6 yr, Abbe 0.42, no discrete events
ZTF g/r seasonal medians wander by about 1-2%, g amplitude above r; post-2020 slopes near zero and change after 2020 under 0.4%
FoV1 and FoV2 fluxes agree within errors throughout; ruwe 1.0, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, normal BP/RP excess
Depth only about 3x the visit noise per visit; trend significance rests on few late visits (t 905-957) at G=17.2
BP/RP depth ratio -1.9 +/- 2.9 and NEOWISE slopes +/- 4% per yr are uninformative
Absolute magnitude and colour place the star on the K-dwarf main sequence at |b| 15-20 deg
Parallax SNR 11, point-like source

explanation: A shallow 1.7% linear fade in Gaia G over 958 d (21 visits, slope_z 4.5, Abbe 0.42) on what looks like a K dwarf (M_G about 6.5 at 1200 pc, bp_rp 1.5). The most likely cause is slow spot or facula coverage change, such as an activity cycle. Later ZTF data show season-to-season level changes of about 1-2%, larger in g than in r, and no ongoing fade after 2020, which fits bounded stellar variability rather than a growing occultation. BP/RP and NEOWISE are too noisy to test colour. No FoV offset, a clean astrometric and blend profile, no recurrence, no IR. Residual Gaia calibration or processing drift at G=17 stays a real alternative.

discriminating_test: Plot the per-epoch G, BP and RP residuals against scan angle (and search Gaia for a neighbour within ~4 arcsec): a scan-angle correlation would confirm a blend, while a ZTF PSF light curve continuing the fade at ~1%/yr after 2018 would point to the star itself.

evidence.feature: BP/RP robust sigma (0.19, 0.069) about 3x median errors; phot_bp_rp_excess_factor 1.44
BP falls ~30% and RP ~8% between the t~835 and t~987 groups while G falls only ~1%, which is inconsistent with a change on the star
Change looks like a step after t~240 d rather than a smooth fade; within each dense group G is flat
Low galactic latitude (5-10 deg) and faint G, so a crowded field
Modest amplitude (~1%/yr, slope_z -4.2) is reachable by spot or activity-cycle evolution in a K/M dwarf at 620 pc
BP/RP depth ratio 6.1 +/- 8.4, so colour is uninformative
ruwe 1.05, parallax_snr 11, low ipd_frac_multi_peak

explanation: A faint (G=18.3), low-latitude star whose 'trend' is a ~2-3% offset of the early visit groups (t<240 d at ~1.02) against later groups (~1.00, final dense group ~0.99), only 4.2 sigma, Abbe 0.56. BP and RP scatter three times their errors (excess factor 1.44), and between the two dense groups BP drops ~30% and RP ~8% while G moves ~1%, which no change on the star can do. So the windows hold variable extra flux that depends on scan geometry, most likely a neighbour or background, and the same thing at a smaller level in G, or residual faint-star calibration drift, explains the trend. A slow activity-cycle change of a reddened K dwarf is the main astrophysical alternative.

discriminating_test: Plot the Gaia G epoch fluxes and per-CCD scatter against scan angle and look for a neighbour within 2-4 arcsec in Gaia DR3 or Pan-STARRS: if the bright early transits share the scan angles that put that neighbour in the window, blending is confirmed.

evidence.feature: Early G epochs (t<240) bright, with 7-12% disagreement between FOV transits 106 min apart and per-epoch errors 2-4x larger than later
phot_bp_rp_excess_factor 1.74 at bp_rp 1.83, galactic latitude 0-5 deg
BP epochs at 191.9, 1.42 and 1.37 times median, all fov 2
Sign of FOV1-FOV2 difference changes between pairs, so it is not a fixed FOV offset
RP depth -0.107+/-0.073 and BP -0.14+/-0.32 (brighter while G fainter)
NEOWISE W2 change -0.019+/-0.025 vs grey prediction -0.088
ZTF r and i repeatedly drop to a fixed floor ~0.61-0.64 and recover within minutes (e.g. t=1525.16, 1522.23, 2173.35)
ZTF after 2020: g -3%, r +0.4%, no continued fade
W1-W2 = -0.5 and strong W3 at low galactic latitude, likely confusion rather than a disk

explanation: The 'drop' is really the first ~230 days of Gaia G being high (1.04-1.22), and those epochs are where transits 106 min apart disagree by 7-12% with inflated per-epoch errors (CCD-to-CCD scatter). A star does not do that, but a neighbour moving partly into the window at some scan angles does. The star sits at |b| < 5 deg with a BP/RP excess of 1.74, and BP has fov-2 epochs at 1.4x and 190x, so contamination is clear. G dims while RP brightens (1.5 sigma), W2 rules out a grey occulter, and ZTF shows no lasting fade. ZTF r/i also flip within minutes to a fixed floor near 0.61, which points to a deblending or crowding artefact. Leading cause: scan-angle-dependent blending.

discriminating_test: Pull the ZTF g/r and TESS light curves to measure rotational modulation. Percent-level spot modulation with a period of days to weeks, plus slow seasonal level changes, would confirm an active spotted star. A quiet star with no modulation would shift weight toward a disk occultation or an unexplained event. A Ca II H&K or X-ray activity check would also discriminate.

evidence.feature: Dip present in G, BP and RP and in both fov at t=127 and t=301.7
fov 1 and fov 2 transits 106.5 min apart agree within errors
ruwe 0.979, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, phot_bp_rp_excess_factor 1.23 (normal for colour)
Duration 175-375 d with 1-2% depth implies crossing speed ~0.07 km/s
Depth grows smoothly from 1.0% to 1.9% then recovers; abbe 0.626
BP/RP depth ratio 1.99 +/- 1.69 (z_grey 0.59, z_dust 0.17)
Outside the episode G scatter only ~0.15-0.3% (small dips at 877, 907 d)
Main-sequence absolute magnitude, W2-W3 shows no mid-IR excess
Calibration drift shared by similar stars already removed from G, BP, RP

explanation: A K1-K2 dwarf (M_G about 5.7, bp_rp 1.18 at 540 pc, ruwe 0.98, no multi-peak, normal BP/RP excess) dims by 1.0% at days 127 and 148 and by 1.9% at day 302, then is back to normal by day 502. Both fields of view and all three bands show it at days 127 and 302, which rules out single-epoch, FOV-offset and blend artefacts. The BP/RP ratio (1.99 +/- 1.69) can't tell grey from reddened. The event lasts 175 to 375 days, so if something passed in front of the star it would have to cross at about 0.07 km/s. That means an extended disk, not a compact body. The likeliest cause is a period of heavy spot coverage on a moderately active K dwarf. A shallow disk occultation is the main alternative.

discriminating_test: Check ground photometry taken at the same time as Gaia days 0-260 (2014-2015, e.g. CRTS, Pan-STARRS or ATLAS), together with the Gaia per-CCD G fluxes and transit flags. This shows whether the 23% G deficit is a real fade (which would also have to show in other bands) or a G-only processing artefact.

evidence.feature: G at 0.77 for days 0-0.93 in both FoV 1 and 2 while BP (mean ~1.02) and RP (mean ~0.98) in the same transits are at normal level
colour_of_change: depth_g 0.037+/-0.003 vs depth_rp 0.003+/-0.012 and depth_bp 0.003+/-0.030; a change in G with no BP/RP counterpart is impossible for a real change in the star's flux
Smooth monotonic exponential-like G recovery (timescale ~90-110 d) across several scanning-law groups with no FoV offset, unlike per-transit window, scan-angle or CCD artefacts
ruwe 1.0, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, phot_bp_rp_excess_factor 1.22 normal for bp_rp 1.14: no sign of a neighbour
Drift shared by stars of similar magnitude and colour already removed; the fade is specific to this star
Ordinary ~K-type main-sequence star at 2300 pc with no IR excess (Ks 15.5, W1 15.5), quiet in ZTF g/r for years afterwards
rep_period 23 d repeat flag is driven by the single early fade, with no repeated events and no recurrence test

explanation: Only Gaia G fades. The first seven transits (both fields of view) sit at 0.77, and G then recovers smoothly: 0.90 at day 94, 0.955 at 145, 0.98 at 200 and about 1.0 from day 260 onward. In the same transits BP shows no deficit (about 1.02 at day 0) and neither does RP (about 0.98); overall depth_rp is 0.003+/-0.012 against 0.037+/-0.003 in G. BP and RP together cover G's passband, so no change on the star, no dust and no occulter can dim G by 23% while leaving both unchanged. Clean astrometry (ruwe 1.0, ipd 0) and a normal BP/RP excess argue against a blend. The only listed route is a G-only artefact, but no known mechanism gives one star a smooth months-long recovery, so this is largely unexplained.

discriminating_test: Run a joint period search on the Gaia G/RP epochs, the full NEOWISE W1/W2 series and any ZTF r/i data. A single coherent period of about 250-400 d, with the IR in step with the optical, would confirm Mira pulsation. Fades with no period from a constant maximum would point instead to R CrB dust.

evidence.feature: G flux range 0.31-3.89 with several separate maxima and minima over 967 d
bp_rp 5.65, Ks 7.23, W1-W4 bright with rising mid-IR excess
