explanation: Gaia G falls in steps: flat near 1.003 until t~440, a plateau near 0.985 from 488 to 824, then 0.96 from 865 to the last visit. Both fields of view and about 13 separate scan groups share it, which a scan-angle or FoV artefact would not do, so the star's flux probably really changed. The dimming is grey within large errors (BP/RP 0.97+-0.38), hot dust shells are excluded and nothing conflicts with cold or confined dust. The star is quiet on short timescales and looks like an old dwarf or subgiant about 0.8 kpc from the plane. The likeliest cause is a slow, structured occultation by dusty material, such as a circumsecondary disk. ZTF shows no continuing fade after 2018. A residual Gaia calibration effect or an injection remains quite possible.

discriminating_test: Run a period search on ZTF g/r (or TESS) photometry to test for a persistent ~3.3 d rotation signal and multi-year mean-level wander, and check whether the r-band amplitude tracks g as spots predict. In parallel, compare Gaia G against RP for same-colour field stars over days 0-200 to rule out a G-only calibration offset.

evidence.feature: Coherent ~3.3 d, ~5% peak-to-peak modulation over days 293-300, consistent between fov 1 and fov 2
Smooth multi-year G fade (abbe 0.10, slope_z -5) then partial recovery, with day-scale scatter (robust_sigma 0.024 >> err 0.005)
bp_rp 1.74, M_G ~6.5 at 1400 pc: K/M dwarf about 1.4 mag above the main sequence (binary or active star), at z ~650 pc
No IR excess (W1-W2 = -0.1, Ks-W1 = 0.2, W3/W4 upper limits); high galactic latitude
W1 visits inside the window are ~3% below the early W1 visits; predicted -9% for grey blocking
RP depth 0.018+/-0.013 (my estimate ~0.04) against G 0.09: low for spots, dust or grey alike
ruwe 0.998, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, BP/RP excess factor 1.3 (normal for this colour)
BP scatter (0.095) far above its errors (0.025), with BP very bright at days 0-37

explanation: Most likely an active, spotted K/M star (BY Dra/RS CVn-like, overluminous for its colour, so possibly a binary). The dense run at days 293-300 shows a coherent ~3.3 d modulation of about 5% peak to peak, seen the same way in both fields of view, which points to rotation. The detected 'drop' is a smooth fade in mean G, from ~1.09 to ~0.97 over about 670 d, followed by partial recovery. That fits a change in spot coverage or an activity cycle. BP is brightest at the start (bluer when brighter), and the W1 drop against the early visits (~3%) matches the prediction for a temperature or spot change rather than grey blocking. Clean astrometry and no IR excess. Caveat: the RP depth looks low compared with G.

discriminating_test: Phase-fold the Gaia epochs with ZTF/TESS photometry, or check a TESS sector, for a period of a few days. If it is an eclipsing binary, the deep primary eclipse and the shallower, redder secondary eclipse should recur at fixed phases and depths.

evidence.feature: Deepest epoch t=0: BP 0.070, RP 0.160, G 0.109, all three bands at once
Shallow dips with RP depth about twice BP depth, about the size of the cool residual light seen at primary minimum
Fast ingress at t~230 and t~553 (0.99 to 0.89 to 0.55 within hours, normal epochs on both sides), seen in fov 1 and fov 2
Deep-dip BP/RP depth ratio ~1.1, close to grey, not dust-like 1.7
No near-IR excess (Ks-W1 0.11, W1-W2 0.03), so no hot inner disk rim
W3/W4 excess (W1-W4 ~3.9) at |b|<5 deg, possibly cool dust or background in the plane
ruwe 1.03, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, normal BP/RP excess factor

explanation: An Algol-type eclipsing binary: a hot (A-type) primary with a cooler, larger companion. Deep, short primary eclipses (G to 0.11 at t=0; ingress caught at t~230 and ~553, 0.99 to 0.89 to 0.55 within ~6 h) appear in G, BP and RP in both fields of view. At the deepest point the remaining light is red (BP 0.07, RP 0.16), as expected if only the cool companion is left. Six shallow dips (t=129.6, 391.7, 592.8, 733.5, 877.3, 896.6) are deeper in RP (~0.06-0.12) than BP (~0.02-0.06), matching secondary eclipses of that companion, and they last no more than hours. The 518-d 'episode' is the slow search averaging sparsely sampled eclipses.

discriminating_test: Compare Gaia epoch photometry of nearby stars of similar magnitude and colour over t=348-656 d. A shared fade would make this instrumental; if they are flat, a Ca II H&K activity or rotation measurement would test the spot/activity explanation.

evidence.feature: Dip seen coherently in both fov 1 and fov 2 and in G, BP and RP over 11 visits
BP/RP depth ratio 2.16 +/- 0.67 (z_grey 1.72, z_dust 0.68, ~1 sigma from cooling value)
300 d smooth fade with gradual onset and recovery; far too slow for orbital crossing of the stellar disk
Out-of-episode variability: second ~0.7% dip at t~840 (also redder), excess fov-pair scatter, slow_change repeat flag
No infrared excess (Ks=W1=W2=12.0, W3 12.3, W4 upper limit); NEOWISE shell-1000K prediction excluded
ruwe 1.04, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, normal bp_rp_excess_factor 1.2
ZTF 2018-2025 shows no clear 1% episode, only 0.3-0.5% seasonal shifts that may be normalisation offsets
Shallow 1% coherent Gaia trend at G=13.5 after shared calibration drift removed; residual systematics still possible

explanation: Most likely the star's own low-level variability: a slow change in spot or facula coverage on an F/G-type, slightly evolved star gives a smooth fade of about 0.8% in G over about 300 d that is redder when fainter. BP/RP = 2.2 +/- 0.7 fits cooling or dust; grey dimming is disfavoured at 1.7 sigma. Both fields of view and all three bands show it, and its timescale matches nothing in the scanning law, so it is neither a field-of-view offset nor a one-epoch defect. The star varies anyway: a 0.7% dip at t~840, extra scatter between paired transits, and ZTF seasons 0.3-0.5% low. A 300 d dip is far too slow for a body crossing the star in orbit, so any occulter must be an extended disk or interstellar structure. That is possible but less likely. Residual long-term Gaia calibration remains an alternative.

discriminating_test: Take an optical spectrum and look for symbiotic emission lines (He II 4686, Raman O VI 6825 plus M-giant bands). Also check archival photometry near day ~1019 for the predicted eclipse, to see whether the fade 903-958 was a separate decline of the hot component.

evidence.feature: Gaia and ZTF dips at 151, 582, ~1880, ~2750, ~3190, ~3622 fit one period of ~434 d
Narrow flat-bottomed dips (~50 d, ~12% of the period), each reaching ~20% of the level just before it
Out-of-eclipse ZTF g ranges ~0.25-5.6, with long low plateaus and brightenings
W2 brighter when optical bright (737, 1296) and fainter when optical faint (566, 1099)
Detected fade 903-958 is 60-120 d before the predicted eclipse; G was 1.07 at 31 d before the previous eclipse
BP/RP depth ratio 1.59 (z_grey 2.2): hot component fading or eclipsed, or dust
Fade seen consistently in G, BP, RP and both fields of view over 3 visits; ZTF confirms large variability
Mid-IR excess (Ks-W4 ~1.9), Galactic plane, poorly constrained distance (luminous)
Isolated BP/RP spikes at 78.36 and 86.11 (fov 2) with normal G

explanation: This looks like an eclipsing symbiotic-like binary. Sharp, flat-bottomed dips about 50 d long recur with P≈434 d: Gaia at 151 and 582, ZTF at about 1880, 2750, 3190 and 3622. Each removes about 80% of the light and is reddened, so a cool giant is eclipsing a hot, variable component. Around the eclipses the system shows large irregular, outburst-like swings: ZTF g varies by a factor of up to about 50, and W2 rises with the optical brightness, so the changes are intrinsic, not dust in front. The detected fade (903-958) comes 60-120 d before the next predicted eclipse (~1019) and starts well before any ingress seen elsewhere. It is most likely the hot component fading. It could also be a broad pre-eclipse decline, which some cycles show.
recognised_as: V1413 Aql (AS 338), eclipsing symbiotic, P ~434 d

discriminating_test: Take one low-resolution optical spectrum, or find one in an archive. Balmer/He emission at z=0 would mean a CV or nova-like, and redshifted broad lines would mean a quasar. Then check the post-2018 ZTF light curve for a deep low state followed by an abrupt return to the high state.

evidence.feature: Smooth fade in G and BP to 0.48/0.41 of the median, accelerating over the last 50 d after a slow rise (abbe 0.096, slope_z -6)
Paired 106.5-min transits differ by 5-13% in G, with BP matching the sign (t=146.7, 357.7, 526.0, 679.3)
BP fades more than RP (depth ratio ~1.3-1.45 late in the fade); G lies between them, so the change is chromatic and consistent across bands
G-W1 = 1.0 and W1-W2 = 0.1 (AllWISE): stellar or disk-like, far bluer than a quasar's roughly flat SED (G-W1 ~ 2.5)
No warm IR excess (W1-W2 ~ 0.1) for a blue source
Parallax SNR 0.72 at G=18.1: luminous, distant object or zero parallax
RP outliers (2.51 at 709.6 d, 1.42 at 0 d) single-epoch, single-band; drive the spurious negative depth_rp
ruwe 0.86, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, BP/RP excess 1.22: no sign of a resolved neighbour

explanation: The most likely cause is an intrinsically luminous accreting binary (a nova-like CV) slowly entering a low state. The source is faint (G=18.1), blue (BP-RP 0.22) and at high latitude, and its insignificant parallax rules out a nearby dwarf nova. G rises gently to a peak at ~357 d and then fades smoothly and faster and faster, by ~0.9 mag, to the last visit (abbe 0.10). BP follows G, and RP fades less, so the source reddens as it dims, as a cooling disk would. Transits paired 106.5 min apart differ by 5-13% in G, and BP agrees in sign: this is flickering, which no occulter or quasar produces. G-W1=1.0 and W1-W2=0.1 are not quasar-like.

discriminating_test: Take a low-resolution optical spectrum to get the spectral type and luminosity class and to check for H-alpha emission, shell lines or Li. Then fit the ZTF g-r versus r slope across the 2024 fade. An ISM-like reddening vector with an unchanged spectral type points to dust occultation. Temperature-driven colour changes with TiO/activity signatures point to spots. H-alpha emission points to a Be star or a YSO.

evidence.feature: Smooth multi-hundred-day fades (abbe 0.07) seen independently in Gaia G/BP/RP and in ZTF g/r in later years
Stable maximum level near 1.02-1.05 with excursions only downward, recovering to baseline in 2025
BP/RP depth ratio 1.48+-0.29 (z_dust -0.78, z_grey 1.66); ZTF g deficit about 1.6x r
Fades at about 640-956, 2760-3010 and 3300-3760 d with no dip near 2300 d: not a strict period
Ks, W1-W3 photospheric (W1-W2 0.03, W2-W3 -0.28): no warm dust or disk
Distance 850 pc with G 15, Ks 9.15: M_Ks about -1, too faint for an AGB or semi-regular giant or an R CrB star
ruwe 1.08, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, BP/RP excess normal: no resolved neighbour
ZTF i flat to about 1% over 167 d and only modest short-term scatter: weak rotational modulation
Colour/IR also fit a B star behind A_V about 8, where BP-stronger fading fits a shell-phase Be disk

explanation: The star is a heavily reddened, low-luminosity source (M_Ks about -1 at 850 pc in the plane), most likely a K giant with A_V about 5-6, though a reddened B star is possible. It has a stable high level (Gaia 2014-15, ZTF 2018-20) and dims smoothly below it for long stretches: Gaia 6.5% over about 300 d, then ZTF fades in 2021-22 and 2024-25 (r about 14%, g about 22%), followed by recovery. The dips are chromatic (BP/RP 1.48+-0.29, ZTF g/r about 1.6-2) and do not recur at a fixed period. It shows no IR excess and has clean astrometry. My leading explanation is variable extinction by a cold, structured occulter, such as a circumsecondary disk on a wide orbit. Spot cycles or Be shell episodes are the main alternatives.

discriminating_test: Take an optical spectrum, or look one up in archival SDSS/DESI, to check for broad emission lines and a redshift. Also check whether Gaia's proper motion is consistent with zero and whether the source has a Gaia QSO-candidate classification.

evidence.feature: W1-W2 = 0.9, W2-W3 = 3.4 (AGN mid-IR colours); W1 far brighter than a blue G=19.3 photosphere
Faint, blue, parallax_snr 1.2, |b| 20-25 deg
Smooth monotonic Gaia fade (abbe 0.065, slope_z -12), consistent across fov 1 and 2
ZTF g/r rise of 15-29% after 2020 after the fade; aperiodic multi-year swings
NEOWISE W1 slope -0.08/yr matches G slope, independent instrument
ruwe 0.98, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, no resolved neighbour signs

explanation: Most likely a quasar/AGN, not a star. It is faint (G=19.3), blue (BP-RP 0.52), at high galactic latitude, and has no significant parallax. Its WISE colours, W1-W2=0.9 and W2-W3=3.4, sit in the AGN locus, and W1=16.1 is far too bright for the photosphere of a blue G=19.3 star. The 'dip' is a smooth 20% fade over 984 d (abbe 0.07) that both fields of view agree on. ZTF later shows large stochastic swings: a 15-29% rise after 2020, with g reaching about 1.3-1.5. That is red-noise behaviour on timescales of years, typical of AGN. NEOWISE W1 also fell during the Gaia years, so the change is real and not a Gaia artefact. The BP/RP ratio is too noisy to discriminate.

discriminating_test: Compare per-transit G fluxes of nearby stars with similar magnitude and colour in the same Gaia transits (and against scan angle/CCD row) to see whether the ~1% drop after ~790 d is shared. Also check whether binned BP and RP drop by the same ~1% once the RP outlier at 949.45 d is removed.

evidence.feature: G fade is a ~1% step after ~730-800 d rather than a linear trend; seen in both fov 1 and 2
G robust_sigma 0.007 vs median error 0.0035, with ~1% differences between transits 106.5 min apart
ztf_after: slopes after 2020 ~0 in g, r, i; no continuation of the -0.4%/yr Gaia trend
ZTF g season medians swing ~1.8% (2018 high, 2020 low), r ~0.6%, i ~0: chromatic low-level long-term variation
colour_of_change ratio null; RP depth driven by single 1.80 outlier at 949.45 d (BP, G normal there)
ruwe 1.03, bp_rp excess consistent with isolated source, ipd_frac_multi_peak 1
Ks, W1, W2 photospheric for a G star; W1-W2 ~ -0.1; parallax SNR 6.7
M_G ~4.2, bp_rp 0.87, |b| 60-65 at 3.1 kpc: old dwarf/subgiant, not a giant or YSO

explanation: The flagged 'trend' is mostly a ~1% G step: flat near 1.003 until ~700 d, then about 0.99 from 809 d on, with partial recovery at 949 d. Both fields of view show it. BP/RP are too noisy (sigma ~2.7%), and the RP fit is wrecked by one 1.80 outlier, so the colour test is null and nothing rules dust or grey out. G scatters about twice its errors even within hours, so small G systematics are present. ZTF shows no continued fade after Gaia, only ~1% season-to-season wander that is strongest in g and absent in i, typical of ZTF offsets or weak activity. Most likely a Gaia calibration/processing residual, or low-level magnetic-activity variability in this old G-type star at 3 kpc. No IR excess. Nothing in the data demands an exotic cause.

discriminating_test: Check Gaia DR4 epoch photometry, which extends to early 2020, for this star and for comparison stars of similar magnitude on the same transits. A fade that persists or recovers on this star alone would point to a real cause. A fade shared with the comparison stars, or one that tracks the window class (G~16 boundary), would point to an instrumental one.

evidence.feature: Fade visits at 663, 696, 888 d are single epochs with errors 0.23-0.26%, deficits only 1.5-2.7 sigma each; 838 d visit is at normal level
sigma_visit 0.00099 is smaller than single-epoch errors (~0.0029) and robust_sigma 0.0038, inflating s_fade
Fade confined to last ~355 d of a sparse 18-visit Gaia series, ending at the last visit
Fade visits include both fov 1 and fov 2
ruwe 0.995, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, bp_rp_excess 1.2, galactic latitude 45-50 deg
Ks, W1, W2 all 14.8: no infrared excess; W1-W2=0 rules out AGN
NEOWISE W1/W2 brightening in the single in-fade visit is within 1.3-1.9 sigma, and early W1 visits are similarly high
BP and RP depths -0.004+/-0.012 and -0.001+/-0.006: colour unconstrained
Absolute G ~4.4, bp_rp 0.84: solar-type dwarf where a ~0.1-0.4% activity-cycle change is possible
355 d, 0.4% shallow monotonic fade: not eclipse-like in depth or duration

explanation: A 0.4% G fade carried by only five sparse visits at the end of the Gaia span. Four of them are single epochs with errors of about 0.25-0.46%, so the real significance is about 3 sigma, not s_fade 6.2: sigma_visit (0.001) comes from multi-epoch visits and underestimates the noise. The 838 d visit is back at normal level. BP and RP are too noisy to give a colour. ZTF cannot measure 0.4%. The star is a quiet, photospheric old G dwarf at high latitude with no crowding indicators. The most likely causes are a statistical or calibration residual near the end of the time series. A modest magnetic-cycle change is the main astrophysical alternative. A real occultation is possible but not required.

discriminating_test: Get an optical spectrum (or look up an archival SDSS/DESI spectrum or a Gaia QSO-candidate classification). Broad emission lines at a cosmological redshift would confirm an AGN and settle the cause of the fade.

evidence.feature: W1-W2 = 1.2, W2-W3 = 3.45, G-W1 = 3.5 with BP-RP 0.56 (AGN mid-IR colour locus)
parallax_snr 0.51 (consistent with zero), G = 18.1, |b| 50-55 deg
smooth stochastic wander (abbe 0.308): rise to 1.07 near day 190, then a gradual fade to 0.935, slope_z -8.2
fov 1 and fov 2 fluxes agree within errors at paired transits (e.g. day 963.6: 0.9359 vs 0.9353); no step
ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, ruwe 1.01, normal BP/RP excess factor
BP/RP depth ratio -0.14 +/- 1.89, uninformative about colour
NEOWISE W1/W2 change consistent with zero; far below the 1000 K dust-shell prediction

explanation: The infrared colours belong to a quasar, not a star. W1-W2 = 1.2 and W2-W3 = 3.45, where stars sit near 0. G-W1 = 3.5 even though BP-RP is only 0.56. The parallax is consistent with zero, the source is faint (G = 18.1) and it lies at high galactic latitude. The G light curve wanders smoothly (Abbe 0.31): it rises to about +7% near day 190, then fades by about 6% to day 964 (-3.9%/yr). The two fields of view agree, and there is no step and no recurrence. This is typical AGN red-noise (damped random walk) variability. BP and RP are too noisy to test whether the source is bluer when brighter. The flat NEOWISE photometry fits a lagged, weaker torus response. No occulter is needed.

discriminating_test: Plot per-transit G flux against scan angle and look at a ZTF/Pan-STARRS image for a neighbour within ~2-4 arcsec. If flux tracks scan angle, or ZTF PSF photometry from 2018 onward is flat at the ~2% level, it is a blend artefact. Real ~10% Be-like variability in ZTF would point to an intrinsic cause.

evidence.feature: phot_bp_rp_excess_factor 3.03 at G=19, |b|<5 deg
early bright fov-1 epochs with huge errors (t=0, 191.4, 357.7: err 0.19-0.27)
fov1 vs fov2 disagreement within the same pair (966.63 vs 966.81: 1.005 vs 0.931; 783.47 vs 783.55)
robust_sigma 0.045 vs median error 0.014; only 16 visits over 967 d
smooth-ish multi-hundred-day bright phase then ~5-8% lower level (abbe 0.43, slope_z -3.8)
BP/RP depths null; no WISE/2MASS/ZTF/NEOWISE coverage
Galactic plane location

explanation: Most likely contamination by a neighbour in a crowded field, not a real fade. The source is faint (G=19), sits within 5 deg of the Galactic plane, and has a BP/RP excess factor of 3.03, far above the ~1.2 expected, which points to strong blending. BP and RP depths could not be measured. The 'drop' is really an early bright phase (t~0-358) carried by fov-1 epochs with very large errors (0.19-0.27) plus a few moderately bright points. Later the level wanders by about 5%, with fov1/fov2 pairs disagreeing at 2-4 sigma within hours (t=783, 967). Scatter is about 3x the formal errors. A real slow variable, such as a reddened Be star with an outburst and decline, remains a smaller possibility. There are no IR, ZTF or NEOWISE data to test either explanation.

discriminating_test: Period search on the ZTF g/r light curve (2018 on; G 19.8 is within reach) for recurring ~0.6 mag eclipses. A strict short period that also phases all four Gaia dips confirms an eclipsing binary; a flat ZTF light curve points to a Gaia transit-level artefact (worth checking the AL/AC centroid residuals of those four transits).

evidence.feature: Three G dips at a consistent ~0.53-0.57 level plus one at 0.69, all other visits flat within noise (robust_sigma 0.035 vs err 0.023)
Dips seen in the same transits in G (small CCD-scatter errors), BP and RP, roughly grey within large BP/RP errors
BP fov2 at t=184.47 is normal (1.14) 106 min after the 0.57 dip at the same scan angle
All four dips are fov 1 transits, mostly unpaired, and clustered within 184-535 d with none in 21 other visits
ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, ruwe 1.02, bp_rp_excess 1.16 normal for a point source at |b| 30-35
No slow trend or red noise (abbe 1.02, slope_z 0.87); drops recover within hours
Blue bp_rp 0.197 with parallax consistent with zero at G 19.8 (distant halo hot subdwarf/CV-like)
Ecliptic latitude 80-90 deg

explanation: The 351 d 'episode' is really four single-transit drops (G 0.53, 0.57, 0.69, 0.53) among otherwise flat visits. G, BP and RP all show them together, the G errors are small (the CCDs agree), the dips are roughly grey, three sit at nearly the same level (~0.55), and a BP transit 106 min after the first dip is back to normal. A flat light curve plus a repeatable deep floor is what short eclipses in a detached binary look like. Given the blue colour and null parallax, a hot subdwarf or CV is plausible. Against: all four dips fall in FoV 1 and inside 184-535 d (each about 5% by chance). That leaves room for a transit-level processing error, such as a misplaced window or a mis-assigned transit.

discriminating_test: Compare the Gaia scan angles (and along-scan centroid offsets) of the five dim transits with those of the normal and BP/RP-excess transits. If they cluster at one scan angle, the dips come from window truncation by a neighbour. If the scan angles are random, a period search in archival ZTF photometry should find strictly periodic ~50% eclipses with a period of order a day.

evidence.feature: Both FoV transits of the same visit are dim at t=193.4/193.5 and 795.6/795.7, with depth changing smoothly over 1.8 h
BP dims at the G-dip transits (fov2: 0.50, 0.38, 0.53 against ~1.0 otherwise); BP depth 0.35+-0.16 matches G 0.30
35 of 41 G epochs flat within a few per cent; discrete deep dips in ~13% of epochs; abbe 1.11
Normal visits at t=214.4/214.5 between the dips at 193 and 251: separate short events, not one 57-d fade
Eclipse lasting more than 1.8 h needs a star of radius >~1 Rsun, not a WD or sdB (eclipses of minutes)
BP/RP excess transits (t=592.7: BP 2.61, RP 2.13 while G is 0.94) and G high outliers (763.7 at +5 sigma) suggest a neighbour entering the windows at some scan angles
Very blue (bp_rp -0.14), G=20, |b| 45-50, parallax SNR 1.3, no WISE or 2MASS match
Flux returns to normal between dips with no stochastic red-noise wandering; blue colour unusual for a QSO
RP depth -0.18+-0.33 is too noisy to constrain colour; no ratio available

explanation: The 57-day 'episode' is really separate short dips: 30-50% G dips at t=193, 251 and 796, a partial one at 734, and a normal visit at 214 in between. Both field-of-view transits 106.5 min apart are dim (0.72 then 0.50; 0.57 then 0.65), with the depth changing in a way that looks like ingress and egress. BP dims at the same transits. The other ~35 epochs are flat within a few per cent. That fits a detached eclipsing binary with eclipses lasting a few hours, a period of order 1-3 d, and dips in about 13% of epochs. Eclipses that long rule out WD or sdB eclipses, so the star would be a distant blue A-type/BHB system. The main alternative is scan-angle-dependent window truncation by a neighbour: some transits show BP/RP excesses.

discriminating_test: Get an optical spectrum, or check the archives (SDSS/DESI spectra, Gaia DR3 QSO candidate tables, X-ray or radio catalogues), for broad emission lines and a redshift that would confirm a quasar.

evidence.feature: WISE W1-W2 = 1.1, W2-W3 = 3.5, large IR excess over the optical photosphere
parallax_snr -1.3 at G = 18.9, high galactic latitude, distance poorly constrained
Smooth, aperiodic Gaia variation (Abbe 0.266, slope -4.4%/yr, no repeating period)
ZTF g amplitude larger than ZTF r in both the fade (days 1960-2110) and the later brightening (days 3500-3940)
ZTF variability of 30-40% on year timescales, larger than the 10% Gaia dip
ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, ruwe 1.12, normal BP/RP excess factor
BP/RP depth ratio 16 +/- 278, uninformative
W1 fades slowly over the decade with no prompt NEOWISE response to the dip

explanation: Almost certainly a quasar showing stochastic AGN variability. W1-W2 = 1.1 and W2-W3 = 3.5 put it on the AGN mid-infrared locus, and W1 = 15.4 is far brighter than a G = 18.9, BP-RP 0.7 photosphere could produce. The parallax is consistent with zero (snr -1.3), it sits at high galactic latitude, and it is a single-peaked point source. The Gaia 'episode' is a smooth 10% low state (Abbe 0.27) inside a meandering light curve. ZTF shows the same random-walk behaviour on longer timescales: a 30-35% fade in g near days 1960-2100, then a 20-40% rise after day 3500, with g changing more than r (bluer when brighter), as quasars do. The BP/RP colour of the dip is too noisy to tell anything.

discriminating_test: Run a periodogram on the ZTF r/i (or ASAS-SN) light curve from 2018 on: a multi-periodic semi-regular signal (about 40 d plus a few-hundred-day term) with amplitude rising toward bluer bands would confirm pulsation. A low-resolution spectrum showing an M-type giant with TiO bands would do the same.

evidence.feature: bp_rp 4.82, G-Ks 6.3, Ks 5.94 at 1800 pc: luminous cool giant/AGB star
Comparable dips outside the flagged window (t=226 at 0.95, t=876 at 0.90) and bright phases up to 1.06: the star varies continuously
Amplitude largest in BP, then G, then RP across the whole light curve (temperature change)
Paired fov 1/2 transits agree within errors during the dips
Dips persist across visits weeks apart in all three bands
Dip ratio BP/RP 0.80 +/- 0.35, z_dust -2.56: not interstellar-like dust reddening
Depths only about 12%, with no strong W3/W4 excess (Ks-W4 about 0.56)
Fast 0.87 to 1.01 recovery in 15 d and unequal dip depths: no fixed eclipse shape
ipd_frac_multi_peak 6%, crowded low-latitude field, BP excess 1.78, bright early BP points and RP outlier at t=876.31
ruwe 1.17: no strong sign of a companion

explanation: A luminous, very red giant (BP-RP 4.8, G-Ks 6.3, M_Ks about -5.5 at 1.8 kpc, near the Galactic plane, W1-W2 negative as for CO absorption in an M giant) showing semi-regular variability. G moves between 0.87 and 1.06 on timescales of weeks to months (a 14% rise in 15 d after t=585, another dip of the same depth at t=876 outside the flagged window). Both fields of view agree, and all three bands show it, with amplitude growing toward the blue (BP range about 0.37, G 0.19, RP 0.17), which points to temperature-driven pulsation, not occultation. The 228-d 'episode' is sparse sampling of a multi-periodic SR/AGB light curve (repeat near 40 d, possibly a long secondary period).

discriminating_test: Get the ZTF g/r (and NEOWISE W1/W2) light curves from 2018 on. Check whether the grey fade keeps going, levels off or recovers, and whether it stays achromatic. Also check for a mid-IR excess. A grey recovery after a long minimum would point to disk occultation. A symmetric recovery to a lower baseline would point to microlensing. A reddened or IR-bright behaviour would point to a YSO.

evidence.feature: BP/RP depth ratio 1.01 +/- 0.18 (z_grey 0.04, z_dust -3.79)
Grey ratio about 2.4 sigma below the 1.4-1.5 expected for a cooling star
Smooth monotonic decline over ~550 d (abbe 0.133, slope_z -8.6), still fading at the last visit
FoV 1 and FoV 2 agree at every paired transit; trend seen in all three bands
Shared magnitude/colour calibration drift already removed
Inferred M_G ~1.5-2.5 with intrinsic bp_rp ~0.6-0.9 after plausible extinction at b 5-10 deg: not a luminous red giant
Low galactic latitude, slightly elevated bp_rp excess 1.25, no WISE match
Low latitude field, a slow grey fade could come from a large-grain YSO disk
Achromatic fall from a flat high state could be the tail of long microlensing
Single RP outlier at t=610.76 (1.118) in one band only
No IR (WISE/NEOWISE) or post-Gaia ZTF data to test dust re-emission or continuation

explanation: Smooth (abbe 0.13), steady grey fade: flat near 1.01 for ~350 d, then about 9% down over ~550 d in G, BP and RP alike (ratio 1.01+/-0.18), with both fields of view agreeing and the fade still going at the last visit. Grey dimming rules out ISM-like dust (z_dust -3.8) and argues against the star cooling (~2.4 sigma). That fits occultation by a large-grain or optically thick disk, with a slow ingress and no egress seen yet. The star is probably a reddened F/G subgiant at 3.5 kpc, not a red-giant pulsator. Weaker options: grey extinction in a YSO, the falling side of a long achromatic microlensing event, or residual calibration or blend trends. There is no WISE or ZTF data to check against.

discriminating_test: Compare the star's per-CCD G window fluxes and background estimates for the t>900 transits with those of nearby stars on the same transits, and check whether ZTF r or Gaia DR4 BP/RP/G show the star 4% fainter after t~990. A deficit only in this source's G processing would make it instrumental. A 4% drop in RP or ZTF r would revive an astrophysical cause.

evidence.feature: G depth 0.044+/-0.0016 while RP depth -0.009+/-0.012 and BP depth -0.002+/-0.019 (BP/RP epoch means stay at ~1.00 in the fade)
No chromatic or grey response in BP/RP: an eclipse, dust or a temperature change would all dim RP by 3-4%
Fade present in both fov 1 and fov 2 at the same level (~0.955)
phot_bp_rp_excess_factor 1.25 (normal for bp_rp 1.38), ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, ruwe 0.997
Fade starts near t~880-903 and is still faint at the last epoch: a monotonic change at the end of the series, slope_z -3.08
Pre-fade G scatter ~0.4-0.5% at the epoch noise level; star otherwise quiet
No IR excess (W1-W2 not red, W3/W4 only upper limits); no NEOWISE visits inside the fade
rep_period 56.3 d from only one fade episode; no second event in the data

explanation: G fades smoothly by 4.4% from about t=900 to the last visit, in both fields of view. BP (-0.002+/-0.019) and RP (-0.009+/-0.012) do not fade at all. Their epoch means stay near 1.00 throughout. G light is essentially BP plus RP light, so a real change on the star has to show in RP: about 4.4% if grey, about 3.3% if dust or cooling. RP misses that by 3.5-4.4 sigma, and by much more if you use per-epoch errors. That rules out every occulting and stellar-variability cause. The BP/RP excess factor (1.25) is normal for this colour, ipd_frac_multi_peak is 0 and ruwe is 1.0, which argues against a blend. What remains is a G-only artefact (processing or calibration) or a signal that no listed process can produce.

discriminating_test: Take a low-resolution optical spectrum (or look for an archival one) to check for Balmer/He II emission lines that would mark it as an accreting cataclysmic variable, and check the ZTF light curve after 2020 for continued fading, outbursts or flickering.

evidence.feature: 5-17% G changes between transits 106 min apart, matched in BP and RP
smooth 18% fade over 930 d, visits at t=831-836 all low, early visits high
BP-RP 0.24 with parallax SNR 3.6 implies sub-main-sequence luminosity
no 2MASS/WISE counterpart, so no strong warm-dust excess
ruwe 0.995, ipd_frac_multi_peak 2, BP/RP excess 1.17 normal
BP/RP depth ratio 1.9 +/- 0.78, consistent with reddening or cooling
no fixed offset between fields of view

explanation: A blue (BP-RP 0.24), faint star that is variable in its own right: G changes by 5-17% within 106 min between transits (e.g. 0.85 to 1.02 at t=907), and the change shows up together in G, BP and RP, with no consistent offset between fields of view. On top of that it fades smoothly by about 18% over 2.5 years (abbe 0.35, slope_z -4.9), and the fade is somewhat redder in BP than RP. A parallax at SNR 3.6 would put it below the main sequence for its colour. Blue, under-luminous, flickering on hour timescales and drifting slowly: that fits a cataclysmic variable (nova-like or old-nova state change) better than dust or eclipses. There is no WISE counterpart, so no strong disk excess (argues against a YSO), and RUWE 1 and normal BP/RP excess argue against a blend.

discriminating_test: Plot the Gaia G epoch fluxes against scan angle (or check the transits' scan angles for the 875-879 and 957 groups). If the high and low G states sort by scan angle relative to a neighbour seen in high-resolution imaging (Pan-STARRS/VVV/UKIDSS within ~2 arcsec), the blend is confirmed. Flat ZTF PSF photometry would also rule out real variability.

evidence.feature: ipd_frac_multi_peak = 31 with phot_bp_rp_excess_factor = 2.08 at |b| < 5 deg
G brightens 13-33% in transit groups at t=783, 875-879 and 957 while RP stays within ~4% of 1 and BP stays near 1
Dip depth G 0.036+/-0.014 but RP -0.003+/-0.026 for a star with bp_rp=3.5, where G flux is dominated by red light
Dip measured against median of outside visits that includes the contaminated high-flux epochs; vs pre-dip baseline only ~2% (about 1 sigma_visit)
Multi-day G excess in both fields of view (875-879), so not a single-FoV offset or a single-epoch hit
Abbe 0.72, slope_z 2.0, repeat signal from only 18 visits
Single RP epoch at 1.20 (t=767.79, fov 2) with no matching G

explanation: The most likely cause is a neighbour blended into the Gaia windows that changes the G flux depending on scan angle. ipd_frac_multi_peak=31%, a BP/RP excess factor of 2.08 and a position in the Galactic plane all point to a close companion source. Around t=783-958, G jumps 13-33% over groups of transits a few days long, while RP (which carries most of this very red star's light) and BP stay flat. No real change in the star can do that. The 3.6% 'dip' (t=409-768, 2.5 sigma) is measured against a median pushed up by those inflated epochs. Against the earlier baseline it is only about 2%, and RP shows no matching dip (-0.003+/-0.026). The 24.6 d repeat at 18 visits is weak.

discriminating_test: A single low-resolution optical spectrum, or an archival Gaia proper-motion and radial-velocity check. Strong H-alpha emission at the SMC's velocity (about +150 km/s) and SMC-like proper motion would confirm Be/B[e] disc variability. Broad, redshifted emission lines and zero proper motion would make it an AGN.

evidence.feature: colour_of_change: BP/RP depth ratio 0.574 +/- 0.069 (RP deeper; z_grey -6.2, z_dust -16.3)
parallax_snr -0.8 at G=14 with ruwe 1.01, |b| 45-50 and |ecliptic lat| 60-70 (consistent with the northern SMC)
bp_rp -0.10 with W1-W2 0.3 and W2-W3 0.8 (hot star plus disc-like near-IR excess, not AGN-like WISE colours)
NEOWISE W1/W2 vary by a factor ~5 (3.1x/3.9x high at t=-113, minimum 0.63 at t=427, slow rise to 1.18), redder when brighter
RP robust_sigma 0.078 vs BP 0.025: a variable red component throughout the light curve (RP 1.16 at t=74-154, 0.72 in the dip)
FoV pairs agree within ~1% (313.46/313.64, 355.37/355.45, 418.60/418.68); dip seen in G, BP and RP with smooth months-long recovery
W3-W4 = 3.05 (W4 = 8.45): cold dust or nebular emission in the 12 arcsec W4 beam

explanation: No parallax is detected at G=14 (parallax_snr -0.8) and the astrometry is clean (ruwe 1.01). Together with the blue colour and a position consistent with the northern SMC, this points to a luminous (M_G about -5) hot star there. Its IR excess (Ks-W1 0.7, W1-W2 0.3, W2-W3 0.8) and the factor-of-5 W1/W2 variability fit a Be/B[e] circumstellar disc. The dip is not an occultation: RP dims more than BP (ratio 0.57; z_grey -6, z_dust -16), so a red emitting component faded, most likely disc emission dissipating and then rebuilding over about 200 d. The whole light curve is redder when brighter and agrees across both fields of view. The main alternative is an FSRQ-like AGN, but the blue optical colour and low W1-W2 count against it.

discriminating_test: Plot the G and BP residuals against scan angle and look for a neighbour within 4 arcsec in a deep high-resolution plane survey. A strong scan-angle correlation, or a neighbour, shifts weight to blending. If ZTF or later Gaia data show the star still wandering by a few per cent over hundreds of days, that confirms red-giant variability.

evidence.feature: Red, luminous giant at 6.2 kpc (bp_rp 2.61, G-Ks 4.6, no W3 excess); slow 3.5% wander with abbe 0.38
G differences of 2-5% between FoV transits 106.5 min apart, far above 0.002 errors
BP is bimodal by visit group (~0.90 vs ~1.10, robust sigma 0.14) and phot_bp_rp_excess_factor is 1.57 in a |b|<5 field
Some visit groups show FoV1 systematically brighter than FoV2 (e.g. 684, 691)
ruwe 1.0 and ipd_frac_multi_peak 0: no resolved close companion in G
Colour ratio 15 +/- 610 tells grey, dust and temperature apart not at all; W2 visits flat, with no NEOWISE slope
Kind is a monotonic-ish trend, not discrete dips; no recurrence

explanation: A luminous, reddened giant (G-Ks 4.6, ~6 kpc, M_G around -3, |b|<5) drifting down about 3% over the first ~600 days and then levelling off at ~0.99 looks like ordinary semi-regular or long-secondary-period variability of a giant. The photometry is also clearly crowded. G differs by 2-5% between transits only hours apart (errors ~0.002), BP jumps back and forth between ~0.9 and ~1.1 by visit group (robust sigma 0.14), and the BP/RP excess factor is high. So a neighbour entering the window at some scan angles could have shaped the weak trend (slope_z 4.2, 20 visits). BP and RP depths have huge errors and say nothing about colour. The infrared shows no excess and W2 is flat, which argues against dust.

discriminating_test: Compare the Gaia G, BP and RP epoch trends of nearby stars with similar magnitude and colour on the same scans, or use the longer Gaia DR4 epoch photometry. If the drop is G-only and shared, it is a calibration residual. If RP and BP follow G and the star keeps wandering, it is stellar activity.

evidence.feature: Smooth 0.5% G decline over ~500 d (abbe 0.27, slope_z -4.8) on an otherwise quiet star (sigma_visit 0.1%)
RP depth 0.03 +/- 0.19% vs G depth 0.57 +/- 0.06%; BP unconstrained (ratio 13.6 +/- 81)
fov 1 and fov 2 epochs fall together; no field-of-view offset
ruwe 1.05, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, normal BP/RP excess factor 1.24
ZTF g and r both change by about -0.28% after 2020 and show correlated seasonal 1-2% wandering
Ks, W1, W2 consistent with a K photosphere, no warm excess; NEOWISE change uninformative
Duration 526 d at 0.57% depth would need an enormous, very slow occulter

explanation: The 'dip' is a shallow (0.57%) slow decline in Gaia G over ~2.4 yr: early visits sit near 1.004, later ones near 0.998-0.999, with a partial recovery near day 580. Both fields of view behave alike. The star is a quiet K-type dwarf or subgiant (M_G ~4.8, bp_rp 1.16) with no IR excess, and ZTF shows similar ~0.3-1% seasonal-scale wandering in g and r. The most likely cause is low-level magnetic-activity or spot variability. A residual G-band calibration drift is a strong alternative, because RP shows no matching drop (0.03 +/- 0.19%) and that is hard to get from a real change. A 526-day eclipse or occultation at 0.5% is implausible, and no listed explanation is ruled out.

discriminating_test: Check the NEOWISE/unWISE images to see whether the brightened W1/W2 flux sits on the star's position and is not a red neighbour within 6 arcsec. Then compare calibrated (not median-normalised) PS1/ZTF magnitudes from 2018-2024 with the pre-fade Gaia level, to see whether the optical extinction persisted alongside the IR excess.

evidence.feature: BP/RP depth ratio 1.9+/-0.3 (z_dust 0.65, z_grey 2.95)
W2 tripled and W1 rose ~45% from 2014 visits to post-fade, in step with the G fade; excess colour ~600 K, energy ~ absorbed fraction
AllWISE 2010 photospheric (Ks-W1 -0.1, W1-W2 0.0); no prior IR excess
IR emission appears with the dimming rather than being present throughout
parallax SNR 22 at 1.6 kpc gives M_G ~4-5, a dwarf, and a slow 9% fade
fade coherent in both fields of view, ruwe 1.01, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, normal BP/RP excess factor
neowise_change reports IR fainter inside the window only because the outside median is set by bright post-fade visits

explanation: A smooth Gaia fade (abbe 0.02), about 9% deep by the last visits, is seen in both fields of view and reddened like dust (BP/RP ratio 1.9+/-0.3, not grey). At the same time NEOWISE W1 rose about 45% and W2 about 200% above the pre-fade level, which matches AllWISE's photospheric colours. The W2 excess grows in step with the G depth (about 22x at every epoch). The excess colour points to dust near 600 K carrying about 8-9% of the star's light, which matches the light lost in the optical. The best fit is new warm dust forming close to an otherwise ordinary G/K dwarf (M_G about 4-5), perhaps collisional debris. The pipeline's neowise_change test misleads here: it compares against the bright post-fade visits.

discriminating_test: Regress Gaia epoch G and RP fluxes against scan angle and FOV. Inspect deep, high-resolution plane imaging (for example DECaPS or Pan-STARRS) for a neighbour within about 2 arcsec. If the fade follows how the scan angles were sampled over time rather than the date, it is a blend. A matching slow fade in ZTF r/i PSF photometry would instead favour intrinsic variability.

evidence.feature: ipd_frac_multi_peak = 44 and phot_bp_rp_excess_factor = 2.15 at |b| < 5 deg, G = 19
RP brightens (depth_rp = -0.24 +/- 0.17; late RP 1.17-1.24) while G fades
G jumps of 5-9% within 106 min (e.g. t = 924.85 vs 924.93), well beyond errors
Late FOV1 transits systematically about 4% below FOV2
Smooth-ish trend (abbe 0.41, slope_z -5.96) in a very red (bp_rp 3.55), probably reddened giant
BP depth 0.21 +/- 0.54, colour ratio undefined; no 2MASS/WISE match, no NEOWISE visits
Galactic-plane location and extreme red colour

explanation: This is most likely a blend in a crowded field near the Galactic plane. The source is faint (G=19) and very red. ipd_frac_multi_peak=44 means a second peak shows in nearly half the transits, and the BP/RP excess factor of 2.15 points to contaminated prism windows. The 6.6% G trend is modest (slope_z about 6 from 18 visits), and the late G scatter is driven by jumps within hours: at t=924.85 versus 924.93, flux goes 0.92 to 1.015, about 4.5 sigma. Late FOV1 transits sit about 4% below FOV2. While G fades, RP brightens, reaching 1.17-1.24 at t=924-932. Intrinsic change in a star this red cannot dim G while RP brightens. That points to neighbour flux entering the windows depending on scan angle. A slow variable red giant is the main astrophysical alternative.

discriminating_test: Measure a rotation period and spot amplitude from TESS or ZTF data within a season, and check chromospheric activity (Ca II H&K or H-alpha) in an archival spectrum. A fast, active rotator would confirm that the dimming follows spot coverage; a quiet, slow rotator would point to dust occultation instead.

evidence.feature: Same-epoch FOV pairs agree inside the dip (203.44/203.51, 305.91/305.98, 581.74/581.81)
Smooth ~1% decline in G and BP over the first 2 days (errors ~0.1%): short-timescale intrinsic variability
ZTF fade from t~3150 to 4080 is deeper in g (3-5%) than r (2-3%), so the star dims repeatedly on year timescales and in a chromatic way
NEOWISE W1/W2 unchanged during dip; 1000 K shell predicted +0.26 in W2; grey predicts -0.0115
Irregular depth over 438 d with a return to normal at t=174; no recurrence at fixed depth
W1-W2 = 0, Ks-W3 ~0.3, no IR excess
ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, ruwe 1.06, normal BP/RP excess factor
Absolute G ~5.5-5.9, a main-sequence K star rather than an evolved giant
BP/RP depth ratio 1.01 +/- 0.56 is uninformative between grey, dust and spots

explanation: Most likely a magnetically active K dwarf (M_G about 5.5-5.9 at 400 pc, no IR excess, ruwe 1.06) whose mean brightness tracks spot coverage. The Gaia episode is shallow (1.2%), irregular (back to normal at t=174, deepest about 2% near t=366-425), the same in both fields of view and in BP and RP, with no NEOWISE change (warm shell excluded, grey blocking mildly disfavoured). The star also varies about 1% within two days at the start, and ZTF later shows a longer 2-5% fade that is deeper in g than r (ratio about 1.5), as cool spots predict. For a 440-day crossing the occulter must be far larger than the star, so occultation is contrived.

discriminating_test: Get the longer ZTF r/i and NEOWISE W1/W2 light curves (2018 on) and check for the same slow, chromatic, roughly cyclic variation on hundreds-of-days timescales typical of a semi-regular or long-period variable.

evidence.feature: bp_rp 5.12, G-Ks 6.8, W1-W2 -0.18, flat W1-W4 with no mid-IR excess

explanation: A very red (BP-RP 5.1, G-Ks 6.8), distant source in the Galactic plane with photospheric-looking WISE colours (W1-W2 negative, no W3/W4 excess): most likely a cool, reddened M giant or AGB star. The 'dip' is a smooth decline-and-partial-recovery over ~800 d (Abbe 0.32) seen in G and RP, deeper in G (0.149) than in RP (0.111), as expected for a cooling pulsating giant. NEOWISE W1 fades far less than G (-0.019/yr against -0.068/yr), matching the star-temperature prediction (-0.015) and ruling out grey blocking at ~12 sigma. That fits semi-regular or long-period (or long-secondary-period) variability, not an occulter. BP is too faint to say anything.

discriminating_test: Compare the archival Gaia per-transit, per-CCD AF G fluxes (with window and quality flags) for t=500-923, and those of nearby stars of similar magnitude and colour, against this light curve. A step that is in the archive and tied to window, CCD or calibration flags points to an instrumental cause. A step missing from the archive means it was injected into G alone.

A neighbour cannot explain it either: G's window sits inside the BP/RP windows, and the excess factor (1.22), ipd_frac_multi_peak (0) and ruwe (1.02) all look clean. That leaves a persistent G-only measurement fault or a signal injected into G only. I know of no Gaia artefact that would produce a step this clean, so most of the weight goes to unexplained.

discriminating_test: Run a periodogram of the dense ZTF r photometry (and any TESS sectors) to look for a rotation period of a few days with an amplitude of about 0.5%, and check an activity indicator such as Ca II H&K or X-ray emission. A clear rotation signal would confirm a spotted active star.

explanation: This is not a discrete dip but a smooth secular fade. BP/RP scatter is twice their errors, but the excess factor and ruwe are normal.

discriminating_test: Check the per-CCD G fluxes and the window AL/AC position of the transit at t=877.81. Flux falling across the strip or a truncated window means an artefact. Separately, search ZTF/TESS for a recurring ~14% eclipse a few hours long.

explanation: Most of the 3.4% 'episode' depth comes from one transit (t=877.81, fov 2) at 0.858 in G, with BP and RP also about 15-19% low. Its G error (0.036) is ten times the usual, which means the CCDs disagreed. The transits 106.5 min before and 4 h after (fov 1) are normal. That points to a single-transit artefact: flux lost at a window edge or a truncated window, a CCD problem, or a neighbour's window conflict. A short real eclipse is the main alternative and the other epochs do not rule it out, but it would not explain the inflated CCD scatter. The rest of the episode (about 1-2.5% low at 886 and 924) is within the star's own slow ~1% wander and the 1% offsets between fields of view.

discriminating_test: Measure a rotation period (TESS or ZTF periodogram) and a chromospheric activity index (Ca II H&K or X-ray). A short period with strong activity would confirm spot or activity-cycle variability. As a cross-check, look at Gaia neighbours of similar G and colour for the same trend.

explanation: This is probably a K dwarf (M_G about 6, BP-RP 1.32) with a slow change in its magnetic activity. Over Gaia's 2.7 years it faded by about 1.3%, in all three bands, with redder-than-grey colour (BP/RP 1.63+-0.66). The NEOWISE W1 slope (-0.0016+-0.002/yr) matches the prediction for a cooling star (-0.0014) better than grey blocking (-0.0047). ZTF shows season-to-season changes of 1-2% that do not keep a steady direction, and the fade did not continue after 2020 (g only -0.4%). So the trend is one phase of irregular spot/facula variability on year timescales, not a lasting occultation. There is no infrared excess (W1-W3 = 0) and no sign of a blend (ruwe 1.01, ipd 0, normal BP/RP excess). Leftover Gaia calibration drift remains the main alternative.

Its WISE colours are AGN-like: W1-W2=1.2, W4 detected, and G-W1 of about 4.2 is far too red in the infrared for an F-type photosphere. The 'dip' is a smooth ~0.6 mag fade over ~1000 d (Abbe 0.12) after a brighter phase near day 176. ZTF later shows the source back near its median level, with no clear further fading, which fits damped-random-walk variability rather than an eclipse or occultation. The flat NEOWISE W1 rules out grey blocking. The BP/RP colour is too noisy to use.

discriminating_test: Pull the TESS or ZTF light curve to confirm a short (about 1-3 d) spot-rotation period with about 1-2% amplitude, and check whether its seasonal mean level wanders by several per cent; also compare same-magnitude, same-colour neighbours' Gaia residuals over the first 100 days to test for a calibration offset.

The near-grey ratio (1.1+/-0.6) allows spots, and so does a change in spot coverage over months. An early-mission calibration residual is the main other possibility. No step-like occulter is needed.

explanation: Most likely a quasar/AGN showing ordinary stochastic variability. W1/W2 dip around t~1800-2700, consistent with a delayed dust-echo response of a luminous AGN. A YSO at |b|>20 deg with no measurable parallax is implausible. ruwe 1.02 and ipd 0 argue against a blend.

A broad-line redshifted spectrum, W1-W2 > ~0.6, or proper motion consistent with zero would confirm a quasar. The 'drop' is not a dip with a shape: Gaia G is about 1.15-1.2 in the first 240 d, about 0.83 at 410-427 d, then about 0.97, and both fields of view agree. explanation: The 'trend' is most likely a red-noise fit to the star's own variability, not a secular fade. G scatters about 2.2% from visit to visit, against errors of about 0.3%, in BP and RP as well, and ZTF also shows about 2-3% excess scatter. The light curve does not fall steadily: it is high early, has a minimum near t=645-720 and recovers by t=860. ZTF after 2020 shows no continued fade (-0.5%). The depth is the same in all bands and the BP/RP ratio is uninformative. There is no infrared excess. For M_G of about 3, this is a reddened F/G star somewhat above the main sequence. discriminating_test: Compare per-CCD G fluxes and the along-scan position in the window against time for this source and for nearby stars of similar magnitude and colour on the same transits. Also check whether Gaia DR4 epoch G, BP, RP and XP spectra over 5.5 yr show the G-only trend, with BP and RP still flat.

evidence.feature: Comparing early and late visits: G drops about 3.2%, RP changes about 0.05%, BP rises about 0.7%; a cooling or dusty fade would dim RP by 2-3%
The fade appears equally in fov 1 and fov 2 and is smooth in time, not scattered by scan geometry
ruwe 1.06, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, bp_rp_excess 1.24 is normal for bp_rp 1.31
No band-consistent physical model fits a change seen in G alone (possible non-physical injection)

explanation: Gaia G declines smoothly by about 4.5% over 892 days (slope_z -19.6, abbe 0.06), but BP and RP do not: early-versus-late RP is flat to about 0.5% and BP is flat or slightly brighter. G covers the same wavelengths as BP plus RP, so a change in the star's own light must show up in at least one of them. A grey, dusty or cooling fade of 2-3% in G predicts RP dims about 2-3%, which is ruled out at roughly 5 sigma. That makes a G-only artefact the most likely cause: residual calibration drift, a G-processing problem such as the window or line-spread fit, or background. The fade is seen in both fields of view, the astrometry is clean and the BP/RP excess is normal, so an FoV offset or a blend is less likely. If no instrumental cause fits, the pattern is non-physical (unexplained).

discriminating_test: Periodogram of the dense ZTF r/g (or TESS) photometry for a rotation period of days to weeks with about 1% amplitude, together with a spectrum for chromospheric activity (Ca II H&K or H-alpha emission). An active, rotating K dwarf would confirm spot-cycle variability; a quiet, non-rotating star would shift weight to Gaia calibration or processing.

That makes a blend, a YSO, a giant's variability or spots unlikely. The best explanations are a dusty structure slowly crossing the sightline or a long-term intrinsic change of the star. A residual Gaia trend cannot be ruled out. ZTF is flat afterwards and shows no recovery.

A Ca II H&K activity spectrum would also help.

explanation: Most likely an intrinsic slow fade of an active star, probably a contact binary or fast rotator whose spot coverage grew. Visit means fall smoothly by about 5% over 919 d (abbe 0.35, slope_z -6.2). Within single 106.5-min FoV pairs, G, BP and RP all change together by 5-10% at the same scan angle, so the star varies fast in its own right and the signal does not look like a blend. It is 2.3 sigma off foreground dust, and BP/RP 1.15+/-0.29 also leans against ISM-like dust. There is no IR excess. W1 keeps falling to t~1300 and then recovers, like an activity cycle.

discriminating_test: Run a Lomb-Scargle periodogram on the dense ZTF r light curve (1108 epochs) or a TESS sector to look for a 10-40 d rotation period with ~1% amplitude. Also check a chromospheric activity indicator such as Ca II H&K, H-alpha or X-ray. A coherent rotation signal would confirm spots, and no signal would raise the blend and instrumental options.

explanation: Most likely a spotted, magnetically active K dwarf (M_G about 6, G-Ks 2.1, no IR excess). The 1% 'episode' is not a coherent dip. Both fields of view agree in every pair. The BP/RP ratio (1.29 +/- 1.12) cannot tell grey from reddened dimming. NEOWISE shows no change. BP/RP depth ratio 0.837+-0.149 (z_grey -1.1, z_dust -5.8): grey dimming

ruwe 1.02, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, BP/RP excess 1.24: no sign of a resolved neighbour

explanation: The 107-day Gaia 'episode' is very likely a sampling coincidence: two single-transit dips (t=783, 876), plus another at t=0, each ~10-13% deep, with normal visits between them. RUWE is 1.02, there is no sign of a second source, and there is no IR excess. That pattern points to a short-period detached eclipsing binary, eclipsing about 10% of the time.

explanation: The star fades steadily and greyly by about 2%/yr over roughly 11 years. Gaia G/BP/RP, ZTF g/r (both -6.7% after 2020) and NEOWISE W1 (about 20% over a decade) each show it independently, on an otherwise very quiet reddened A/F star with no infrared excess. Three instruments agreeing rules out most artefacts. Equal g and r fades, plus a W1 fade that matches the optical, rule out spots, cooling of the star and ISM-like dust. The best fit is the slow ingress of a long-period occultation by an extended screen of large grains or optically thick clumps, such as the diffuse edge of a disk around a companion. A sharp-edged body would have to cross the star at about 0.002 km/s, so the screen needs a gradual edge. The extreme linearity keeps unexplained substantial.

Each band also jumps on its own (RP low at 541, 953 and 965 while G is normal), G changes by up to 11% within one 106-min pair, the field is crowded (|b|<5), and the BP/RP excess is raised. Together these hint the deficit lasted for years. No IR excess, so a YSO is unlikely.

The low state at t 650-700 shows up in G, BP and RP, and BP drops more (about 1.4% against 0.7%), which fits cooler spots. ZTF after 2020 is flat, so the fade did not continue. discriminating_test: Take one spectrum to check chromospheric activity (Ca II H&K or H-alpha emission, lithium), and look for a rotation period in TESS or ZTF. A strongly active dwarf makes a few-percent multi-year spot or cycle variation natural. An inactive star would shift weight to a blended variable neighbour or circumstellar dust.

evidence.feature: G fade of 2.5% at ~0.1% errors, consistent between fov 1 and fov 2 transits 106.5 min apart
Smooth multi-year wave in G (pre-fade hump to 1.015, Abbe 0.139, slope -1.1%/yr), not a box-shaped event
BP/RP depth ratio 1.44 +- 0.66: matches star cooling (~1.4-1.5), dust allowed, grey mildly disfavoured

G=15.2 at 730 pc with bp_rp 1.3 implies a dwarf, not a giant

Single-epoch BP drops at t=541.0 and 654.7 (fov 1) absent in G and RP
Early ZTF g (t~1250) ~3.7% low but ZTF r at the same time near 1.0

explanation: Most likely slow intrinsic variability of an active G/K dwarf (M_G ~5-6 at 730 pc), such as changing spot coverage over an activity cycle. The Gaia G curve is a smooth multi-year wave (Abbe 0.14). It rises about 1.5% to t~350, then declines, and steps down to 2.5-3% below median after t~750, with paired fields of view agreeing at 0.1% precision. BP/RP depth ratio 1.44+-0.66 fits a cooling star and also fits dust. ZTF 2018-2025 keeps showing seasonal +-1.5-2% level changes in g and r together, so the star keeps varying and the fade is not a one-off occultation. With no WISE excess (W1-W2 ~ -0.1), a dusty disk or YSO is unlikely. A blended neighbour at low latitude remains possible.

discriminating_test: Get an archival optical spectrum (SDSS/LAMOST/DESI) or check Gaia proper motion: broad emission lines at a cosmological redshift, or proper motion consistent with zero, would confirm a quasar.

evidence.feature: W1-W2 = 0.8, W2-W3 = 3.8 (AGN wedge colours)

explanation: Most likely a quasar/AGN showing ordinary stochastic variability. WISE colours W1-W2 = 0.8 and W2-W3 = 3.8 put it in the AGN region, and the mid-IR is far brighter than any G = 18.9 photosphere with bp_rp 0.79 could give (W3 = 11.0, W4 = 9.1). The parallax is negative (snr -1.3), ruwe is 1.0 and the source is at high galactic latitude, all as expected for an extragalactic point source. The 'dip' is a smooth monotonic fade (abbe 0.08, slope -6.6%/yr, about 12-20% over ~2.7 yr), which fits damped-random-walk quasar variability and is not an occultation. BP/RP are too noisy to constrain colour. The NEOWISE W2 'change' comes from one outlier with a huge error.

discriminating_test: Plot the G epoch residuals against scan angle and look for a neighbour within ~2 arcsec in deeper high-resolution near-IR/optical imaging; if the residuals do not depend on scan angle, also check whether a long-baseline ZTF-r/i or near-IR light curve continues the slow variation (it should if this is a giant).

explanation: A faint (G=18.9), very red (BP-RP 3.5, G-Ks 5.7) source deep in the Galactic plane with negative parallax, most likely a distant reddened giant. A 13-17% G decline over ~2.6 yr with abbe 0.44 is typical long-period/semi-regular giant variability. Crowding is a strong competitor: the BP/RP excess factor of 1.94 is about 7 sigma above expectation, BP is chaotic (a 10x spike in both fields of view at t=957), RUWE is 1.42, G scatter within 106-min pairs is 3-4x the errors, and RP does not follow G (RP depth 0 +/- 0.105; G and RP anticorrelate at several epochs). A bluer neighbour whose share changes with scan angle would move G more than RP. Neither an occultation nor anything exotic is needed.

discriminating_test: Measure the depth in red and near-IR (ZTF i or ATLAS o, plus J/H) through the next predicted event at t~4060-4075 and take radial velocities to check for a 267 d orbit. Small-grain dust predicts a depth that falls steadily with wavelength (only a few per cent in J). A blended or hot-component stellar eclipse would show a different colour signature and a different RV behaviour.

evidence.feature: ZTF g/r dip events spaced ~265-270 d (or multiples) from t~1392 to 3794; predicted events at ~1659 and ~2726 fall in seasonal gaps; Gaia dips at 318.9, 577, 845.6 lie on the same ephemeris; renewed fade at t~4051-4069 matches the next predicted event
Each event lasts ~15-25 d at P~267 d around a main-sequence G/K dwarf (parallax SNR 32, M_G~5.5), so the occulter is ~0.3-0.5 AU across, not a star
Strongly chromatic: ZTF g depth ~12.5% vs r ~6.5% (tau ratio ~2); Gaia at t=318.9 BP 12.2%, G 7.7%, RP 5.1%; at t~577 BP ~4% vs RP ~1.5%
Flat-bottomed events with nearly identical depth over ~8 events and ~7 years, with gradual multi-day ingress and egress
No near-IR excess (Ks-W1 ~0, W1-W2 ~-0.1), and high galactic latitude at ~1 kpc
W3=12.5 vs W1=13.8 (W1-W3~1.3 mag): a possible warm (~300 K) excess, as expected for dust ~1 AU from a G dwarf; could also be a marginal W3 detection
The t~577 dip spans both fields of view and 10 transits in G, BP and RP, and is seen independently by ZTF in two bands at the same phase
ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, ruwe 1.05, normal BP/RP excess factor 1.22; ZTF PSF depth matches the Gaia depth
Star is quiet outside the events (Gaia G robust sigma 0.28%, abbe ~1.1, no trend)

explanation: The dips repeat at a strict period of about 267 d. ZTF shows about 8 events (t~1392, 1925, 2190, ~2455, 2990, 3256, 3523, 3794), and the predicted ones at ~1659 and ~2726 fall in data gaps. Each lasts 15-25 d with a flat bottom at ~12.5% in g and ~6.5% in r. The Gaia dips (318.9, 577, 845-871) fit the same ephemeris, with BP ~2.4x deeper than RP, and ZTF fades again near t~4060 as predicted. The host is a G/K dwarf (M_G~5.5 at 960 pc). A stellar eclipse of a dwarf at P=267 d would last ~1 d, so the occulter must be ~0.3-0.5 AU across and made of small dusty grains. The best fit is a circumsecondary disk around a faint companion at ~1 AU, which also fits the possible ~300 K W3 excess.

discriminating_test: Run a season-by-season periodogram on the ZTF r/g (or TESS) photometry to confirm the ~1.85 d rotation period and check that its amplitude anticorrelates with the mean brightness level (spot-cycle signature); a single low-resolution spectrum showing Ca II H&K/H-alpha emission would also confirm an active star.

evidence.feature: Smooth monotonic G trend -1.26%/yr (slope_z -6.28, abbe 0.24) over 28 visits, mirrored in RP (depth 0.034+-0.013) and BP
Coherent ~1.85 d, ~1-2% periodic modulation in dense Gaia transit runs (t 104-109, 487-492), present in both FoVs, amplitude changing between runs
ZTF g and r fainter in 2018-2019 than after 2020 (+2.0% g, +2.25% r), later slow few-percent wanders
No systematic offset between FoV 1 and FoV 2 epochs in G
ruwe 0.982, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, phot_bp_rp_excess_factor 1.25 normal for bp_rp 1.23
W1-W2 = 0.0, W4 only an upper limit: no hot inner-disk dust
Multi-year smooth fade rather than a discrete eclipse; recurrence not applicable
W3 12.7 (W1-W3 ~1.5) hints at warm excess but is likely a low-SNR/confused detection at |b| 10-15 deg
BP/RP depth ratio 0.54 +- 0.72 uninformative (z_grey -0.63, z_dust -1.6)
ZTF brightenings clustered at season edges (high airmass) and large intra-night scatter at t~1484.7

explanation: The detected 'dip' is a smooth ~3% G fade over 921 d (slope_z -6.3, abbe 0.24), also seen in RP (~3-4%) and noisily in BP, with no FoV1/FoV2 offset and clean astrometry (ruwe 0.98, no multi-peak, normal BP/RP excess). The dense Gaia runs at t~104-109 and ~487-492 show a coherent ~1.85 d, 1-2% modulation in both fields of view, marking a rapidly rotating spotted G/K star (or synchronised active binary). ZTF finds the star still faint in 2018-19 and ~2% brighter after 2020, then further slow few-percent wanders: a multi-year mean-level change typical of spot-coverage/activity cycles. Colour ratio is unconstrained; W1-W2=0 argues against inner-disk dust. Residual chance of Gaia calibration drift or a slow disk occultation.

discriminating_test: ATLAS or ASAS-SN forced photometry for 2015-2018. It would confirm the reddened ~6% fade independently of Gaia calibration and show when the star recovered (a smooth egress means an occultation; no fade there means a Gaia artefact or injection).

evidence.feature: Smooth monotonic G decline 1.015 to 0.951 over 921 d, abbe 0.1, slope_z -15
BP/RP depth ratio 1.56 +- 0.29 (z_dust -0.48, z_grey 1.95)
FoV 1 and 2 pairs agree throughout the fade
ruwe 1.01, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, bp_rp excess 1.22 normal for colour
NEOWISE W2 change -0.058+-0.027 excludes 300K/1000K re-emitting shells; W1-W2 ~0, no IR excess
sigma_visit 0.34%: no rotational modulation; ZTF flat to ~1% over 2018-2025
Multi-year ingress implies transverse speed far too slow for a sharp-edged body
Early ZTF g points (t~1300-1400) ~3% low, then normal: possible egress
M_G ~4.2-4.7 at 1500 pc: dwarf/subgiant, not an evolved or R CrB star

explanation: Smooth, monotonic ~6% fade over the whole Gaia baseline (abbe 0.1, -2.4%/yr), matched between fields of view and coherent in G, BP, RP. BP/RP depth ratio 1.56+-0.29 fits small-grain dust (1.7); grey is disfavoured at ~2 sigma. Clean source (ruwe 1.01, ipd 0, normal excess factor) argues against blending. No IR excess, and NEOWISE rules out warm re-emission (300K and 1000K shells), so the absorber is confined to the sightline. ZTF 2018-2025 is flat to ~1%, with possibly low g points near t~1300-1400, which points to a one-off multi-year episode rather than an activity cycle. A sharp-edged eclipser cannot take years to ingress. A diffuse dusty disk around a wide companion crossing the star fits best.

discriminating_test: Run a Lomb-Scargle period search on the 192 ZTF g and 192 ZTF r epochs over 0.02-0.5 d. A coherent ~0.05 d signal with a g/r amplitude ratio of about 1.4-1.6 would confirm SX Phe/delta Sct pulsation. A ~0.25 d double-wave with equal amplitudes would point to a contact binary. No signal would point back to a Gaia field-of-view calibration artefact.

evidence.feature: Within each Gaia transit group, flux alternates by field of view (e.g. 0.961/1.049/0.963/1.043) with pair sums constant near 2.01; sign flips between groups and some groups are near the mean (319, 701 d)
Pattern tied to the 106.5 min field-of-view spacing
ZTF robust scatter well above errors (g 0.060 vs 0.027, r 0.041 vs 0.024), larger in g than r
BP and RP mostly follow the G sign in high-amplitude groups (542, 681, 867, 889 d); BP excess slightly above RP
Detected fade depends on the single last G transit at 917.8 d (0.955); paired visits at 867.8 and 889.1 d have normal sums; s_fade only -1.18
RP at 917.8 d = 1.028 +/- 0.030; BP and RP change depths consistent with zero
ZTF after 2020 shows no lasting change (g -0.002, r -0.018)
ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, ruwe 1.09, normal BP/RP excess factor 1.18
W1-W2 about 0.2, no infrared excess, high galactic latitude, NEOWISE change only 1.7 sigma from one visit

explanation: This F-colour, distant star varies by about +/-4-5% in G on a short timescale. In every transit group, consecutive transits 106.5 and 253.5 min apart move in opposite directions around a constant mean (pair sums about 2.01). The sign flips between groups, and some groups sit near the mean, which is what a ~0.05 d SX Phe/delta Sct pulsation sampled by the scanning law would give. BP and RP mostly follow G. ZTF shows its own excess scatter, larger in g than in r. The flagged fade rests on one final single transit (0.955) caught near minimum. The paired visits at 868 and 889 d show no deficit, RP at 918 d is not faint, and ZTF after 2020 shows no lasting change. A field-of-view offset or a contact binary are the main alternatives.

discriminating_test: Run a period search on the ZTF g and r epochs and phase-fold them. If the ~0.5-depth dips recur at one strict period with a stable depth, and Gaia's episode epochs (548-784) fall at eclipse or ellipsoidal-minimum phases, the eclipsing-binary explanation is confirmed.

evidence.feature: ZTF g/r: dozens of short dips reaching a consistent floor near 0.45-0.5 flux in both bands, no bright outliers
ZTF r fast sequences (e.g. t~2154.6 smooth minimum 0.49; t~2441.25 and 2529.58 recovering 0.50->0.60 in ~10 min)
Gaia dims outside the episode (t=224.7, 885.6, 972.5/972.75) with normal fov-pair partners 106.5 min apart

Ks-W1 = 0, W1-W2 = 0, no NEOWISE change: no warm dust
ruwe 1.0, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, normal BP/RP excess; ZTF PSF photometry shows the same dips
Some dims appear in one field of view only

explanation: This looks like a short-period eclipsing binary, and the 236-day 'episode' is an artefact of Gaia's sparse sampling. ZTF g and r (2 arcsec PSF photometry) show many short, nearly grey dips that bottom out at a repeatable floor of about 0.45-0.5. Several fast-cadence sequences trace smooth minima and egresses within tens of minutes. The flux distribution has only a faint tail (no bright excursions), which points to eclipses rather than pulsation. Gaia catches the same thing: values of 0.57 and 0.83 six hours apart on day 972 (primary and secondary?), with normal epochs 106.5 min apart, and dims outside the episode at days 224 and 885. The episode visits sit at about 0.92 with abbe 0.90, i.e. noise-like, so they are not a smooth fade. There is no IR excess.

discriminating_test: Take one low-resolution optical spectrum now and compare it with any archival spectrum, or with pre-Gaia SDSS/PS1 colours. If the spectral type and TiO band strengths are unchanged and the continuum is simply more reddened, a dust screen is crossing the line of sight. If the star now has a later spectral type, it is cooling intrinsically. Pre-Gaia photometry would also show when the fade began.

evidence.feature: Smooth monotonic fade coherent in Gaia G, BP, RP (both fov) and continuing in ZTF g/r/i to t~4000 d; no steps at ZTF field/CCD boundaries
colour_of_change ratio_bp_over_rp 2.19+/-0.52 (z_grey 2.26, z_dust 0.93); ZTF fade rates roughly g:r:i = 0.10:0.065:0.045 mag/yr, ISM-dust-like or slightly steeper
neowise_change W1 +0.008+/-0.024 vs pred_grey -0.055 and pred_star_temperature -0.016; late W1 visits only ~5% below early ones while ZTF g dropped ~50%
M_G ~7.3, bp_rp 1.57, ~850 pc above the plane: old main-sequence field dwarf, not a giant or young star
Short-timescale quiet: G scatter ~0.5% across the dense t=35-41 d sequence; no periodicity, single ongoing episode with no recurrence
Parallax SNR 15, W1-W2 ~ -0.1, ruwe 1.07, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, normal BP/RP excess
Same fade in PSF photometry (ZTF ~2 arcsec) and Gaia windows; no scan-angle or fov dependence

explanation: A quiet K7/M0 dwarf (M_G about 7.3, 960 pc, |b| 60-65 deg) fades smoothly and monotonically through the whole Gaia span (G -4.4%/yr, slope_z -34, abbe 0.025). ZTF shows the fade continuing for about 7 more years: g fell about 50%, r about 37%, i about 26%. The BP/RP ratio of 2.2+/-0.5 and the g>r>i fades look like ISM-like dust, not grey blocking (z_grey 2.3). W1/W2 stay nearly flat, which fits dust in front better than grey blocking or a cooling star. The fade appears in every band, both fields of view and two independent surveys, so it is not instrumental. Best guess: a dust screen, such as a disk edge, slowly crossing the line of sight. Such a screen is unusual for an old field dwarf, so unexplained keeps a large share.

discriminating_test: Check whether ZTF g/r photometry from 2018 onward continues the fade (and whether it reddens), and whether Gaia stars of similar magnitude and colour in the same field show the same residual slope (which would point to calibration).

evidence.feature: Smooth monotonic G trend of 1.6% over 995 d, Abbe 0.36, no recurrence

FoV 1 and FoV 2 epochs fade together

explanation: The detected 'dip' is a slow, smooth fade of about 1.6% in G across 995 days (-0.6%/yr, slope_z -6.4, Abbe 0.36). Both fields of view fade together, so an FoV offset is unlikely. ruwe 1.02 and ipd_frac_multi_peak 0 argue against a blend, and the 1.6% amplitude is ordinary. The BP and RP depths are pure noise (ratio -0.5 +/- 2.5), so colour cannot separate grey, dust or temperature, and there are no WISE, NEOWISE or ZTF data to test anything. A percent-level change over years in a G=17, roughly solar-type, mildly reddened dwarf is most plausibly a magnetic activity cycle or other slow stellar variability, or a residual magnitude- or colour-dependent calibration drift at the 1% level. The packet cannot tell these apart.

discriminating_test: Compare Gaia G epoch residuals of nearby stars of similar magnitude and colour (and of the same scan/CCD rows) over days 750-900. A matching ~1 mmag deficit would make the dip instrumental; per-CCD G photometry for the three dip visits would show whether one CCD or one window position drives it.

Calibration drift removal applied; 1 mmag residual trends are at the level of photometric systematics for G~15.4
BP/RP depths -0.0003 +/- 0.0067 and -0.0012 +/- 0.0055: no colour information
ruwe 1.03, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, bp_rp excess 1.2: no sign of a neighbour or companion
abbe 0.79, slope_z 1.25, s_fade 2.0: no coherent slow fade
G robust_sigma 0.0023 vs median error 0.0018: slight excess scatter, possible low-level intrinsic variability
