evidence.feature: bp_rp 5.97, Ks 4.03, W1 3.49, W3/W4 excess: dusty cool giant
Repeated broad minima in Gaia G (t~540-558 and t~919-931) and maxima between; robust_sigma 0.13
ZTF r quasi-periodic large-amplitude cycles (~380-390 d), changing amplitude, up to factor ~3
BP/RP depth ratio 1.93 +/- 1.91, BP amplitude much larger than RP over the whole light curve
Both fields of view agree within each visit during the dip
At t=507 RP is 1.057 while G is 0.84; ipd_frac_multi_peak 2, bp_rp_excess 1.99, crowded plane field
No NEOWISE visits inside the dip, so the IR cannot test dust against temperature

explanation: This is an extremely red (BP-RP 5.97, G-Ks 7.7), IR-bright source in the Galactic plane with mid-IR excess (W3, W4). That points to a dusty, probably reddened AGB star. The whole light curve varies a lot (robust sigma 0.13 in G, 0.35 in BP). The Gaia 'episode' at t~507-558 is one minimum among several (another at t~919-931, about 374 d later), with maxima in between. ZTF r shows large seasonal swings (0.73 to 2.18), with peaks roughly every ~380-390 d and changing amplitude, which is typical of a semi-regular or Mira-like pulsator. The dips are deeper in BP than in RP, which fits the cooler star at minimum light. Pulsation explains the dip without anything else.

discriminating_test: Look at the per-transit G fluxes (AF CCD level), window class and scan angle for epochs before and after day ~700, in Gaia DR4 epoch data. Also compare G with the integrated BP+RP spectrum flux for each transit. A G-only step that tracks window class or scan angle would confirm an instrumental cause.

evidence.feature: G depth 0.0168+/-0.0010 vs BP -0.0009+/-0.0037 and RP 0.0068+/-0.0045: G fades more than both BP and RP, impossible for a real flux change
Fade present in both fov 1 and fov 2 epochs after day 732
Abrupt step (abbe 0.089) then flat plateau near 0.983-0.985, no recurrence
ruwe 0.975, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, BP/RP excess 1.21 normal for bp_rp 0.9
Photospheric Ks-W1-W2, W3/W4 upper limits, NEOWISE W1/W2 change consistent with zero, 1000 K shell excluded
ZTF 2018-2024 quiet, only ~0.5% higher after 2020 in g and r
BP scatter (1.8%) twice its quoted errors, but BP mean during fade is +0.3%

explanation: A step-like G fade of 1.7% starts around day 700-730 and lasts to the last visit, seen in both fields of view (abbe 0.09). BP shows no change (-0.09+/-0.37%) and RP only 0.7+/-0.45%. Because G covers the BP plus RP passbands, any real change in the source's flux must show in BP or RP at a similar depth. G exceeds their combined change by about 4 sigma, so the fade is most likely a G-only instrumental artefact. Candidates are a calibration or window-class offset (G=16 sits at a window-class boundary) or processing, not occultation or stellar variability. RUWE, ipd_frac_multi_peak and the excess factor are all clean, which weakens blending. There is no IR excess and ZTF stays quiet. Some unexplained probability is kept for an unphysical G-only signal.

discriminating_test: Plot the G epochs against scan angle and check the Gaia catalogue for neighbours within ~3 arcsec. If the low transits (t~130, 896, 928) share a scan-angle range along which a neighbour lies, or their windows were truncated, the dips are a blend artefact. If the low transits show no scan-angle pattern, ZTF r/i photometry would test for a real fade or dipping.

evidence.feature: repeat period 31.8 d, close to half the 63 d scanning-law precession, from only 23 visits
at P=31.8 d the epoch t=34.38 (G 0.999) falls within ~0.2 d of the dip phase yet is normal; implied eclipse shape inconsistent (0.873 then 1.005 a fraction of a day later in phase)
RP in the low-G transits averages ~0.97 vs G ~0.92; RP depth -0.007 +/- 0.058, a shallower response than a real dimming of a red star predicts (~2 sigma)
phot_bp_rp_excess_factor 1.66 at bp_rp 3.07, |b| 0-5 deg, G 18.8, BP robust sigma 0.36 and RP robust sigma 0.053 (twice its errors)
G transits at t=130.16 and 130.23 missing while BP/RP exist, during the t~130 dip (window conflict or truncation in a crowded field)
fov1 fainter than fov2 by ~2-4% in most transit pairs (130? no; 229, 592, 680, 896); the deepest end-of-span point (928) is a single fov1 transit
t~130 dip of 8-12% seen in both FoV transits 106 min apart and gone 6.5 d later: not a single-transit cosmic ray, could be a dust dip
negative parallax (snr -0.68) and G-Ks 5.1: distant reddened giant or luminous young star; no WISE photometry to test for IR excess

explanation: The most likely cause is a crowding artefact in G. The source is faint (G=18.8), very red and at |b|<5 deg, and its BP/RP excess (1.66, about 2 sigma above what its colour predicts) points to a neighbour inside the larger BP/RP windows. The dips are driven by G: RP in the same transits is only about 3% low on average, against about 8% in G, and BP is unusable. The low G points come as FoV pairs at the same scan angle (t~130 and t~896) plus one transit (t=928). G is missing at t=130.16 and 130.23 although BP and RP exist there. fov1 runs about 2% fainter in pairs, and the 31.8 d repeat is about half the 63 d precession period. Without IR or later photometry, a real fade of a reddened giant or a young star cannot be ruled out.

discriminating_test: Check quasar catalogues (e.g. SDSS spectroscopic or Milliquas) or take a spectrum for broad emission lines and redshift; also check whether ZTF g/r over 2018+ shows continued damped-random-walk variability rather than a stable baseline.

evidence.feature: parallax_snr -0.1 at G=20.2, high galactic latitude
blue colour bp_rp 0.553, typical of quasars
smooth aperiodic wander: abbe 0.151, levels 0.70-1.20 including bright states well above median after the dip
dip and surrounding levels agree between fov 1 and fov 2 pairs
BP depth 0.40+-0.11 deeper than G 0.245 (chromatic, bluer when brighter)
phot_bp_rp_excess_factor 1.48, elevated for this colour (host galaxy or extended emission)
no 2MASS/WISE match; faint source with very noisy BP/RP outliers

explanation: Most likely a quasar showing stochastic red-noise variability. The source is faint (G=20.2) and blue (BP-RP 0.55), sits at high galactic latitude, and its parallax is consistent with zero (SNR -0.1). Its BP/RP excess factor of 1.48 is high for its colour. The G light curve wanders smoothly between 0.70 and 1.20 (abbe 0.15, robust sigma 0.18), with a bright phase at 0.83-1.2 after the dip, so the 262-day 'dip' is just one low state in continuous aperiodic variability. It is not a discrete event on a stable baseline. Both fields of view agree, which rules out an FoV offset. BP dims more than G, consistent with quasars being bluer when brighter. The 595 d 'repeat' is a red-noise alias and gets no eclipse-period support.

discriminating_test: Inspect per-CCD G fluxes, scan angles and window positions for the low transits at 322.8, 547.34 and 646.4 d (and compare same-magnitude neighbours at those times). A single-CCD or window-edge flux loss, or a shared dip, would settle it as instrumental; a consistent drop on all CCDs would favour a real short event.

evidence.feature: Visits inside the episode at 374 d (5 transits, mean ~1.0015) and 441 d (~1.002) are at baseline, contradicting a sustained 0.5% dimming
Deficit driven by a few isolated low transits; 547.34 d G at 0.981 (fov 2) while the transit 0.18 d later is 0.996 and BP/RP at 547.34 are 1.011/1.015
Colour of change: BP depth -0.024+/-0.015, RP -0.014+/-0.015 (both slightly brighter, consistent with zero), ratio undefined
Flagged by 'repeat' at 107 d with only 20 visits; abbe 0.83 and slope_z 0.27 indicate essentially noise-like visit series
G scatter within the 69-74 d cluster (~0.99-1.017) somewhat exceeds quoted errors; bp_rp 1.56 at ~1 kpc implies a K dwarf that may have low-level spot variability
ZTF g/r show no level change (-0.6%, -0.07%) and symmetric outlier counts; NEOWISE W1/W2 changes consistent with zero; no IR excess (Ks-W1 0.2)
ruwe 0.99, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, BP/RP excess 1.27 near normal for this colour, but |b| 5-10 deg and BP/RP scatter about 2x errors

explanation: The 'episode' is a marginal 0.48% mean deficit built from a few low single or double transits (322.8, 547.3, 646.4 d; each ~2-3.5 sigma on 0.3-0.5% per-transit errors). Visits inside it (374, 441 d) sit at or above baseline, so it is not a coherent dimming. The flag came from a 'repeat' search on only 20 visits, where many trials make false alarms likely. BP and RP show no matching dip (both slightly brighter, within errors). The 547.3 G low has no RP counterpart, which points to a G-only transit artefact. ZTF and NEOWISE show nothing. Most likely this is noise, single-transit artefacts or calibration residuals, possibly mixed with low-level spot variability of this faint K dwarf. No real occultation is indicated.

discriminating_test: Check for H-alpha emission, either from the IPHAS/VPHAS+ r-Halpha colour or from one low-resolution spectrum. Emission whose equivalent width changes alongside the ZTF brightening would confirm a Be-disk cause. Its absence would shift weight to an irregular supergiant or a YSO.

evidence.feature: BP/RP depth ratio 0.634+-0.201 (RP fades more than BP; z_dust -5.32)
Bluer-when-fainter colour, about 3.8 sigma below the ~1.4 expected for a cooling star
IR excess: Ks-W1 0.3, W1-W2 0.2, W1-W4 1.73 mag on a luminous hot star at low Galactic latitude
Smooth monotonic Gaia decline (abbe 0.152, slope_z -12.1, -1.74%/yr) in G, BP and RP after drift removal
ZTF faint in 2018-19, then brightens around t~1780-1820, more in r (+4.7% after 2020) than in g (+1.6%): independent confirmation, redder when brighter
Few-per-cent stochastic ZTF variations on 100-300 d timescales that do not repeat season to season
ruwe 0.91, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, normal BP/RP excess; fades are not tied to field of view
Within-pair FoV1/FoV2 differences of ~1% and single-band RP outlier at t=811.4
One-night ZTF g and r drops to ~0.25 at t~3195 with normal epochs around them, outside the detected dip; likely a bad-frame artefact

explanation: Most likely a Be star (or similar hot emission-line star) whose circumstellar disk is fading. At 3.8 kpc in the Galactic plane, G=12.6 makes it a luminous, reddened hot star. It has a near- and mid-IR excess (Ks-W1 0.3, W1-W2 0.2, W1-W4 1.7). The Gaia fade is smooth (abbe 0.15) over about 2.5 yr and appears in all three bands, but it is bluer when fainter: BP/RP depth ratio 0.63+-0.20 rules out interstellar-like dust (z=-5.3) and also a cooling star (about 1.4). ZTF then sees the star faint in 2018-19, followed by a recovery that is larger in r (~6%) than g (~2%), so redder when brighter, plus stochastic variations of a few per cent. That pattern is what disk free-free emission building and decaying produces. It is not eclipses or calibration drift.

discriminating_test: Plot the per-transit G and BP fluxes against Gaia scan angle and check deeper imaging (or Gaia neighbours) within ~2 arcsec for a fainter, bluer source; flux tracking scan angle confirms the blend.

evidence.feature: G elevated 10-23% only in first 8 epochs (t 0-213 d), flat ~0.97-1.0 after; trend is a step, abbe 0.54
RP depth -0.053+/-0.098 vs G 0.187+/-0.047; RP early mean ~0.98 vs late ~1.00 for a very red star whose G light is mostly RP-band
BP wildly erratic (0.2 to 4.4, robust sigma 0.54) and high in the same early epochs as G
phot_bp_rp_excess_factor 2.08, well above the ~1.5 expected for BP-RP 3.35; |b| 0-5 deg crowded field
RP and G differ by ~7-8% between fields of view 106.5 min apart (e.g. t=762, 942, 183)
ruwe 1.02 and ipd_frac_multi_peak 0: no close resolved companion, so the neighbour must sit at ~1-2 arcsec, in the window but not a double peak
ZTF r: -0.06 change after 2020 with +0.02/yr slope, scatter close to errors; no continued fade
Very red (BP-RP 3.35, G-Ks 6.1), faint, in the plane: likely reddened giant that may vary at a low level

explanation: The 'trend' is not a smooth fade. G sits 10-23% high in the first eight epochs (t<213 d, both fields of view) and is flat near 1.0 afterwards. RP, which carries most of the light of a star this red (BP-RP 3.35), does not follow (depth -0.05+/-0.10; early RP mean slightly below late), while BP is erratic (0.2-4.4) and highest in the same early epochs. A faint, bluer neighbour falling inside the windows at the early scan angles would add ~15% in G, a lot in the faint BP, and only a few per cent in the bright RP. phot_bp_rp_excess_factor 2.08 (strong excess for this colour) at |b|<5 deg confirms contamination. ZTF r shows no continued fade. A low-amplitude red-giant variable is the main alternative.

discriminating_test: Get absolutely calibrated photometry that bridges 2017-2019 (Gaia DR4 epochs running to 2020, or ATLAS/Pan-STARRS on a fixed zero point) to see whether and how the star recovered. A gradual egress mirroring the ingress points to a dust structure. A level tied to a processing or scan-angle change points to an instrumental cause. Check the Gaia scan angles for the same epochs.

evidence.feature: Smooth ~120 d ingress then flat plateau at -6.5% for >=430 d to the last visit (abbe 0.046, s_fade 26.2)
Fields of view 1 and 2 give the same level both before and during the fade
Fade appears in G, BP and RP, coherent over 22 visits, not a single epoch or band
BP depth 0.075+-0.017 vs RP 0.026+-0.009 (ratio 2.9+-1.2, z_grey 1.6, RP well below G): chromatic, dust- or temperature-like
ZTF 2018-2025 flat (g -0.3%, r +0.03%), robust sigma about equal to errors: star otherwise quiet
Quiet star with no irregular dips in Gaia or ZTF
ruwe 1.02, ipd_frac_multi_peak 1, bp_rp_excess 1.24 (mild): no close neighbour
Low galactic latitude, no WISE match, ZTF bright outliers near season edges suggest a crowded field
M_G about 3-5 at 2.6 kpc with bp_rp 1.16, G-Ks 1.8: ordinary F/G/K dwarf, not a giant, B star or R CrB
No WISE/NEOWISE data, so no IR-excess or energy-budget test

explanation: Gaia G declines smoothly over ~120 d (days ~380-490) to a flat level ~6.5% fainter, which lasts at least 430 d to the last visit. Both fields of view show it, and so do BP and RP. The dimming is chromatic (BP ~7.5%, RP ~2.6%, grey disfavoured), as small-grain dust would make it. A stellar or planetary eclipse cannot last this long with a flat bottom: it would need a sub-km/s speed. The star looks like an ordinary reddened F/G dwarf and is otherwise quiet in Gaia and in ZTF 2018-2025, which argues against spots, pulsation or YSO activity. Best fit: an optically thin, diffuse-edged dust structure (a disk) crossing the star. A Gaia processing or crowding artefact in this low-latitude field cannot be ruled out, because the packet has no scan-angle or IR data.

discriminating_test: Run a periodogram on a TESS sector (or dense ZTF) to look for a rotation period of a few to tens of days with about 1% amplitude and flares, and check for Ca II H&K or H-alpha emission. Either would confirm an active, spotted K dwarf whose spot coverage explains the fade.

evidence.feature: Same-size rises and falls elsewhere (+0.8% in 12 d at days 621-633, -0.9% at day 203), robust_sigma 0.52%
Fade seen in both fov 1 and 2 and in G, BP and RP; ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, normal bp_rp_excess, ruwe 1.04
BP/RP depth ratio 1.63+-0.56 (z_grey 1.14, z_dust -0.12)
NEOWISE W1 change -0.59+-0.81% vs star-temperature prediction -0.45%, grey -1.46%
Flat fade of 100 days or more at 1.4% depth implies a crossing speed of about 0.1 km/s for a stellar-size occulter
No IR excess (Ks 12.2, W1 12.1, W2 12.2, W3 12.5); 1000 K shell excluded
Fade lasts to the last Gaia visit; ZTF per-field normalisation cannot show whether it persisted
ZTF season-to-season level changes of 1-2% (high near days 2473-2503, low near 2821-2849 and 3265-3487)

explanation: A main-sequence K dwarf (M_G about 6.2, no IR excess, ruwe 1.04) that is itself variable at the 0.5-1% level, with smooth red-noise-like changes (abbe 0.32), rises and falls of 0.4-0.9% within 10-15 days (days 304-314, 459-474, 621-633), an earlier 0.9% dip at day 203, and season-to-season ZTF level changes of 1-2%. The detected 1.46% fade starting between days 840 and 855 is the largest of these excursions, but it is not different in kind. It appears in both fields of view and in G, BP and RP, with BP/RP 1.63+-0.56 and W1 -0.6+-0.8%, which fits a star getting cooler (more spot coverage). It is too long and flat for an eclipse (it would need about 0.1 km/s). Likely an episode of spot or activity variability.

discriminating_test: Run a period search on the dense ZTF r/g data to confirm a rotation period of hours to a day, and check whether the modulation amplitude follows the mean level. Also look for an eROSITA/ROSAT X-ray detection or H-alpha/Ca II emission in an archival (e.g. LAMOST) spectrum as evidence of strong activity.

evidence.feature: Smooth multi-year fade of about 5-8% (abbe 0.234), followed by a partial recovery
Variations of 4-6% within hours (e.g. t=625.5-625.8, 988.7-989.1), coherent in G, BP and RP and seen in ZTF r over about 3 h
ZTF g has 30 epochs above 3 sigma against 17 in r; single bright points of 15-20%
BP/RP depth ratio 1.77±0.47: non-grey at 1.65 sigma, consistent with cooling or dust
NEOWISE: no W1/W2 brightening (1000 K shell excluded); grey blocking excluded; W1 fell about 2% within the Gaia span
W1-W2 = 0.0 and Ks-W1 = 0.3: no inner-disk excess
ruwe 1.01 and a normal BP/RP excess factor; shared calibration drift already removed
Absolute G about 5.8 minus extinction, which rules out a giant
Low galactic latitude field, where crowding and residual Gaia trends are possible

explanation: Most likely a magnetically active, spotted (reddened K/G) dwarf with a slow change in spot coverage, like an activity cycle. The detected 'dip' is a smooth decline of about 8% over roughly 850 d (abbe 0.23, slope_z -8) with a slight recovery at the end. The star also varies by about 5% within hours. That fast variation is coherent in G, BP and RP and shows up again in dense ZTF sampling. ZTF g also has bluish upward outliers that look like flares, and the slow wandering of a few per cent continues through later years. The colour ratio of 1.77±0.47 is non-grey and fits spots or a cooling star. W1 dimmed by about 2% during the Gaia span (W1/G about 0.3), which matches a temperature change better than grey blocking or dust in front.

discriminating_test: Run a 0.5-30 d period search on the dense ZTF/TESS data and measure ZTF g-r against brightness in same-night pairs. A few-day rotation period with a spot-like colour slope would confirm activity. No period and a colour slope matching interstellar reddening would favour variable circumstellar extinction (YSO).

evidence.feature: G fades and recovers on 100-250 d timescales (abbe 0.37, s_rep period 248 d) rather than following one straight trend
ZTF g and r, in other years, show 5-10% multi-year swings (low 2018-19, high after t~2750)
Both fields of view agree within each pair and RP dips at the same epochs (416-442, 678-695)
ruwe 1.03, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, corrected BP/RP excess about 0
BP/RP depth ratio 0.81 +/- 0.79, consistent with grey, dust or a temperature change
W3=11.6, W4=8.97 near detection limits in the Galactic plane, with W1-W2=-0.4 and Ks-W1=0.2 (no hot inner-disk excess)
Absolute magnitude places the star on the main sequence, not among giants or B stars
Step of about 5% in ZTF g and r across the t~2620-2750 season gap; ZTF normalises each field and CCD separately

explanation: A reddened dwarf (M_G about 6.8 before extinction, 1.2 kpc, in the Galactic plane) that varies slowly and irregularly at the 5-10% level. The Gaia 'trend' is not monotonic: it fades in episodes near t~430, ~695 and ~900 and recovers in between. Paired fields of view agree, and RP tracks G. ZTF independently shows the same amplitude in later years (low in 2018-19, about 1.05 by 2022-25). So this is long-term variability of the star itself, most likely changing spot coverage or an activity cycle in a young active star. Variable extinction around a YSO is the next option. The faint W3/W4 'excess' combined with a blue W1-W2 looks like contamination from Galactic-plane nebulosity, not a disk. The colour ratio is too uncertain to separate these options.

discriminating_test: Compare calibrated (not median-normalised) ZTF/Pan-STARRS magnitudes from 2018 onward, and the Gaia G trend of neighbouring stars of similar magnitude in the same field, with the star's early and late Gaia G level. That would show whether the fade is real and persists or recovers, or is a Gaia crowding/processing drift.

evidence.feature: Smooth monotonic G decline over 922 d (abbe 0.215, slope_z -6.8), accelerating at the end
Late faint G epochs in both fov 1 and fov 2 (866, 894 x2, 922)
BP/RP robust_sigma 0.069 vs errors 0.016-0.028 at |b| 0-5 deg; colour ratio meaningless (-0.26 +/- 0.48)
ruwe 0.99, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0: no close resolved neighbour or astrometric companion
Gradual pre-dip trend rather than a sharp ingress; 55 d faint state with no recovery seen
ZTF 2018-2025 quiet (r robust_sigma 0.027 ~ errors), only -0.9% change after 2020
No WISE detections, so dust re-emission and IR excess cannot be tested
Inferred M_G ~4-5 after plausible extinction: a dwarf, not an evolved star

explanation: G shows a smooth, accelerating secular fade rather than a discrete dip: about 1.007 near t~200, 0.997 near 540, 0.992 near 700, then 0.965 at 866-922 (abbe 0.22, slope -1.6%/yr, z=-6.8), seen in both fields of view, with the star otherwise quiet. BP and RP are dominated by crowding scatter (about 7% against 2-3% errors, |b|<5 deg), so the colour is unconstrained, and there is no WISE photometry to test for dust. The likeliest single cause is long-term activity/spot evolution on a reddened K-type dwarf at 1.7 kpc. A Gaia crowding/processing drift in a dense field and a slow dust occultation are close competitors. ZTF (later years, median-normalised) is quiet with a weak decline and cannot fix the absolute level.

discriminating_test: Phase-fold the ZTF r/i and NEOWISE W1/W2 light curves at P~375 d to confirm that the brightness maxima and minima recur on the Mira period (and look for a catalogue Mira/OH-IR entry). A strictly periodic recurrence would essentially rule out R CrB fades and instrumental causes.

evidence.feature: G and RP brighten and fade by factors of 5-8 with maxima about 375 d apart (t~358, ~733) and minima ~190, ~575, ~960
Detected drop at t=955-967 sits at the expected phase of the next minimum after the maximum at ~733
BP-RP 5.79, G-Ks ~8.8, bright W3/W4 (Ks-W4 ~4.8): cool AGB photosphere with a circumstellar dust shell
Both fields of view agree within errors at paired transits (e.g. 357.62/357.70, 733.42/733.49)
ruwe 1.82 and BP/RP excess 2.42 at low galactic latitude; but ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, and a large excess is expected for very red sources
BP depth 0.46+-0.50 with ratio 0.27+-0.29: BP at noise level, so the colour test is uninformative

explanation: A large-amplitude long-period variable, most likely a dusty Mira (AGB star). It is extremely red (BP-RP 5.8, G-Ks 8.8) and has a strong mid-IR excess (Ks-W4 about 4.8). G swings by a factor of about 8 (about 2.3 mag) with maxima near t=0, 358 and 733 and minima near 190, 575 and 955-967, which gives a regular period of about 370-380 d. The RP light curve tracks G in step. The 'drop' at 955-967 is just the star going into its next pulsation minimum, measured against a median that is dominated by minimum-phase visits. BP is too faint and noisy (ratio errors of about 0.3) to constrain the colour. Instrumental causes cannot produce a coherent periodic factor-of-8 change in both G and RP.

discriminating_test: Take one optical spectrum, or use archival OGLE/MACHO I-band monitoring of this position, to look for H-alpha emission and long-term outbursts of the disk. Strong H-alpha emission, and an emission equivalent width that grows with brightness, would confirm a Be-star disk.

evidence.feature: Depth ratio BP/RP = 0.78 (z_grey -5.6, z_dust -23): RP changes more than BP, so the source is redder when brighter
NEOWISE W1 change -0.54 against grey -0.34, dust in front -0.02, star cooling -0.18: the IR varies more than the optical
W1 rises with a lag of hundreds of days after the optical rise (0.48 to 1.16), holds a plateau, then declines over years
Late Gaia data: BP falls from 1.12 to 1.00 while RP climbs to 1.09 (outer disk persists)
Hot-star colours with a small near-IR and mid-IR excess (Ks-W1 0.2, W1-W2 0.3); G-W1 0.3 is far too blue for a quasar or blazar
Parallax SNR 1.3 at G=15.1, |b| 40-45, |beta| 60-70: a luminous, distant blue star consistent with the SMC
Coherent change in G, BP, RP and an independent survey (NEOWISE), both fields of view agree, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, normal BP/RP excess
Smooth change (abbe 0.04); the 647 d 'repeat' rests on fewer than two cycles in a 971 d span

explanation: The 'dip' is not an occultation. It is a low state lasting more than 350 d, followed by a brightening that lasts years, as in a Be star building a disk. The brightening is redder (RP 0.37 against BP 0.29, ratio 0.78, which is anti-dust). W1 rises later and further, by a factor of about 2.4 against about 1.6 in G, stays high about 1700 d and then fades. Late in the Gaia span BP falls back while RP keeps rising, which fits an inner disk dissipating while the outer disk persists. The colours (bp_rp -0.09, G-Ks 0.1, Ks-W1 0.2, W1-W2 0.3) are those of a hot star with a modest free-free excess, far too blue for an AGN. The negligible parallax at G=15.1 and the coarse position fit a luminous B star in the SMC.

discriminating_test: Plot the Gaia per-transit G flux against scan angle and look up the Gaia DR3 neighbour within ~2 arcsec. Then check ZTF PSF light curves of the resolved components for a real fade. If flux follows scan angle and ZTF is flat, it is confirmed as a blend.

evidence.feature: ipd_frac_multi_peak = 1.0: a double peak in every transit
Flux changes of 50-100% between the transits of one pair 106.5 min apart, with 1-2% errors
Which FoV reads high flips between pairs (fov1 high at 593, fov2 high at 733 and 872)
phot_bp_rp_excess_factor 1.55, high for bp_rp 2.37
Robust sigma 0.22 against median errors of 0.013; abbe 0.47, not a smooth fade
Red, faint, low-latitude source; parallax SNR 0.65; some slow trend possible
No BP/RP depths, no WISE/2MASS match, no NEOWISE visits in the window

explanation: A faint (G=18.8), red source in the Galactic plane with ipd_frac_multi_peak = 1.0 (every transit shows a double image) and an elevated BP/RP excess (1.55): a close neighbour is in the window. The G flux jumps by up to a factor of 2 between the two transits of one pair 106.5 min apart (733.42: 0.80 vs 733.49: 1.58; 593.21: 0.85 vs 593.39: 1.41; 872.71: 0.80 vs 872.79: 1.37), while the quoted errors are 1-2%. No star does that. Which field of view reads high changes from pair to pair, so this is the neighbour entering or leaving the window with scan angle, not a fixed FoV offset. The 'drop' is the high early epochs, the same blend at different scan angles. There is no BP/RP or IR data to test anything else.

discriminating_test: Pull the ZTF g/r (and TESS) light curve from 2018 on to confirm the ~1.2 d rotation period, see whether the mean level keeps wandering by a few per cent with spot-like reddening (g dimming slightly more than r), and check whether the star recovers rather than staying faded.

evidence.feature: Coherent ~1.2 d, ~4% peak-to-peak modulation in G and RP within the t=685-690 dense sequence, consistent between fov 1 and 2
Fade is smooth and part of a long-term decline (slope -1.94%/yr, slope_z -3.71, earlier high at t~390)
Both fields of view equally faint at t=733 and through the fade
phot_bp_rp_excess_factor 1.26 is about the expected value for bp_rp 1.3; ruwe 0.999; low ipd_frac_multi_peak
BP depth 3.2+/-1.0% matches G 3.7+/-0.5%, RP 1.2+/-1.3%; ratio 2.75+/-3.3 unconstraining
Ks-W1 ~0.2, W1-W2 ~-0.1: no clear warm-dust excess, but low galactic latitude
Only 6 visits in the fade, faint to the last visit, no ZTF/NEOWISE coverage of it
Parallax SNR 4.3 at G=16.9 implies a dwarf/subgiant, not a distant giant

explanation: The star is clearly variable on its own: during the dense run of visits at t~685-690, G and RP rise and fall together by about +/-2% with a period of roughly 1.2 d, and paired fields of view agree. That points to a fast-rotating spotted (active) dwarf. The detected fade is smooth (abbe 0.30) and part of a longer trend: brighter near t~390, then a decline to about -3.7% from t=733 onward. FOV1 and FOV2 dim alike, and the BP depth matches G. That fits a change in spot coverage or an activity cycle. The colour ratio is uninformative (2.75+/-3.3). The excess factor is normal, ruwe~1 and multi-peak is low, so a blend is unlikely. There is no NEOWISE or ZTF coverage of the fade and no IR excess, which weighs somewhat against dust.

discriminating_test: Get a long-baseline red/near-IR light curve of the source (e.g. VVV Ks or a later Gaia release's epoch photometry) to see whether the fade reverses cyclically, as semi-regular or LSP giant variability would, or continues. Also check whether nearby stars of similar magnitude and colour show the same Gaia G trend.

evidence.feature: bp_rp 3.11, G-Ks 5.2, parallax_snr 1.9 at G 17.5, |b| < 5 deg: distant reddened giant, not a dwarf
sigma_visit 0.0189 vs within-pair (106.5 min) G rms ~0.0177 (about 0.0125 per transit): intrinsic variability on week-to-month timescales
Detected change is a shallow steady trend (depth 0.061 over 920 d, slope -2.42%/yr) with no discrete deep or reddened fades
Large single-transit G disagreements inside pairs (781.2: 0.959 vs 0.994; 883.4: 0.976 vs 1.004) and FOV2 brighter in 8 of 11 pairs (~1%)
BP robust_sigma 0.29 vs err 0.083 and bp_rp_excess 1.56 slightly above expectation: BP window contaminated in a crowded field
ruwe 1.04, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0: no resolved close neighbour in the G window
Trend leans on high early points (t=0 at 1.068, t=219 at 1.045); colour depths uninformative (RP 0.018+/-0.028, BP 0.20+/-0.24)
No ZTF, NEOWISE or TESS epochs, so continuation or reversal of the fade cannot be tested

explanation: A faint, very red (BP-RP 3.11, G-Ks 5.2) source in the Galactic plane with parallax SNR 1.9 at G 17.5 is most likely a distant, reddened red giant. The 'dip' is a modest 6% linear decline over 920 d (slope_z -4.1 with only 15 visits, abbe 0.56), on top of ~1.7% intrinsic visit-to-visit variability: within-pair G scatter (~1.25% per transit) is well below sigma_visit 0.019. A slow drift of this size is typical of semi-regular or long-secondary-period giant variability sampled sparsely. Colour constraints are uninformative (RP 0.018+/-0.028, BP very noisy and probably contaminated). Residual calibration drift or crowding in a faint red plane field remain plausible alternatives; nothing requires an unknown cause.

discriminating_test: Run a period search on the dense ZTF g/r light curves (or check the Gaia DR3 RR Lyrae/VSX catalogues). A coherent 0.4-0.7 d period with a sawtooth RRab shape that phases all epochs, including the Gaia fov=1 and fov=2 points, would confirm pulsation.

evidence.feature: Flux distribution: flat floor ~0.85-0.95 with brief peaks to 2.2-2.8x in G, BP, ztf_g; about 18% of epochs above 3 sigma
Rise from 0.93 to 2.25 within one 106.5-min fov pair, decay to ~1.16 after ~4 h and ~1.0 after ~6 h
Amplitude ordering BP (2.53/0.87) > G (2.25/0.90) > RP (1.75/0.89), and ztf_g amplitude > ztf_r
ZTF PSF photometry reproduces the same brightenings in many seasons
Floor level in 357-918 d (0.94-0.97) matches the pre-357 floor (0.90-0.96): no true drop, only missing maxima
bp_rp 0.79, G-Ks 1.3, M_G about 1 at 2500 pc, |b| 25-30 deg
All five bright Gaia epochs are fov=2 and before day 330
W1-W3 about 0.1 mag, photospheric; NEOWISE shows no significant change
ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, BP/RP excess 1.24 near normal for this colour

explanation: This looks like a large-amplitude RRab-type pulsator. Most of the time the light sits on a flat floor near 0.80-0.95 of the median, with short peaks up to 2-2.8x. Those peaks rise within one 106.5-min pair and fade within hours, the shape of a sub-day pulsation. Mean bp_rp 0.79 and M_G around 1 at 2.5 kpc fit the horizontal branch. The amplitude falls from blue to red (BP > G > RP, ztf_g > ztf_r), so the star is hotter at maximum. ZTF shows the same behaviour with its own 2-arcsec PSF, so the variability is real and not a Gaia window effect. The detected 'drop' (357-918 d) only reflects that no Gaia epoch after day 357 happened to land on a maximum. The faint-state level is the same before and after, so there was no real fade.

discriminating_test: Run a periodogram on the ~926 ZTF r and ~418 ZTF g epochs to find the sub-day period, check the light-curve shape (sawtooth RRab, sinusoidal RRc/HADS or double-minimum EW), then fold the Gaia epochs on it to see whether the 589-764 d visits fall at minimum phase.

evidence.feature: 10-26% G changes between paired transits 106.5 min / 4.2 h apart, in both fov 1 and fov 2
Amplitude falls with wavelength: ZTF g 0.76-1.36, r 0.82-1.27, i 0.96-1.22; within Gaia pairs the BP change is ~1.3-1.5 times the RP change
ZTF i and r per-bin minima form a stable floor (~0.96 i, ~0.85 r) with upward excursions, unlike an EB ceiling with downward dips
Episode visits (0.796, 0.804, 0.838 in G) sit no deeper than the out-of-episode floor (0.799, 0.809) and have the faint-phase BP/RP colour
NEOWISE W1 change 0.000 +/- 0.026 vs grey prediction -0.174
No IR excess (Ks-W1 0.1, W1-W2 0.0); hour-scale chromatic changes
ruwe 1.03, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, variability also in 2-arcsec ZTF PSF photometry; BP/RP excess 1.33 adds BP noise only
fov 2 median lower than fov 1, mostly from fov1->fov2 declines within pairs

explanation: A short-period, large-amplitude pulsator (likely a reddened RR Lyrae or HADS in the disc). Gaia flux changes 10-26% between transits 106.5 min to 4.2 h apart, in both fields of view, so the star varies on a timescale of hours. The amplitude depends on colour (ZTF g ~0.63, r ~0.47, i ~0.26 mag; Gaia BP > G ~ RP), which fits a temperature change and not grey eclipses. ZTF i and r show a floor with brief brightenings. The 'episode' is three single fov-2 transits that sit at the out-of-episode floor (0.80-0.84 vs 0.80 minimum elsewhere) with the faint-phase colour, so it is sparse phase sampling. The 31 d 'repeat' is an alias. NEOWISE visit means do not change.

discriminating_test: Get the TESS 2-min/FFI or ZTF light curve and check for a coherent hours-period (delta Scuti) signal at the ~1% level; if there is none, regress the Gaia G residuals against scan angle and check the Gaia catalogue for neighbours within ~4 arcsec to test for crowding.

evidence.feature: G robust_sigma 0.0034 vs median error 0.0012; differences within a pair up to ~1.3% at 106.5 min, both brighter and fainter, not tied to one fov
Episode includes a normal visit at t=200.4 (1.001); depth 0.67% is only ~2x the per-epoch scatter; abbe 0.77
Excess scatter larger in BP (~0.0045) than RP (~0.0020), as for temperature-driven pulsation
G brightenings at t=39.3, 377.8, 513.2, 694.6 not confirmed in BP/RP; dip depth BP 0.0015+-0.0032, RP 0.0030+-0.0027 vs G 0.0067+-0.0007
Galactic latitude 0-5 deg at 2.2 kpc (crowded field), though ruwe 0.97 and ipd_frac_multi_peak 0
No IR excess: Ks-W1 0.1, W1-W2 0.0; no NEOWISE visits in episode
Lowest point t=231.39 seen in G, BP and RP simultaneously
Absolute ecliptic latitude 60-70 deg, parallax SNR 30

explanation: The 'episode' is a 0.67% deficit over four visits, one of which (t=200.4) is normal, in a star whose G scatter (robust sigma 0.0034) is three times its errors, with differences within a pair up to 1.1-1.3% across 106.5 min, in both directions. Most likely this is a sparse sampling of the star's own short-timescale variability. It is a reddened A/F star near M_G~1.7, possibly a delta Scuti pulsator; BP shows more excess scatter than RP. The alternative is G-band systematics from crowding in the Galactic plane: several G excursions are not matched in BP/RP, and the BP/RP dip depths fall about 2 sigma short of G. Eclipses and dust do not fit: there is no recurrence, there are brightenings too, and there is no IR excess.

discriminating_test: Get a quiescent low-resolution optical spectrum (or check archival LAMOST/SDSS/Gaia XP data and CV or outburst-alert catalogues at the position) for broad Balmer and He I emission, which would confirm a dwarf nova.

evidence.feature: Repeated ~100x (5 mag) brightenings in G, BP, RP and ZTF g/r/i, lasting days and recurring every ~300-600 d
Outburst amplitude larger in ztf_g (~160x) than ztf_i (~49x): bluer when bright, as from a hot accretion disc
M_G~10.8 at bp_rp 0.60 (G=19.6, 580 pc): far too faint for a main-sequence star of that colour, as expected for a CV
Detected 'dip' is one visit at t=925 with flux 1.29, depth -0.349 (brighter than median), 55 d after a 100x outburst and following a 2.6-3.5x visit at t=893
Same outbursts seen in both Gaia fields of view and in independent ZTF photometry from other years
Quiescent scatter 0.26 against per-epoch errors ~0.02 in G: strong flickering
Parallax SNR 6.2 and multi-day outbursts recurring at irregular intervals

explanation: A dwarf-nova-type cataclysmic variable. Gaia and ZTF g/r/i show repeated ~5 mag outbursts (flux ~80-160x quiescence at t~376, 870, 1275, 2362-2370, 2971, 3331-3337, 3677) that last days to ~2 weeks and decline through 2-3x before returning to quiescence, with larger amplitude in g than i (bluer in outburst). At 580 pc the quiescent G=19.6 gives M_G~10.8, far below the main sequence for bp_rp=0.6, which puts it between the main sequence and the white-dwarf sequence where CVs sit. The quiescent scatter (0.26 vs errors ~0.02) fits flickering. The 'detected dip' at t=925 is one visit 1.29x the median on the decline after the t=870 outburst. It is a brightening (depth -0.35), not a dip, and the 28.2 d repeat comes from sparse sampling of the outbursts.

discriminating_test: Run a period search over 0.5-10 d on the Gaia G epochs, or on ZTF photometry of the field. If every deep and partial epoch folds into one or two narrow eclipse phases at about 40% depth, it is an EB. Also check the scan angles and window positions of the fov-2 deep transits for window conflicts with the close neighbour.

evidence.feature: Within each 106.5-min FoV pair, one transit is deep (0.57-0.63) and the other partial (0.82-0.98), consistent with ingress or egress timing
Per-epoch depths are equal in G, BP and RP, including the partial epochs; BP/RP ratio 1.01 +/- 0.35
The minimum level repeats at about 0.57-0.63 in four separate events, suggesting a fixed eclipse depth
Flat at about 1.00 between events (robust_sigma 0.008), with short events at a low duty cycle (~20% of epochs)
ipd_frac_multi_peak = 1.0 at low galactic latitude, bp_rp excess 1.29: a close resolved neighbour in every transit
The deepest transit of every event is fov 2 (chance about 1/16 if eclipse timing alone decides), a mild hint of an FoV- or window-assignment artefact
Ingress of ~0.3 in flux within 1.8 h is too fast for a disk or dust occultation

explanation: Most likely a detached eclipsing binary that Gaia samples sparsely. The 65 d 'episode' comes from averaging visits. The real signal is six short events (t=24.8, 278.6, 473.5, 538.6, 752.7, 915.9). In each, one transit of the 106.5-min pair sits near a floor of about 0.57-0.63 and its partner is partial (0.82-0.98), as expected during ingress or egress lasting a few hours. The deeper transit is always the one nearer mid-eclipse, whichever FoV comes first. Every epoch, partial ones included, has the same depth in G, BP and RP (ratio 1.01), which fits twin-like components, while G and BP/RP window geometry would differ. About 20% of epochs are affected, suggesting P of a few days. The star is normal at all other epochs.

discriminating_test: Check a decade of archival ground-based photometry (ASAS-SN, ZTF, ATLAS) for repeated slow cycles of similar amplitude, which would point to an activity cycle, against a single isolated dip, which would point to an occultation. Add a Ca II H&K / H-alpha activity spectrum.

evidence.feature: Smooth, gradual decline and recovery over hundreds of days, Abbe 0.199, with the pre-dip level about 0.5-1% above the post-dip level
Depth ratio BP/RP 1.31 +- 0.54, consistent with spots, grey material and dust alike
216 d duration at 1.3% depth on a dwarf would need a transverse speed of about 0.08 km/s for a stellar-sized occulter, so only a very large extended body fits
fov 1 and fov 2 agree within each visit throughout the dip; ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, ruwe 1.04, normal BP/RP excess factor 1.21
Calibration drift shared by similar stars already removed; dip seen coherently in G, BP and RP
Abs. M_G about 4.5-5 with G-Ks 1.8 (photospheric), so not a giant, Be star or galaxy
No WISE match despite Ks 13.1, so mid-IR excess and dust re-emission cannot be tested; possible WISE confusion at low galactic latitude
Short-term visit-to-visit scatter small (sigma_visit 0.3%), little rotational modulation for a star with a 2% slow change

explanation: A smooth (Abbe 0.2), shallow 1.3% fade lasting about 200-380 d on what looks like a reddened G dwarf (M_G about 4.5-5). Before the dip the star sits about 0.5-1% above the later baseline, so this looks more like slow intrinsic variation than a flat star with one discrete dip. The likeliest cause is a magnetic activity or spot-evolution cycle. The BP/RP depth ratio of 1.31 fits spots, but its large error (+-0.54) also allows grey or dust. The leading alternative is a slow occultation by a large disk or dust structure: the dip lasts far too long for any eclipse of a dwarf (v about 0.08 km/s for t=2R/v). An instrumental cause is unlikely: both fields of view agree, RUWE, IPD and BP/RP excess look clean, and calibration drift has been removed.

discriminating_test: Get the ZTF/ATLAS/Pan-STARRS g and r light curve from 2015 to 2024. A fade that holds steady at the faint level points to a microlensing tail or disk ingress. A recovery or cycle with colour change points to activity. Behaviour shared by Gaia neighbours of similar magnitude points to calibration.

evidence.feature: Smooth monotonic decline flattening toward the end, abbe 0.158, both fov agree
sigma_visit 0.005 about equal to per-epoch errors; dense 3-day cluster at t~81 shows no short-term modulation
ruwe 1.01, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, BP/RP excess 1.25 normal for colour and magnitude
depth_g 0.039 equals depth_rp 0.040; BP depth -0.03 +/- 0.044, ratio unconstrained
Early BP visit at t~81 elevated about 13% with large BP/RP scatter (3x errors) and BP outliers at 2.1 and 2.8
Parallax SNR 5 at 2.3 kpc gives M_G about 5 (dwarf), b 10-15 deg, no IR data
Parallax detected at 5 sigma
Single 690-d drop with no recurrence information

explanation: A smooth, decelerating fade of about 5% over 990 d (abbe 0.16, slope_z -9.5). Both fields of view agree and the scatter about the trend matches the errors, so this is not a FoV offset or a one-off defect. ruwe 1.01, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0 and a normal BP/RP excess argue against a blend. The star is a distant, roughly solar-type dwarf that is otherwise quiet on short timescales. Ordinary explanations remain open: a long activity cycle (little rotational signal, though), the achromatic tail of a long microlensing brightening, the ingress of a slow disk occultation, or a residual time-dependent calibration error. G and RP fade alike, and BP is too noisy to tell grey from reddened. There is no IR, ZTF or NEOWISE data to separate these.

discriminating_test: Take an H-alpha spectrum, or check the archival OGLE/ASAS-SN long-term optical light curve and colour, to see whether the star has Be emission and whether its optical level and colour track the multi-year NEOWISE fade and recovery.

evidence.feature: parallax_snr -1.3 at G=14.1 with |b| 45-50 and |beta| 60-70: very distant, luminous blue star (likely SMC)
Modest IR excess rising Ks-W1 ~0.4, Ks-W2 ~0.6, Ks-W3 ~1.2 mag; W1-W2 only 0.2
NEOWISE W1 and W2 both fade ~19% over ~2019-2023 and recover smoothly, grey across W1/W2
BP/RP depth ratio 0.95 +/- 0.24 (z_dust -3.2): grey fade, not interstellar-like dust
Trend present consistently in G, BP, RP and both fields of view, with drift shared by similar stars removed
Extra short-term scatter (robust_sigma 0.011 vs err 0.0024, ~2% differences within 106-min FoV pairs)
Crowded-field possibility if Magellanic; WISE 6 arcsec PSF could include a variable neighbour

explanation: A G=14.1 blue source (bp_rp 0.11) whose parallax is consistent with zero sits at |b| 45-50, |beta| 60-70. That makes it very distant and luminous (M_G about -5 if it is a Magellanic Cloud member): an early-type star rather than a nearby dwarf. Its modest excess rising from Ks to W3, with W1-W2 0.2, looks like free-free emission from a Be decretion disk, not a quasar or dusty disk. The 3% Gaia fade is grey, shows in G, BP and RP and in both fields of view, and lasts the whole span. NEOWISE then shows a smooth ~19% fade and recovery over several years in W1 and W2. That pattern is typical of a Be disk dissipating and rebuilding, with the optical changing first.

discriminating_test: Compare calibrated absolute magnitudes from Pan-STARRS1/SDSS (pre-2014) and ZTF/Gaia DR4 (post-2017) with Gaia's early bright and late faint levels. That shows whether the star returned to the bright level (an occultation with egress, or a transient brightening) or stayed faint. Also check field stars of similar magnitude for the same early-epoch trend.

evidence.feature: Smooth monotonic ramp ~9% over ~300 d then flat plateau, abbe 0.029, consistent between fov 1 and 2
BP drop larger than RP (ratio 3.5+-2.3, by eye ~1.8), G in between
NEOWISE W1 in-change shift -0.002+-0.024 vs grey prediction -0.07
Early W1 visits (t=-172, 7) about 4-8% high, hinting W1 tracked the early bright state
ruwe 1.04, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, bp_rp excess consistent with colour
Plateau scatter ~0.6% with sigma_visit 0.005: little rotational modulation for a star with a 9% activity-level change
No IR excess (Ks-W1 ~0, W1-W2 ~0.1), |b| 15-20 deg at 1.9 kpc
Parallax gives a dwarf luminosity
ZTF 2018-2024 flat, but normalised to its own median so the absolute level relative to Gaia is unknown

explanation: A quiet, unblended K dwarf (M_G about 6, ruwe 1.04, normal BP/RP excess) whose G flux sits about 8.5% higher for the first ~100 d, then falls smoothly over ~300 d and stays flat to the end of Gaia (abbe 0.03, no field-of-view offset). The change is chromatic: by eye BP drops ~11% and RP ~6% (test ratio 3.5+-2.3), so it is not grey, which fits either small-grain dust or the star cooling or getting more spotted. W1 is ambiguous (the two early visits are high). No eclipse or YSO signature, no IR excess. The best fits are a long, slow dust occultation or a change in activity or spot coverage. A residual calibration problem stays plausible. Without knowing the absolute level, I cannot tell which state is normal.

discriminating_test: Compare absolute, non-renormalised photometry from other surveys (Pan-STARRS or Catalina epochs, and ZTF absolute magnitudes) covering days 200-305 and after day 911 with the Gaia-era level. Also check whether Gaia neighbours of similar magnitude and colour on the same transits show the same step around day 200-300. A shared step means calibration. A step on this star alone that recovers later means an occultation.

evidence.feature: Sharp step between day 198 and 305, then flat at about 0.96 for at least 606 d, in both FoVs and many scan groups
abbe 0.136, quiet star (sigma_visit 0.0028) with no rotational modulation before or after the step
RP depth 2.6+-0.9% below G depth 4.4%, BP/RP ratio 2.16+-1.19, near the dust value of 1.7
NEOWISE W1 change +0.005+-0.022 against grey prediction -0.044; fits dust in front (-0.003) or a cooler star (-0.013)
W1-W2 = 0, Ks-W1 = 0, high galactic latitude, about 0.65 kpc from the plane: no disk-bearing young star
A clean single step with no ingress structure, on one star, could come from an unremoved calibration or processing change
ruwe 0.957, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, normal BP/RP excess: no sign of a resolved neighbour
ZTF level is flat from 2018-2019 to after 2020 (normalised): the dip ended before day 1293 or never ended

explanation: The G flux drops 4.4% (about 16 sigma) at some point between days 198 and 305. It stays flat at about 0.96 through the last epoch (day 911), and both fields of view agree. Seven earlier scan groups are all bright and eleven later ones are all faint, so this is a step in time, not a scan-angle effect. The colour is reddened: RP 2.6+-0.9% against G 4.4%, ratio 2.2+-1.2. W1 does not dim (+0.5+-2.2%), which disfavours grey blocking at about 2.3 sigma. That fits small-grain dust in front, for example a long occultation by a companion's disk (ingress under 107 d, duration over 600 d). The star is a quiet K dwarf with no IR excess. An unmodelled calibration or processing step, or an injection, remains quite possible.

discriminating_test: Run a period search on the ZTF g/r and Gaia epochs for a 0.4-0.8 d period. Check that the folded curve is an RRab sawtooth (fast rise, slow decline) and that the 462-638 d visits fall at minimum phase. Or check whether Gaia DR3 lists it as an RR Lyrae.

evidence.feature: Flux floor ~0.92-0.94 with frequent upward spikes to 1.8 (G); none below 3 sigma
Changes of 0.9 in normalised flux within ~4-6 h between FoV pairs (t=0.07 to 0.50)
Amplitude BP > G > RP (2.9 / 1.84 / 1.63 peaks), BP/RP depth ratio 2.0
Dip visits (0.939, 0.912-0.939, 0.929-0.938) equal the normal minimum level seen at other epochs
Same spiky pattern in ZTF g and r over 2600 d, larger in g
Faint, distant, high galactic latitude, BP-RP 0.74: halo horizontal-branch colours
Abbe 0.74 and s_rep period 25 d from only 20 visits, consistent with undersampled short-period variability

explanation: This looks like a high-amplitude pulsator, most likely an RRab Lyrae star in the distant halo (G=15.8, parallax SNR 1.1, high latitude, BP-RP 0.74). The light curve sits at a floor near 0.93 and rises in sharp spikes to 1.84 in G, 2.9 in BP and 1.6 in RP. Brightness changes by up to 2x within hours (FoV pairs), and the amplitude is larger in BP than RP. ZTF repeats this pattern for years with g amplitude above RP. The 'dip' covers just three visits (462-638 d), all at the normal minimum-light level (0.91-0.94), the same level seen at 0, 137, 173, 266 and 859 d. The pipeline compared them with a median pulled up by the spikes. It is not a real dimming below the star's normal floor.

discriminating_test: Compare the absolute, survey-calibrated brightness before, during and after Gaia (Pan-STARRS 2010-2014, Gaia DR4 epoch photometry to 2020, absolute ZTF/PS1 magnitudes 2018+) along with same-CCD comparison stars. That shows whether the ~5% drop is a lasting level change on the star or a Gaia calibration step. A Ca II H&K spectrum would then test the activity-cycle option.

evidence.feature: Monotonic G decline (slope_z -12.6, abbe 0.11) with plateaus and drops near t~270, ~650, ~805 d
RP and BP fade by a similar amount to G (RP ~6%, BP ~4%, G ~5%), roughly grey
FOV1 and FOV2 agree within ~0.4% in the dense runs at 233-240 and 617-623 d; ruwe 1.01, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, normal BP/RP excess
No rotational modulation above ~0.5% within multi-day dense runs; ZTF robust sigma equals its errors
Calibration drift for similar stars already removed; the same change appears in G and in the separate BP/RP instruments
Steps could still be residual time-dependent calibration specific to this source
NEOWISE W1 shows no brightening near the 1000 K shell prediction (+0.086 +/- 0.055 vs +0.33); Ks/G normal for a reddened dwarf
ZTF 2018-2025 flat in g and r (change ~0.2%, slope ~0.1%/yr), so the fade stopped or reversed after Gaia

explanation: The detected 'dip' is the end of a secular, step-like fade over the whole Gaia span: G goes from about 1.020 (t<240) to 0.998 (300-623) to 0.990 (676-783) to 0.968 (830-995). RP (1.025 to 1.000 to 0.962) and BP (about 1.025 to 0.986) follow it, so the colour is roughly grey. Both fields of view agree and ruwe/ipd are clean, so the fade looks real. The star is a quiet F/G dwarf: there is no rotational modulation in the 6-day dense runs, ZTF shows no excess scatter, and 2018-2025 is flat. Spots in a quiet star, a slow disk ingress, or residual calibration could each explain it, but none fits well. This looks like secular dimming in the style of Boyajian's star, so unexplained gets the largest share.

discriminating_test: Get the per-transit scan angles and check whether the G and RP fluxes correlate with them. Also look in high-resolution plane imaging (e.g. DECaPS or Pan-STARRS) for a neighbour within ~2-4 arcsec that would fall into the G or BP/RP windows at the early scan angles.

evidence.feature: RP brightens by 11% (depth_rp -0.11) while G fades by 7.7%, in a star where RP dominates G

Very red, distant source in the plane: plausibly a reddened giant capable of slow low-amplitude drifts

explanation: The 'trend' is most likely contamination that depends on scan angle, in a crowded field in the Galactic plane. The G fade (7.7%, only 4 sigma) comes from a handful of early visits that sit high, set against one dense 3.5-day group at t~960 that dominates the median. RP moves the opposite way (early visits ~0.82-0.86, brightening by 11%). For a source this red (bp_rp 3.76), G flux is mostly RP light, so no real change on the star or occulter can do that. At t=195.9, G (+9%) and BP (x5) jump together, which looks like a bluer neighbour entering the window. The BP/RP excess factor (1.93) points to contaminated windows. ZTF shows no continued fade. A slow change of a reddened giant remains a minor alternative.

discriminating_test: Plot the per-transit G and BP flux against scan angle and look for a Gaia or Pan-STARRS neighbour within 2-4 arcsec. Then check whether ZTF PSF photometry (2 arcsec) shows any real fade or offset after 2018.

explanation: Most likely a neighbour contaminating the Gaia windows at some scan angles, not a real fade. Most G epochs sit at 1.00. The 'drop' exists only because the first eight epochs (t<230) are 4-15% bright, mostly in fov 2. Positive outliers depend on the field of view: in the dense 685-690 d run, fov 1 reads 1.06-1.14 while fov 2 stays near 1.00, and BP jumps to 1.27-1.31 at the same moments. BP is bimodal (0.6-0.8 versus 1.0-1.3, robust sigma 0.28), the BP/RP excess factor of 1.85 is high for G=17.3, the field is crowded (|b| 5-10 deg), and the BP and RP depths are inconsistent. W1 shows no matching change, and the W2 decrease rests on one visit. Intrinsic slow variability of a distant red star remains a minor alternative.

discriminating_test: Look for the same 2014.6-2017.4 slow 1% fade in independent long-baseline photometry (ATLAS or Pan-STARRS yearly means), and compare against Gaia epoch photometry of nearby stars with similar magnitude and colour on the same scans. A matching fade elsewhere, plus chromospheric activity (H-alpha or Ca II emission, or X-ray), would point to an activity cycle. No fade elsewhere, or the same trend in comparison stars, would point to an instrumental cause.

Only 15 visits; trend partly driven by the last visit (0.983 point) and the selection was made by the trend search itself

explanation: A shallow 1% G-band decline (-0.37%/yr, slope_z -4.3) across only 15 Gaia visits of a quiet G=17.5 K7/M0 dwarf (M_G about 8.4, bp_rp 1.92). Colour gives no information: the BP and RP depth errors (11%, 2.9%) are far larger than the 1% signal. There is no IR excess and no sign of a neighbour (ruwe 1.06, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, normal excess factor). The ZTF median level and slope are flat from 2018 on, so the fade did not continue at the Gaia rate. That fits a magnetic-activity or spot-coverage cycle on a cool dwarf, or a star-specific calibration or processing residual, or a look-elsewhere fluctuation that a trend search over many faint stars will turn up. There is no recurrence, depth structure or energy-budget problem that would call for anything unexplained.

discriminating_test: Check the TESS light curves, or ask for one quick spectrum, for a rotation period of a few days and chromospheric activity (Ca II H&K or H-alpha emission, Li). Strong activity and rotational modulation would confirm a spotted active star. A quiet slow rotator would raise the dust and unexplained options.

explanation: A roughly solar-type dwarf (BP-RP 0.92, M_G about 4.5, no IR excess) that varies on its own. Gaia shows a 1.5% fade over three years that gets redder as it dims (BP/RP 1.9+/-0.7, also consistent with cooling). On top of that, the visit-to-visit scatter (0.46%) is far above the errors, and there are changes of about 1% within a day or two (t~430-433). ZTF in other years shows the same few-percent behaviour over years: low in 2018-19, brighter after 2020 (g +1.6%, r +1.2%, with g changing more than r), then a redder 3-4% fade and recovery around t~3700-3990. Changing spot coverage plus rotation on an active star explains all of it. Without IR excess, dust is unlikely.

discriminating_test: Absolutely calibrated photometry spanning 2016-2019 (Gaia DR4 epoch photometry, or ATLAS/Pan-STARRS) would show whether and when the 4.5% fade ends, its egress shape and its colour. A symmetric egress with a reddened or grey colour would favour a disk occultation. A level that never recovers, or a step matching a Gaia calibration epoch, would favour an intrinsic or instrumental cause.

explanation: Gaia G drops from ~1.01 to ~0.965 between t~488 and ~545 d, then stays on a flat plateau to the last visit (t=922). Both fields of view show it, and scatter within visits stays low. RP also dims (2.6+/-0.8%). The negative BP depth comes from a single BP outlier (1.93 at t=718.6, with no G epoch). Without that point, BP dims ~4-6%, so the fade is consistent with grey or mildly reddened extinction. A smooth step with a ~50 d ingress and a >375 d flat bottom on an otherwise quiet K-type dwarf best fits partial occultation by an extended circumsecondary disk or dust structure. A star-specific calibration step or an intrinsic long-term change are the alternatives. No WISE data exist to test dust re-emission.

discriminating_test: Check quasar catalogues or archival spectroscopy (SDSS/DESI) for a redshift and broad emission lines, or look in the ZTF g/r light curve for continued damped-random-walk variability that gets bluer when brighter.

explanation: Most likely a quasar/AGN whose stochastic variability looks like a dimming episode. The source is faint (G=20.2), has no measurable parallax, sits at high galactic latitude, is blue in the optical (BP-RP 0.52) and point-like (RUWE 0.99), yet has WISE W1-W2=1.5 mag and W3=12.2. G wanders smoothly by about 10% (abbe 0.18): faint at the start (~0.90), bright from day 166 to 376 (~1.1), the flagged low from day 431 to 641 (~0.85), then brightening to 1.14. This is red-noise behaviour, not a one-off occultation. The 557 d 'repeat' is spurious with only about 1.7 cycles in the data. The BP/RP ratio (1.2 +/- 0.66) tells us nothing.

discriminating_test: Run a period search on archival ZTF or TESS photometry of the star. A rotation period of about 0.5-3 d with several-per-cent amplitude, whose mean level and amplitude change over years with spot-like g-r colour, would confirm an active spotted star. Continued reddened fading with no periodicity, or an infrared excess in WISE, would shift weight to dust or a disk.

explanation: This looks like a magnetically active K dwarf (M_G about 6.8 at 760 pc, bp_rp 1.49, close to the main sequence, normal G-Ks). On top of the fade, G changes smoothly by 3-5% within hours, and the paired fields of view agree (t=477, 494, 699, 807, 876). That points to fast rotational spot modulation of about 8% peak to peak. The 15% drop in mean level over 2.5 years fits a growth in spot coverage, as active-star cycles do. The fade is redder in BP than RP (ratio 1.81+/-0.43), which fits cooler spots (about 1.4-1.5) as well as dust. A 3% fade between late 2014 and mid-2015 that only this star shows would be real stellar activity, especially with a Ca II H&K or X-ray/UV activity check. If the fade does not appear, or the comparison stars share it, it is Gaia's early-mission calibration.

explanation: This is a slow secular fade, not a dip. G holds steady near 1.029 for the first ~95 days (both fields of view agree), falls about 3% by day ~300, then drifts down about 1% per year (abbe 0.12). The star looks like a K3-K5 dwarf (M_G ~6.2 at 1.2 kpc) with no infrared excess, so a change in magnetic-activity and spot coverage is the most likely cause. ZTF also shows slow 1-2% wanders in later years, larger in g than in r (+0.94% vs +0.56%), which points the same way. The main alternative is a residual Gaia calibration problem confined to the early mission. BP and RP are too noisy (3-4x their errors) to measure colour. NEOWISE is low S/N and rests on one low visit.

Comparing early and late visit means gives BP 2.2+/-0.4%, G 1.8%, RP 1.2+/-0.2%: it gets redder as it fades, and G sits between BP and RP as a real change on the sky should. The pipeline's ratio of 0.34 is pulled down by low BP visits at t=177-315. NEOWISE W1 and W2 drop about 3% at the same time and stay low, and ZTF is flat from 2018 to 2025. The two fields of view agree, ruwe is about 1 and the multi-peak fraction is low. My best guess is a change in the star's spot level, but an infrared drop this large does not fit spots well.

For a star this red, G is mostly RP light, so real intrinsic or occultation changes would move them in step. A neighbour entering the windows at some scan angles fits this. explanation: A faint (G=18.4), very red (BP-RP 3.3) source with no measurable parallax in the Galactic plane. It is most likely a heavily reddened distant giant in a crowded field. RP, which should carry most of this star's flux, does not follow the hump (it is low at day 162). The best options are slow giant variability or scan-angle neighbour contamination. A low-magnification microlensing-like hump also fits the shape. Nothing requires an unexplained cause.
