fov 1 and fov 2 transits agree within each early visit
Excess epochs confined to the very start of the Gaia series; later epochs at many scan angles show no repeat
ZTF g/r 2018-2025 flat (change after 2020 ~0.2%), no recurrence of a 7% excursion
No IR excess (Ks-W1 0.1, W1-W2 -0.3, W3/W4 upper limits), colour/distance imply a reddened FGK dwarf, not a Be star or YSO
Faint state lasts >800 d at 7% depth with flat bottom; would need an enormous occulter if it is a dimming
NEOWISE W1 at t=30 not brighter than later visits (+0.07+-0.04 opposite to grey prediction), weakly against a real achromatic change
|b| 0-5 deg, 2 kpc: high microlensing optical depth and crowding

explanation: The flagged 'drop' is not really a dip. The first 12 Gaia epochs (t=0-86) are 4-8% bright, and they fade smoothly through t~150-350 to a level that then stays flat in Gaia to t=959 and in ZTF to t~4050. The change is achromatic (BP/RP ratio fits grey, z_grey -0.65) and shows equally in both fields of view, and the star is otherwise quiet in G. Its location in the Galactic plane makes the decaying tail of a low-amplification microlensing event (A~1.08 at t=0, tE~80 d) the most natural single cause, filed under other_astrophysical. The main alternatives are an early-mission Gaia photometry residual, a variable unresolved neighbour, or a grey long-disk ingress.

discriminating_test: Look for an archival optical spectrum (SDSS/LAMOST/DESI) or a quasar catalogue match: broad emission lines at a measurable redshift would confirm an AGN; a stellar spectrum would reopen the case.

evidence.feature: W1-W2 = 0.9, W2-W3 = 2.3 with optical bp_rp 0.65 (strong mid-IR power-law excess)
parallax_snr = -3.8 at |b| 40-45, distance poorly constrained
smooth rise to 1.15 then fade to 0.86 over ~1000 d, abbe 0.153, no sharp ingress or egress
fade seen consistently in both fields of view and in G, BP and RP
BP/RP depth ratio 2.32 +/- 2.2 (bluer when brighter, poorly constrained)
RP outliers 4.73 and 3.06 with no counterpart in G or BP
NEOWISE W1/W2 change consistent with zero, ruling out a warm dust shell
phot_bp_rp_excess_factor 1.24, slightly high for this colour (possible host galaxy)

explanation: Almost certainly a quasar/AGN showing ordinary red-noise variability. The infrared colours are AGN-like and impossible for a bp_rp 0.65 photosphere: W1-W2 = 0.9 (above the ~0.8 AGN cut) and W2-W3 = 2.3. The parallax is significantly negative (SNR -3.8), consistent with zero, at high galactic latitude, with a slightly elevated BP/RP excess. The G light curve is not a dip: it rises smoothly by ~15% to t~360, then declines ~25% to t~927, with low Abbe (0.15) and a 'repeat' at 285 d that is just the undulation. BP/RP depth ratio 2.3 +/- 2.2 fits bluer-when-brighter. Isolated RP spikes (4.7, 3.1) at t~360-372 are single-band cosmic rays. NEOWISE shows no matching change, as expected for a lagged, diluted IR response.

discriminating_test: Phase-fold all ZTF g/r/i (and any TESS) epochs at P about 2.0726 d, T0 about 548.63, to confirm a coherent box-shaped eclipse of about 6-7% lasting 3-4 h at fixed depth in every band, and look for a secondary at phase 0.5 that would separate P=2.07 d from an equal-eclipse P=4.145 d.

evidence.feature: Six deep G dips (0.932-0.948) all phase to P about 2.0726 d within about 0.04 d; partial-depth epochs fall at ingress or egress
ZTF i dips of about 7-9% (e.g. three points at 0.913 at t=2094.80, two at 0.92 at 2121.7) recur at integer cycles of the same 2.0726 d period
A dipped transit is followed or preceded by a normal one 106.5 min to 4.2 h away, giving an eclipse of about 3-4 h, consistent with t ~ 2R/v at P about 2 d
Dips occur in both fov 1 and fov 2, and some pairs are dipped in both FoVs
Depth about the same in G, BP and RP (grey), although the BP/RP windows are larger than G's; ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, ruwe 0.945
Depth about 6.5% on an F/A-type primary (M_G of about 1-3 at 3.2 kpc) implies a companion of about 0.25 R*, too large for a planet
Epochs at phase 0.50-0.54 (t=309.27, 309.34, 477.22) are normal and the light outside the dips is quiet (robust_sigma 0.0033)

explanation: The 'episode' is really a set of short, deep, grey dips seen in single Gaia transits. All six deep G dips (about 6-7%, near t=289.6, 453.3, 548.7, 612.9, 621.2, 762.1) fit one ephemeris, P about 2.0726 d with T0 about 548.63, to within about 1 h. Shallower epochs (76.16, 243.91, 778.78, and BP/RP at 190.14) fall at ingress or egress. The other transit of each pair, 1.8-4.2 h away, is normal, so each eclipse lasts about 3-4 h. That matches 2R/v for an F/A primary with an orbital speed of about 200 km/s. ZTF i dips (1984.95, 2038.88, 2040.88, 2067.82, 2094.80, 2121.7, 2125.86) land on the same period. The depth is the same in G, BP and RP. Phase 0.5 shows no secondary. Best reading: a detached EB with a low-mass companion.

discriminating_test: Get a multi-year red/near-IR light curve (ZTF i/r or a near-IR plane survey in Ks). Semi-regular variation at the few-per-cent level would confirm intrinsic LPV behaviour. A flat light curve would point to crowding or calibration effects in the Gaia epochs; to check this, plot Gaia G against scan angle and look for neighbours within 2 arcsec.

evidence.feature: bp_rp 4.05, G-Ks 7.4, parallax_snr 0.08, |b|<5 deg: distant reddened cool giant
Slow G level changes of +-4-5% over hundreds of days (abbe 0.51), the amplitude typical of semi-regular M giants
phot_bp_rp_excess_factor 1.95, well above the ~1.63 expected at this colour: BP/RP windows contaminated
RP robust_sigma 0.14 vs errors 0.036, and RP brighter while G is fainter (357-409 d) and fainter while G is brighter (t<220 d)
G differs by 5-7% between the two fields of view 106 min apart (e.g. t=195, 219, 957)
Drop depth measured against only ~4 early 'outside' visits; colour test inconclusive (BP S/N ~1, RP depth -0.12+-0.13)
Drop lasts 609 d with no repeating eclipse shape; 25.4 d period from only 14 visits
ruwe 1.02, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0: no resolved neighbour in G itself

explanation: A faint (G=19.3), very red (BP-RP 4.05, G-Ks 7.4) source with no detected parallax, at |b|<5 deg: most likely a distant, heavily reddened M giant. The 'drop' is really four early visits at ~1.04-1.05 followed by later visits near 0.97-1.00, with a 0.93 point near 919-957 d. That looks like slow, few-per-cent semi-regular variation, which M giants commonly show. Crowding is the main alternative. The BP/RP excess is significant, RP scatters 4x its errors and runs opposite to G, and G differs by 5-7% between the two fields of view 106 min apart. The 25.4 d repeat period comes from only 14 visits and is not credible. A 609-day step does not fit an eclipse.

discriminating_test: Run a Lomb-Scargle periodogram on the dense final ZTF g/r/i season (or a TESS sector). If it shows a coherent ~11 d rotation signal of ~3-5% that drifts in phase and amplitude, it would confirm spots and account for the Gaia group-to-group changes. A spectrum showing Ca II H&K or H-alpha emission would confirm chromospheric activity.

evidence.feature: G moves 3-4.5% between visit groups 10-15 d apart (69.6 vs 79.1 d; 215.6 vs 359 vs 374.5 d), and the pairs from the two fields of view agree
Dense ZTF season (t~3950-4025): g and i are bright together (e.g. ~1.06 at 4008-4010) and faint together (~0.96 at 3956), repeating about every 11 d
ZTF seasonal means fall ~3-4% in g, less in i, around t~2800-3300, then rise to ~1.02 by t~4000: slow and chromatic
CMD position: M_G ~4.2, intrinsic BP-RP ~1.25, about 2 mag above the main sequence (subgiant / sub-subgiant region of active binaries)
BP/RP depth ratio 1.21 +/- 0.38; dip at 940 d is redder (BP ~10%, RP ~7.5%)
NEOWISE W1 change +0.6 +/- 1.4% against -3.9% predicted for grey blocking
No IR excess (Ks = W1 = W2 = 13.7); about 800 pc from the Galactic plane
BP/RP excess factor ~1.26 matches the colour expectation (C* ~ 0), ipd_frac_multi_peak low, ruwe 0.90
Duration of 593 d with a gradual multi-season level change, far too long for an eclipse of a K subgiant

explanation: Most likely a spotted, active K star. It sits about 2 mag above the main sequence (M_G ~4.2 at BP-RP ~1.3), where RS CVn-like subgiants live. It varies all the time: Gaia changes by 3-4.5% between groups only 10-15 days apart (both fields of view agree), and ZTF scatters well above its errors. In the dense last season, g and i rise and fall together with a quasi-period of ~11 d and ~3-5% amplitude. Seasonal means drift: ZTF is ~3-4% fainter around t~2800-3300 and deeper in g than in i, then recovers. That looks like spots evolving or an activity cycle. The detected 'drop' (bright early, fainter later, a 6% low point at 940 d) is this variability. BP/RP ~1.2 is mildly red, and W1 rules out grey dimming.

discriminating_test: Extract the multi-year ZTF/Catalina/PS1 light curve. Repeated stochastic wandering of similar amplitude means intrinsic variability. A single long grey event that recovers points to a disk occultation. Add one low-resolution spectrum (H-alpha emission, log g) to separate a Be star from a BHB or post-AGB star.

evidence.feature: Fade seen coherently in G (2.9%), BP (3.0%) and RP (3.5%) with BP/RP ratio 0.85+-0.25 (z_grey -0.59, z_dust -3.36)
Coherent ~1-2% pre-fade hump in all three bands around t=300-500 d; low abbe 0.17; star wanders smoothly rather than having one isolated event
Duration >=309 d with gradual ~200 d ingress and no egress; t~2R/v requires v~0.1 km/s for a stellar-size occulter
RP varies slightly more than BP (bluer when fainter), weakly; W1/W2 scatter (~9-10%) larger than optical, as Be disk changes would produce
Parallax SNR -0.22 at G=15.7 with blue colour: rules out nearby WD/CV/sdB, so the source is luminous and distant
G-Ks~0.2, G-W1~0.2, W1-W2~0, BP/RP excess 1.16 normal for a point source
Large single-band outliers between paired FoV transits (e.g. G at t=153.8, 907.4; BP at 74.2; RP/BP at 282.7) not mirrored in other bands
Shared calibration drift already removed; similar depth in all bands with separate BP/RP windows argues against blending or window effects
NEOWISE W1/W2 change consistent with grey and with zero (one visit in); no warm-shell brightening

explanation: Most likely the star's own slow variability. The ~3% fade lasting at least 300 d is grey (BP/RP ratio 0.85+-0.25; interstellar-like dust excluded at 3.4 sigma). Before it, G, BP and RP rise and fall together by ~1-2% (abbe 0.17), so the source wanders on its own. Its parallax is consistent with zero and its colour is late-B/A, so it is luminous and distant, probably a halo BHB, post-AGB or Be-like star. A compact eclipser is ruled out: t~2R/v gives v~0.1 km/s. A large grey disk could cause the fade but needs an unlikely geometry. Calibration drift was removed and the three bands agree, so instrumental causes are less likely. Stellar IR colours (G-Ks~0.2, W1-W2~0) argue against an AGN.

discriminating_test: Run a periodogram on the dense ZTF r-band seasons (t~1580-1880, ~2170) to look for a stable rotation period of days whose amplitude tracks the long-term level, and take a low-resolution spectrum to check for Ca II H&K/H-alpha emission and lithium (activity versus youth, and luminosity class).

evidence.feature: Gaia G trend -1.78%/yr (slope_z -4.49) in both FoV 1 and FoV 2, drift shared with similar stars removed
ZTF g and r both show a few-percent low state in 2018-2019 and ~2.5% brightening after 2020, so the star varies on its own over years
G robust_sigma 0.02 vs median error 0.004, with transit pairs 106.5 min apart agreeing: real variability on week-to-month timescales
ZTF dip slightly deeper in g than r (ratio ~1.3), not grey
Smooth multi-year change, no eclipse-shaped events; rep_period 65.1 d is near the 63 d scanning-law precession
W2-W3 = 2.5 mag with no Ks/W1/W2 excess, at galactic latitude 5-10 deg; W3=12.4 near the detection limit
Parallax SNR 2.9 at G=17.1 with bp_rp 1.39 implies a dwarf/subgiant rather than a luminous red giant
ruwe 0.97, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, excess factor 1.25 normal for the colour
W1-W2 = -0.2 and a significant parallax

explanation: The detected 'dip' is a ~5% G fade over Gaia's 1020 days, seen in both fields of view, with calibration drift already removed. ZTF independently shows the same kind of behaviour: a ~5-7% low state around t~1760-1950 in both g and r (slightly deeper in g), then recovery and a further ~5% brightening by t~3500-4100. On top of that, G shows ~2% scatter from visit to visit (errors 0.004) while paired transits agree. That points to a spotted, active dwarf/subgiant (distance and colour argue against a giant) whose activity level drifts over years. BP/RP colour and NEOWISE are uninformative. The W3 excess, with no Ks/W1/W2 excess, is marginal and possibly nebular at low latitude, so it gives the YSO reading only modest weight. The 65 d repeat matches the scanning-law precession.

discriminating_test: Run a period search on the ZTF g/r light curve (and fold the Gaia epochs) to confirm the hours-long ~40% grey eclipses recur at a fixed period of a few days with constant depth.

evidence.feature: Dips last hours with gradual ingress/egress across consecutive 106.5-min FoV transits (357, 870, 961)
Per-epoch BP, RP and G depths nearly equal (~0.40-0.44); ratio 0.655 +/- 0.236, z_grey -1.47, z_dust -4.43
Dips seen in both fov 1 and fov 2 and in all three bands
Normal visits at 389 and 408 inside the 182-d 'episode'; it is two separate short events, not a long fade
Four separate events of similar depth (~0.40-0.43) over 961 d
Quiet out of dip (robust_sigma 0.015, no epochs above 3 sigma, max flux 1.024)
ruwe 0.938, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, BP/RP excess 1.23 unremarkable
Depth ~40% too deep for a planet around a bp_rp 1.07 star

explanation: Four short, deep (~40%), grey dips: t=357 (both FoVs, egress 0.60 to 0.70 in 106 min), 540 (G, BP, RP agree), 870 (0.95 to 0.72 to 0.98 within ~6 h) and 961 (0.81 to 0.58 to 0.99 within ~10 h). Each lasts hours, not 182 d; the pipeline's 'episode' just spans two eclipses with normal visits (389, 408) between. Smooth ingress/egress across consecutive transits and both fields of view, equal per-epoch depths in G, BP and RP (z_grey -1.47), an otherwise quiet star with no brightenings, ruwe 0.94 and no multi-peak point to a detached eclipsing binary with a period of a few days; the in-eclipse duty cycle (~7/42 epochs) fits that. Artefacts would not track smoothly across bands and transits.

discriminating_test: Get long-baseline ground photometry (ZTF/ASAS-SN) and a TESS light curve. A rotation period of days with spot-level amplitude, and a fade that later reverses (an activity cycle), would confirm spots. A fade that is grey and keeps going would point to occultation. A fade only in Gaia would point to calibration.

evidence.feature: G robust_sigma 0.0058 vs median error 0.00067; ~1% changes within 3 days in G, BP, RP (t 833 to 836)
Light curve rises to day ~300 then fades; abbe 0.40, smooth multi-year change rather than a single straight fade
BP/RP depth ratio 1.8 +/- 0.62 (z_grey 1.29, consistent with a temperature/spot change)
Fade seen in BP and RP as well as G; BP/RP windows would include any sub-arcsec companion, and bp_rp excess factor is normal, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0
ruwe 4.01 and M_G ~0.5 mag above a single K dwarf: likely binary, can host active (BY Dra/RS CVn-like) components
Ks, W1, W2, W3 flat (no infrared excess), W4 only an upper limit
NEOWISE W2 slope -0.0115 +/- 0.0047 /yr, closer to grey prediction than to temperature (2.1 sigma) or Gaia-only drift (2.4 sigma), but only 4 visits
Final dense group (t 984-991): G fov 2 ~0.5% brighter than fov 1, not seen in BP/RP
G = 12.2 close to the gating/window-class boundary, slow trend of 0.56%/yr is near the calibration-drift level

explanation: This looks like a K dwarf (bp_rp 1.24, M_G about 5.6, slightly overluminous, ruwe 4 so probably a binary) that is magnetically active. It varies well above the noise (G robust sigma 0.58% against 0.07% errors), with changes of about 1% over a few days that show in G, BP and RP alike (days 833 to 836). The detected fade is not a clean line: the star brightens until about day 300, then fades about 2% in all three bands, more in BP (ratio 1.8 +/- 0.6). That fits a change in spot or activity level, like a cycle. There is no IR excess. The W2 trend leans grey, but it rests on only 4 visits. Gaia calibration drift is the main instrumental alternative.

discriminating_test: Compare the Gaia G epoch fluxes of nearby stars of similar magnitude and colour over t=164-358 d, and check the scan angles of the five low transits against any Gaia neighbour within ~4 arcsec. A shared drift or a scan-angle match would make the fade instrumental; neither would leave slow stellar activity as the cause.

evidence.feature: 1.7% G fade over 4 visits, both fov 1 and fov 2 low at t=215.6, gradual recovery
Source is a dwarf (M_G ~7, bp_rp 1.61), not an evolved star
ZTF median fades after 2020 by 4% in g and 2% in r (redder when fainter)
RP +18.6% at t=164.66 (fov 2) while G dims; BP/RP robust scatter 2-5x their errors; excess factor 1.28 at |b| 5-10 deg
Dip only 1.7x G robust sigma per epoch, significance rests on a run of 5 points among 17 visits
ruwe 1.0, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, G-Ks ~2.9 with no K excess
Single ~200 d, 1.7% non-recurring fade with no flat bottom

explanation: A shallow (1.7%) G fade, deepest at its first visit and recovering gradually over ~200 d, seen in both fields of view. The star is a K/early-M dwarf (parallax distance 1100 pc, M_G about 7; G-Ks normal, so no sign of a disk). The colour test cannot be used: BP/RP scatter far exceeds their errors, and the RP 'brightening' comes from a single fov-2 outlier (1.186) that cannot be physical while G dims. That points to contaminated BP/RP windows in a crowded low-latitude field. ZTF shows a slow multi-year fade (g -4%, r -2%, redder when fainter), so the star varies slowly at the percent level. The most likely cause is a change in spot coverage or activity. Low-level calibration or crowding residuals at G=17.8 remain the main alternatives.

discriminating_test: Check the scan angles of the t=0 and t=219 FoV-1 transits against the later ones, together with Gaia/VVV sources within ~4 arcsec. If a neighbour lies along those scan directions, it is a blend. A multi-epoch near-IR (VVV Ks) light curve over the same years would show whether the star itself faded.

evidence.feature: Trend depth 0.14 set by only two early G transits (t=0, 219), both FoV 1, then flat G for ~600 d
Early RP epochs (0.93-1.02) show no brightening matching the +14-17% G excess, although G flux of a bp_rp=4 star is mostly RP-band light
phot_bp_rp_excess_factor 1.89, |b|<5, RP scatter (0.08) far above its errors and above G scatter
BP flux at noise floor (errors ~38%, values 0.12-19.3); colour ratio 9730 +/- 1.76e6 is meaningless
FoV 1 points often slightly above FoV 2 in the same transit pairs (593, 782, 873, 964)
Very red, IR-bright (Ks 11.4) star in the plane, consistent with a reddened giant/AGB star that can vary slowly
ZTF r after Gaia flat (change +0.03, slope ~0) but with 16% errors; no NEOWISE visits

explanation: The 'trend' comes almost entirely from two early single-transit G points, both FoV 1 (t=0: 1.17, t=219: 1.14). After day ~360 G is flat to a few per cent. In a crowded field at |b|<5 with BP/RP excess 1.89, the most likely cause is flux from a neighbour entering the G window at those scan angles, or a calibration artefact. The star is very red (G-Ks 7.5, bp_rp 4), so its G flux is mostly RP-band light. A real 15% brightening would show in RP, but the early RP points sit at ~0.97, not higher. BP is at the noise floor and tells us nothing. An intrinsic slow decline of a reddened red giant is the main alternative. ZTF data are too noisy to decide.

discriminating_test: Plot G epoch flux against scan angle, and check Gaia DR3 for a resolved neighbour within ~1-2 arcsec. If the bright G epochs cluster at the scan angles that put the neighbour inside the window, the blend is confirmed.

evidence.feature: ipd_frac_multi_peak = 67 (double image in most transits)
phot_bp_rp_excess_factor 2.05, far above normal for bp_rp 1.82, at |b| 5-10 deg
G change 0.091+/-0.015 but BP 0.007+/-0.012 and RP -0.009+/-0.007: no change in the larger-window bands
Change caused by bright G outliers outside it (1.27, 1.24, 1.16, 1.43, 1.26) against a steady ~0.98-1.00 level inside
Big scatter within same-day transit groups at 618, 629 and 779 (0.74-1.18), in G only
W2 visits inside the change show no change (+0.017+/-0.023), and no IR excess in W1/W2
Isolated single-band spikes: RP 1.236 at 88.12, BP 1.216 at 995.38

explanation: A close neighbour moving in and out of the narrow G window. ipd_frac_multi_peak = 67 means most transits show a double image, and a BP/RP excess factor of 2.05 at bp_rp 1.82 points to strong contamination in the larger BP/RP windows. The 'drop' is not the star fading. Out-of-change G visits (t = 80, 88, 154, 995) are 12-27% bright, plus a single +43% visit at 466. These pull the outside median up, so the quiet visits in between look 9% faint. BP (0.007+/-0.012) and RP (-0.009+/-0.007) show no change, and neither does W2. G also scatters inside same-day groups (0.74, 0.83, 0.85 next to ~1.05), which fits a dependence on scan angle rather than anything on the star.

discriminating_test: A period search on an archival ZTF g/r light curve. A strict sub-day period with a stable shape would point to a pulsator, contact binary or rotator, and would show whether the mean level keeps fading. Aperiodic flickering would point instead to a YSO, CV or AGN, and WISE colours could then separate those three.

evidence.feature: Pairs 106.5 min apart differ by 0.07-0.18 (e.g. 695.44 -> 695.51: 1.079 -> 0.900) with errors ~0.005; no consistent fov1/fov2 sign
Same-FOV transits 6 h apart also differ by 0.11-0.16 (592.17 vs 592.42; 609.43 vs 609.68), at essentially the same scan angle
phot_bp_rp_excess_factor 1.72 at bp_rp 1.23, far above an isolated star's ~1.25; BP/RP depths null
ipd_frac_multi_peak 0 and ruwe 1.06: no close neighbour inside the G window
Trend slope_z -4.29, abbe 0.499 over 23 visits: correlated slow variation in the visit means, with scatter of 0.03 per visit
Smooth hour-scale swings, flux range 0.90-1.11 (~0.23 mag peak-to-peak)
Galactic latitude 5-10 deg, parallax_snr 1.2: distant star in a disc field, consistent with zero parallax
No 2MASS/WISE photometry, no ZTF or TESS epochs: no colour or IR test of dust vs temperature

explanation: The source itself varies on a timescale of hours. Transits 106.5 min apart, and same-FOV transits 6 h apart, differ by up to 18% against errors of about 0.5%, with no consistent FOV sign. Both fields of view share a scan angle, so neither blending nor an FOV offset explains this. The detected 'dip' is a -4.6%/yr trend (4.3 sigma, Abbe 0.5) in the visit means, most likely the slow, red-noise part of that variability: spot evolution, YSO accretion or extinction, CV-like state changes, or chance sampling of a pulsator or contact binary. It is probably not a separate fading event. BP/RP depths are missing and the excess factor of 1.72 shows contaminated BP/RP, so colour cannot discriminate. No IR or other-survey data. The type stays uncertain.

discriminating_test: Retrieve the ZTF r/i (or Gaia DR4) multi-year light curve. Continued semi-regular cycles of 5-10% with larger amplitude in bluer bands would confirm red-giant variability; a flat light curve would point to a Gaia G-band instrumental or blend trend.

evidence.feature: bp_rp 4.18, G-Ks 6.8, parallax_snr about -1, |b| 0-5 deg: distant, reddened, cool evolved star
Smooth multi-hundred-day fade (abbe 0.48, s_fade 3.1), no repeating short dips
Early RP visits (t=0-219) do not sit above the late level the way G does; RP has isolated low points not matched in G
phot_bp_rp_excess_factor 2.04, well above about 1.6 expected for this colour, in a crowded low-latitude field
ruwe 1.03 and ipd_frac_multi_peak 0: no resolved neighbour in the G window
FoV 1 and FoV 2 agree within about 1% at the early bright visits and in the dense late cluster
Only 16 visits, with the trend significance at about 4 sigma and driven by the first three visits
BP depth 0.13 +/- 0.65, no WISE or NEOWISE data: dust versus temperature untestable

explanation: Most likely a distant, heavily reddened red giant in the Galactic plane (BP-RP 4.18, G-Ks 6.8, parallax not measured, |b|<5) with slow, low-amplitude semi-regular or long-secondary-period variability. The 'dip' is a smooth G decline of about 3%/yr (8% total, slope_z -3.9, abbe 0.48) from about 1.06 in the first three visits to about 1.0 later. That is ordinary for such a star and nothing like an eclipse or transit. BP is pure noise, so colour cannot be tested. RP does not clearly show the early bright level, and the BP/RP excess of 2.04 (about 1.6 expected at this colour) points to a crowded field. That leaves real weight on a blend or a G calibration residual for an extreme-colour faint source.

discriminating_test: Measure the rotation period and spot-modulation amplitude in TESS or dense ZTF data, and look for chromospheric activity (Ca II H&K or H-alpha) in archival spectra. An active, spotted star whose modulation amplitude follows the slow lows would settle it as spots or activity. A quiet, inactive star would push the probability toward dust or instrumental causes.

evidence.feature: Fade present in both fov 1 and fov 2 and in G, BP and RP, with paired transits agreeing
BP/RP depth ratio 1.71 +/- 0.56 (z_grey 1.27): chromatic but not decisive between spots, cooling and dust
ZTF g and r show repeated season-long 1-3% lows, larger in g, so slow variability is normal for this star
sigma_visit 0.0059 far above per-epoch errors (about 0.001); one in-fade visit at t=821 back to normal level
NEOWISE W1 change +0.008 +/- 0.010 against grey prediction -0.017
W1-W2 = 0, Ks-W1 = 0: no inner-disk excess; W3 is only marginally bright
Absolute magnitude about 6 with bp_rp 1.28: a dwarf, not an evolved star

explanation: A quiet-looking K dwarf (M_G about 6 at 450 pc, ruwe 1.04, no near/mid-IR excess in Ks-W2) fades 1.7% in G for about 300 d, seen in both fields of view and all three bands, with BP deeper than RP (ratio 1.7 +/- 0.6). Most likely this is the star's own slow variability: changing spot coverage or magnetic activity. The star already shows week-scale scatter (sigma_visit 0.6%), the dip is irregular (one visit at t=821 back at normal level), and ZTF shows similar 1-3% season-long lows that are deeper in g than in r. The one NEOWISE visit inside the fade shows no W1 dimming, which argues against grey blocking. Dust or an instrumental cause is still possible.

discriminating_test: Gather archival multi-epoch photometry from before 2014 (2MASS, SDSS, Pan-STARRS, photographic plates) and take a new optical/near-IR SED or spectrum now. This would show when the fade began, whether it is still linear and grey, and whether any curvature, colour structure or companion lines appear, as a disk ingress would predict.

explanation: The detected fade belongs to a steady decline over the whole record: Gaia G -1.4%/yr (z=-17.7), ZTF g/r/i about -1.5%/yr to the end of the data, and NEOWISE W1 at a similar rate. Seeing it in three independent facilities rules out instrumental drift. The star is a quiet F/G turnoff star (M_G about 3.5) at high latitude, with clean astrometry and no IR excess. The only listed natural cause that fits is a slow grey ingress of an optically thick disk around a wide companion, which is unlikely a priori, so I give similar weight to no listed cause fitting.

A residual long-term calibration drift is the main instrumental rival. ZTF later shows no significant change, so the fade is not ongoing.

explanation: The G light curve is dominated by fast periodic variability. FoV pairs 106.5 min apart differ by up to 10% (10-20 sigma), with signs that alternate, yet the pair means after t=221 stay tightly near 1.0. That anticorrelation implies a photometric half-cycle of about 106.5 min (or an odd fraction of it): a W UMa binary with P about 0.30 d, or a delta Scuti star. The 'drop' compares about seven early visits that sat near 1.055, four of them single random-phase epochs, with later pair-averaged visits. So it reflects sparse sampling plus a modest mean-level shift (spots, a neighbour, or calibration), not an occultation. NEOWISE W1 shows no matching drop, which disfavours grey dimming at 3.4 sigma.

discriminating_test: Look up an optical spectrum (SDSS/DESI) or a Gaia/Milliquas quasar classification and check that proper motion is consistent with zero: broad emission lines at a cosmological redshift would make this certain.

The signal is therefore not physical for the star. It is either a G-only processing or calibration artefact, or an injected change that no real process makes. explanation: A 0.4% G deficit over three visits on a G=16.9 dwarf, near the noise floor (epoch scatter 0.0047 exceeds the 0.0037 errors). The search flagged it through a 351 d repeat: G is equally low (~0.5%) at t=0-54, mildly low at t~402, and low again at t=700-751, so the dimming returns at the same time of year. For a given source, Gaia's scan angle is set mostly by the Sun's position, so yearly recurrence points to an effect that depends on scan angle, such as a faint neighbour entering the window or background. BP/RP scatter 4-5x their errors, a mild BP/RP excess and dips in BP/RP that G does not share back this up. The colour and NEOWISE data cannot tell the explanations apart. The star's own low-level spot variability is the second choice.

Gaia also shows 3-6% changes within 1-2 days (t 649-653), which points to an active, spotted, fairly fast-rotating star. Changes in spot coverage over an activity cycle are the simplest cause. They match the fades being deeper in blue and the NEOWISE response (cooling-like, not grey, no warm shell). Variable dust extinction with no IR emission, or survey normalisation offsets, remain alternatives.

The fade is reddened (BP/RP ratio 2.4+-0.4: not grey; closest to small-grain dust) and W1 does not change (rules out grey blocking and a hot shell). On a main-sequence K dwarf about 380 pc off the plane, with no W1/W2 excess, the best fit is optically thin dust crossing our sightline, for example the diffuse edge of a circumsecondary disk. A spot or activity-cycle change fits the colour and W1 less well. Neither explanation is secure.

discriminating_test: Take a low-resolution optical spectrum to check for H-alpha emission and Li 6708 absorption. Youth and accretion would confirm a disk-bearing YSO. Also measure the ZTF g-r and r-i colour change across the later ZTF fades, to separate grey disk occultation from dust reddening and from spot or temperature changes.

ZTF r and i show similar slow, irregular +/-5-7% swings over later years, so the star itself varies on these timescales. G and RP depths are near equal (RP slightly deeper), which mildly favours large grains or opaque structure over ISM-like dust or spots. Instrumental causes are unlikely. A giant is ruled out by the luminosity.

A neighbour that enters the BP window and the G background area at later scan angles would raise BP and over-subtract G, which explains both. The other leading option is a real activity-cycle change at the 0.5% level, which BP/RP are too noisy to check. A one-off flat-bottomed grey depression would instead point to an occultation.

W1-W2 is stellar, so not an AGN. ruwe, ipd and the excess factor show no blend. The BP/RP ratio cannot tell the causes apart.

NEOWISE rules out only a hot (1000 K) shell, and there is no IR excess. The leading natural reading is a long-term change of a roughly solar-type dwarf (activity or spot cycle), but 7% with under 1% short-term scatter is large for a quiet star about 0.5 kpc off the plane. A slow disk ingress or a star-specific instrumental drift remain possible, so a substantial unexplained share stays.

discriminating_test: Look for an archival optical spectrum (SDSS/DESI) or a quasar-catalogue match (e.g. Milliquas, Gaia QSO candidates) showing broad emission lines at a cosmological redshift. A ZTF light curve with continued damped-random-walk variability would also confirm it.

If the year-scale grey +-3% changes appear in every field and not in the comparison stars, the variability is on the star. A low-resolution spectrum (Ca II H&K/H-alpha emission, Li) would then separate a young active star from dust-driven dimming.

If the slope stays significant (and no comparable drift appears in a TESS/ground mean level), the trend is real; otherwise it was pulsation sampling.

The main alternative is a YSO dipper: low latitude, possible Ks excess (G-Ks 3.8 at BP-RP 1.23).

discriminating_test: Cross-match against archival spectroscopic quasar catalogues, or take one low-resolution optical spectrum, to look for redshifted broad emission lines; Gaia proper motion consistent with zero would also support it.

discriminating_test: Pull the archival OGLE-bulge I-band or VVV Ks light curve for this position. If it shows long-period/semi-regular variability whose phase matches the Gaia G and RP decline, this is pulsation. If it is flat while the Gaia G residuals track scan angle, a neighbour blended into the G window is the cause.

RP fades too (depth 0.074 +/- 0.040; late visits ~0.90-0.97 vs early ~1.04-1.08), and RP field-of-view pairs mostly agree to a few per cent

explanation: This looks like a luminous, heavily reddened red giant or AGB star in a crowded field near the Galactic plane: BP-RP 5.37, G-Ks 7.9, Ks 8.5 and a parallax consistent with zero. Stars like this almost always vary semi-regularly or over long secondary periods. The slow 29% fade in G is matched by a smaller (~7%) but significant fade in RP, and RP agrees between fields of view. A larger amplitude at shorter wavelengths fits temperature or molecular-band changes in a cool star, and grey occultation does not fit. Seventeen visits over 2.6 years can make part of a semi-regular cycle look like a trend. The scatter between fields of view in G (10-28%) and the high BP/RP excess point to some blending in G on top of this.

discriminating_test: Compare absolutely calibrated photometry (Pan-STARRS1 2010-2014, ZTF calibrated magnitudes 2018 onward, Gaia DR4 epochs past 2017) with Gaia's pre-fade level to see whether the star recovered (occultation), stayed faint or cycled (activity), plus one low-resolution spectrum for H-alpha activity.

explanation: Faint, quiet mid-M dwarf (M_G about 9.7, bp_rp 2.34, high latitude, no IR excess). The one NEOWISE visit in the fade shows W1 unchanged, which disfavours grey blocking and fits a change in spot coverage or temperature, or chromatic dust. Activity-driven secular dimming is the most likely cause but weak, since the star shows no rotational scatter. A disk occultation or a Gaia systematic for faint sources remain possible.

discriminating_test: Get the ZTF g/r (or ASAS-SN) light curve for 2018 onward. A rotation period and repeated 1-3% year-scale shifts in the mean level would confirm a spotted, active star. A flat star after the event would favour a one-off occultation. Also check the Gaia catalogue for neighbours within 3 arcsec, which bears on crowding.

evidence.feature: Irregular ~1% month-scale fluctuations throughout, plus a broad low state, not a clean single dip; abbe 0.43

explanation: The 'trend' is really a broad, shallow (~2-2.5%) low state from day ~600 to ~1000 (minimum ~0.980 near days 774-786, back to ~1.00 by day 1003), with ~1% month-scale wiggles before and during it (e.g. 357 vs 395, 704 vs 733, 936 vs 988) and visit noise (0.7%) above the photon errors. BP and RP both drop by similar amounts, and there is no fov offset, so it looks like a real change in the source's flux rather than a calibration drift. Red-noise wandering of a moderately active G/K dwarf (spot or activity evolution) is the simplest explanation. The colour ratio (1.13+/-0.66) does not tell grey from dust, so a long shallow occultation or a crowding effect in the plane is still possible. With WISE missing, nothing tests the dust case.

discriminating_test: Take an optical spectrum, or use archival H-alpha photometry (e.g. IPHAS/VPHAS+ r minus H-alpha): H-alpha emission or shell lines would confirm a Be star with disk variability. A non-emission star with a flat baseline would point to a disk occultation.

evidence.feature: Coherent fade in G, BP, RP and in both fields of view, confirmed and followed through recovery by ZTF g at 2 arcsec
ruwe 0.78, low ipd_frac_multi_peak, normal BP/RP excess factor

explanation: A luminous, reddened hot star (M_G around -2, in the Galactic plane, probably late B/A from its BP-RP versus G-Ks) went through one long, irregular fade: about 10% in Gaia from t~480 to the last visit, down to about 15% in ZTF g near t~1290, then recovering by t~2300 and still slowly brightening afterwards. G, BP, RP and both fields of view all show it, and ZTF confirms it, so it is not instrumental. The BP/RP depth ratio of 1.3 is neither grey nor ISM-like dust, but fits a temperature or disk change in a hot star, or an occulting disk made of fairly large grains. Leading cause: disk variability of a Be/shell star. Second: a long occultation by a circumsecondary disk. The star also varies by about 1% over hours.

discriminating_test: Fold ZTF g/r light curves (2018 on) in a period search to see whether short dips of 15-20% recur at a fixed period, which would confirm an eclipsing binary. Also check the scan angles of the fov1 dip transits for a neighbour at the window edge.

evidence.feature: Two deep single-epoch G dips (14.5%, 18%) with normal visits in between; the 319 d 'episode' is an artefact of merging them
RP dips 13% and 15.5% at the same epochs, BP roughly consistent: grey-ish dimming in all bands
fov1 dip of 4.8% at t=133.34 recovered by the fov2 transit 106.5 min later: short event, consistent with eclipse egress

explanation: The 319-day 'episode' is not a slow fade. It is two isolated single-transit dips (t=318.0: G -14.5%; t=637.4: G -18%) with normal visits in between (mean about 0.997), plus a weaker fov1 dip at t=133.3 that is gone 106.5 min later. That rules out a cosmic ray or one-band defect. Short, deep, grey dips caught sparsely by Gaia, from a star that is otherwise quiet (ruwe 1.0, normal BP/RP excess), look most like eclipses in a binary. The remaining weight goes to a crowded-field window or processing artefact and to a dipper.

discriminating_test: Get the ZTF r/i PSF light curve (2018 on), or the VVV/NEOWISE light curve, for this position. Continued irregular variation of 0.1-0.3 mag on timescales of hundreds of days, larger in the bluer band, confirms a red long-period variable. A flat light curve in PSF photometry that resolves the neighbour would point to Gaia blending.

It shows whether 2-3% fades keep recurring as wandering variability with a spot-like colour (BP deeper than RP), whether the dip tracks scan angle (blend), or whether it stays one isolated occultation.

Additional ~1-2% low excursions outside the episode (t~84, t~832) and slow 0.5% wandering of baseline

discriminating_test: Run a period search on the ZTF g/r PSF photometry (2-arcsec resolution, nightly cadence) for a 0.25-0.37 d orbital period with two near-equal minima and grey g-r amplitude. BP and RP drop in step with G with similar fractional amplitude (grey); G amplitude slightly larger, consistent with constant extra light diluting the larger BP/RP windows

Which field of view is low changes from pair to pair, and the same field of view flips within 6 h (the 677-678 d group), so a fixed field-of-view offset or a scan-angle blend does not explain it. The flux values fall in a continuous, arcsine-like distribution, not two discrete levels, and BP and RP change together with G with roughly equal amplitude (grey). This points to a contact binary (EW) with a photometric period near 0.15 d (orbital about 0.3 d). The 'dimming episode' and the 342 d 'repeat' come from averaging this undersampled variability into visits: high points inside the dip are as bright as those outside it.

discriminating_test: Check archival ground-based photometry overlapping Gaia days 577-1012 (e.g. Pan-STARRS or Catalina), or Gaia per-CCD G fluxes, to see whether the star really faded by ~3.7%. A real fade there would bring astrophysical classes back. No fade, with neighbours unaffected, points to an artefact or injection confined to the G pipeline.

A source-specific G calibration or processing artefact is possible but unusual. An unphysical injection into G is the most likely reading.

discriminating_test: Look for an ~8% fade in red-optical photometry from another survey taken during Gaia's interval, such as ATLAS o or Pan-STARRS. Also compare this star's per-CCD G epochs with nearby stars of similar magnitude and colour. A real fade, or a fade that field stars share, would move probability away from the G-only artefact or unphysical-injection reading.

evidence.feature: RP depth -0.0195 +/- 0.008 against G depth 0.053 +/- 0.004; a red star's G flux is mostly RP
BP late-epoch mean no fainter than early; BP depth 0.037 +/- 0.053 cannot supply the G deficit
Smooth monotonic G trend in both fields of view (abbe 0.06), no recurrence, no scan-angle-like scatter
ruwe 0.983, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0, BP/RP excess factor normal for colour

RP gets slightly brighter (depth -0.020 +/- 0.008), and BP is flat to brighter (early mean ~0.99, late ~1.03). For a red star (bp_rp 1.86), most of the G flux falls in RP, so a real 5% G fade needs either RP to dim about as much or BP to dim by over 25%. Neither happens. That rules out occultation, dust, spots and changes in the star's temperature. Astrometry is clean (ruwe 0.98, no multi-peak, normal excess factor) and there is no IR excess. What remains is a G-only artefact or an injection that no physical process would make. Between those, I lean to the injection, because star-specific monotonic G drifts are rare.

BP/RP depth ratio 1.36+-0.13 (z_grey 2.66, z_dust -2.57), matching temperature or spot reddening
W1/W2 fade ~8% from t~29 to t~578, a fraction of the G fade (more than dust-in-front predicts, less than grey)

W1-W2 = -0.1 and Ks-W1 = 0.3: no clear warm-disk excess
Gaia, ZTF PSF photometry and NEOWISE agree; ruwe 1.01, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0; the change is smooth, not scan-angle scatter

explanation: The 'dip' is a smooth (abbe 0.08) ~18% fade from a bright state over ~500 d with partial recovery. The star does this repeatedly: ZTF g, r and i show another ~10-17% high state near t~2400-2750 and lows before and after, and W1/W2 follow at roughly a third to a half of the optical amplitude. BP/RP ratio 1.36+-0.13 and the ZTF g/r amplitude ratio (~1.4) fit cooler spots or a temperature change, not grey or ISM-like dust. The visit-to-visit noise (2.3%, much larger than the 0.4% errors) and 1-3% changes within hours point to a rapidly rotating, magnetically active K/M dwarf (parallax SNR 4.5 rules out a distant giant). Most likely: a multi-year activity cycle with changing spot coverage.

discriminating_test: Phase-fold all Gaia and ZTF dip epochs (the recurrence period search) to find one strict period of a few days that aligns the deep primaries and puts the shallower, redder dips near phase 0.5.

Field-of-view pairs 106.5 min apart show ingress (0.85 to 0.30) and egress (0.30 to 0.84); ZTF r on day 1756 deepens gradually over about 1 h

Shallow dips at 773.7 (G 0.84, RP 0.71) and 778.04, and a mild ~7% sag in the ZTF g high-cadence night near 1418, consistent with secondary eclipses of a redder companion

Primary dips roughly grey to slightly bluer (575.5: BP 0.24, RP 0.29; 880.8: BP 0.32, RP 0.34), so not a planet-sized occulter

explanation: The 305-day 'episode' is just the slow-change search averaging a few short, deep dips. These are Algol-type eclipses. The flux stays flat near 1 apart from brief drops to 0.11-0.30 in Gaia G, BP and RP and in ZTF g and r, roughly 16 events spread over 2700 days. Field-of-view pairs catch ingress (575.44 at 0.85, then 575.51 at 0.30) and egress (880.78 at 0.30, then 880.85 at 0.84). ZTF r on day 1756 deepens from 0.47 to 0.17 within about an hour. Each dip lasts hours, under a day. About 5-10% of epochs fall in a dip, which suggests a period of a few days. Shallower dips that are deeper in RP (773.7) look like secondary eclipses of a cooler companion. Depths over 80% mean the eclipsed star supplies most of the light.

discriminating_test: Take an optical spectrum, or cross-match with quasar catalogues (Milliquas / Gaia DR3 QSO candidates / SDSS), to look for broad emission lines and a redshift. Alternatively, fit the ZTF light curve with a damped-random-walk model.

evidence.feature: W1-W2 = 1.1 and W2-W3 = 2.4, AGN wedge colours with detections in W3/W4
G-W1 = 4.5 with blue BP-RP 0.58: huge mid-IR excess for an optically blue source
parallax_snr -0.81, distance poorly constrained, ruwe 0.99, ipd_frac_multi_peak 0
Smooth, aperiodic G variation of about 40% over years (Abbe 0.146); start of light curve fainter than the detected fade
Pairs of FoV 1 and 2 transits agree to within errors throughout
NEOWISE W1/W2 brighter during the optical fade, peaking roughly 200-500 d after the optical peak (dust echo lag)
Strong IR excess at galactic latitude 10-15 deg could also be a disk-bearing young star
phot_bp_rp_excess_factor 1.28, mildly elevated (host galaxy or faint-source noise)

explanation: Most likely a quasar/AGN showing ordinary stochastic variability. The WISE colours (W1-W2 = 1.1, W2-W3 = 2.4) sit in the AGN locus, and G-W1 = 4.5 is far too red for a star with BP-RP 0.58. The parallax is consistent with zero and RUWE is about 1. G changes smoothly by about 40% over 930 d (low at the start, peak near 500 d, then a fade; Abbe 0.15), which looks like a damped random walk, not a discrete occultation. The 24.3 d 'repeat' is an artefact of sparse sampling. W1/W2 run higher during the optical fade, peaking around 700-1050 d after the optical peak near 500 d. That fits a dust-torus reverberation lag. The BP/RP depths are too noisy to constrain colour.
